questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC was established by Decree No. 22 of ____
questions.explanation: The NDIC was created by Decree No. 22 of 15 June 1988, following the earlier recommendation for a depositors' protection fund. It is easy to pick 1989 (option C), but that is the year the corporation actually began operations. 2006 and 2023 are the years of later Acts that repealed and replaced the original law, not the year the NDIC was set up.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC Act 2006 was repealed and replaced by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation Act of ____
questions.explanation: The NDIC Act No. 33 of 2023 repealed the 2006 Act and is now the main law governing the NDIC. Option D is the Act that was replaced, not the replacement, and 1988 is the year of the original decree that created the NDIC. 2016 is not the year of any NDIC Act.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In 1983, a committee set up by the ____ recommended a depositors' protection fund, which led to the creation of the NDIC.
questions.explanation: In 1983 the Board of the Central Bank of Nigeria set up a committee to review the banking system, and it recommended a Depositors' Protection Fund, the idea that became the NDIC. Option A and option D are tempting because the Federal Government and the Ministry of Finance were involved in later legislation and ownership, but the committee itself came from the CBN. The Stock Exchange in option C had no role in it.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC began operations in ____
questions.explanation: Although the NDIC was legally created in 1988, it actually opened for business in March 1989. Option A, 1988, is the year of the decree that established it, which is why many students mix the two up. 1986 is the year the Structural Adjustment Programme started, and 1990 has no special link to the NDIC's start.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The US Banking Act of 1933 (often called the Glass-Steagall Act) brought about the establishment of the ____
questions.explanation: The Banking Act of 1933, signed in June 1933 after the wave of US bank failures during the Great Depression, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which began insuring deposits on 1 January 1934. Option A is Australia's scheme, set up in 2008 during the global financial crisis. Option D began operating in 1962 and Brazil's fund (option B) was set up in 1995, both under their own countries' laws.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The current law governing the NDIC is the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, No. ____ of 2023.
questions.explanation: The NDIC Act No. 33 of 2023 repealed the NDIC Act No. 16 of 2006 and is now the law governing the Corporation. Option B, 22, is the number of the original 1988 Decree that first established the NDIC, which is why it is a tempting choice. Options A and C are not the numbers of any NDIC law.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC Act No. 33 of 2023 repealed and replaced which earlier law?

options.b: Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Decree 1994
options.c: Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020

questions.explanation: The NDIC's legal history runs from Decree No. 22 of 1988, to the NDIC Act No. 16 of 2006, to the NDIC Act No. 33 of 2023, which repealed the 2006 Act. Option C (BOFIA 2020) is the law under which banks are licensed, and option A governs the Central Bank; both remain in force. Option B was a 1990s law for recovering debts owed to failed banks, not the NDIC's establishing law.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The financial panics that led to many bank collapses between 1893 and 1907 occurred in:
questions.explanation: The United States suffered repeated banking panics in this period, notably the Panic of 1893 and the Panic of 1907, with runs that closed many banks. These episodes, followed by the collapses of the early 1930s, built the case for nationwide deposit insurance, which came with the FDIC in 1933. Options A, B and D did not experience this series of panics.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) commenced operations in the year:
questions.explanation: The NDIC actually started operating in 1989, a few months after the law creating it was made. Option B (1988) is the tempting trap: that is the year NDIC was established by Decree No. 22, not the year it began operations. 1987 and 1990 do not match either milestone.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC was established in 1988 by:

options.c: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020

questions.explanation: The NDIC was created by Decree No. 22 of 15 June 1988, during military rule, and started operations in 1989. Option B is a much later law that repealed and replaced the NDIC Act 2006, so it could not have created the NDIC in 1988. Option A established the Central Bank of Nigeria, and option C is the current law for licensing and regulating banks.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In 1983, a committee set up by the Board of the Central Bank of Nigeria to examine the operations of the Nigerian banking system recommended the establishment of a ____.
questions.explanation: The 1983 CBN committee recommended a Depositors Protection Fund, and that recommendation eventually led to the creation of the NDIC. Option D and option C name later rescue arrangements: a Financial Stability Fund for bank resolution costs and AMCON (2010) for buying bad loans. Option A is not what the committee proposed.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The committee whose report first recommended a deposit protection arrangement for Nigeria was set up by the Board of the Central Bank of Nigeria in which year?
questions.explanation: The committee was set up in 1983 and recommended a Depositors Protection Fund. Option A is 1986, when the Structural Adjustment Programme began, and option B is 1988, when the NDIC itself was established by decree. Option D predates the committee.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The CBN committee that recommended a Depositors Protection Fund was set up in 1983, and the NDIC opened its doors for business in 1989. How many years passed between the two events?
questions.explanation: From 1983 to 1989 is 1989 - 1983 = 6 years. Option A (5 years) measures from 1983 to 1988, the year the decree was promulgated, not the year operations began. Options B and D are simple arithmetic slips.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The decree establishing the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation was dated ____.
questions.explanation: Decree No. 22 creating the NDIC is dated 15 June 1988; the Corporation then started operations in 1989. Option A confuses the decree with the start of operations, and option B has the right day but the year SAP began. Option C borrows the day and month of the 2023 Act.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The 1988 decree that created the NDIC was repealed and re-enacted as ____.
questions.explanation: The 1988 Decree was repealed and re-enacted as the NDIC Act No. 16 of 2006. Option D is the 2023 Act, which in turn repealed the 2006 Act rather than the decree directly. Options A and B are banking and central bank laws, not the NDIC's own statute.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which option lists the NDIC's governing laws in correct chronological order?

options.a: Decree No. 22 of 1988, Act No. 16 of 2006, Act No. 33 of 2023
options.b: Act No. 16 of 2006, Decree No. 22 of 1988, Act No. 33 of 2023
options.c: Act No. 22 of 1983, Act No. 16 of 2006, Act No. 33 of 2023
options.d: Decree No. 22 of 1988, Act No. 33 of 2006, Act No. 16 of 2023

questions.explanation: The NDIC began under Decree No. 22 of 1988, which was replaced by the NDIC Act No. 16 of 2006, which was in turn repealed by the NDIC Act No. 33 of 2023. Option D swaps the numbers of the 2006 and 2023 Acts, and option B puts the 2006 Act first. Option C wrongly dates the first law to 1983, the year of the CBN committee.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which of the following was introduced by the NDIC Act 2023 and was absent from the NDIC Act 2006?

options.a: A power for the NDIC to act as liquidator
options.b: An explicit statement of the NDIC's public policy objectives
options.c: A limit on the amount paid per depositor
options.d: A requirement that banks insure their deposits

questions.explanation: Section 2 of the NDIC Act 2023 states the public policy objectives of the deposit insurance system, which the 2006 Act did not do. Options A, C and D describe compulsory membership, the liquidator role and a coverage limit, all of which already existed under the earlier law.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, when can the NDIC begin paying insured deposits of a deposit-taking institution?

options.a: Only after a court has wound up the institution
options.b: On revocation of its licence or on its actual suspension of payments
options.c: Only after the institution's assets have been sold
options.d: Only when shareholders approve the payment

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act allows insured deposits to be paid when the licence is revoked or when the institution actually suspends payments (with CBN concurrence). Option A and option C would make depositors wait for long court or asset-sale processes, which is exactly what fast payout tries to avoid. Option D is wrong because shareholders have no say in deposit insurance payouts.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The setting up of the NDIC in 1988 is best described as part of ____.

options.a: the economic liberalisation efforts of the then military government
options.b: the IADI's programme for African deposit insurers
options.c: the recapitalisation of banks after the 2009 crisis
options.d: the banking consolidation exercise of the civilian government

questions.explanation: The NDIC was created as part of the economic liberalisation efforts of the military government of the time, to restore public confidence in banks. Option D refers to the 2004-2005 consolidation, option B to a body that was only formed in 2002, and option C to events two decades later.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which economic programme, introduced in Nigeria in 1986, liberalised bank licensing and led to a rapid rise in the number of banks before the NDIC was created?
questions.explanation: The Structural Adjustment Programme of 1986 liberalised bank licensing, so the number of banks grew rapidly, which strengthened the case for explicit deposit insurance. Option A was a 1970s policy on Nigerian ownership, option D came in 2004-2005 and reduced the number of banks, and option C is a later strategy plan.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Following the liberalisation of bank licensing under SAP, the number of banks in Nigeria rose to about ____ by the early 1990s.
questions.explanation: Bank numbers grew rapidly under SAP to about 120 by the early 1990s. Option A is the number of banks left after the 2005 consolidation, and option B is the number of banks before that consolidation. Option D is far below the early-1990s peak.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The proliferation of banks during the SAP era is linked to all of the following problems EXCEPT ____.

options.b: fraudulent activities in the foreign exchange market
options.d: excess capital and very strong corporate governance

questions.explanation: Rapid growth in bank numbers heightened competition and led to sharp practices, window dressing, inadequate manpower and fraud in the foreign exchange market. Options A, B and C are all named consequences. Excess capital and strong governance are signs of a healthy system, not problems caused by proliferation.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The main impetus for establishing a deposit insurance scheme in Nigeria was the need to ____.

options.a: raise revenue for the Federal Government from bank premiums
options.b: replace the CBN as the regulator of all deposit-taking banks
options.c: guarantee shareholders' investment in banks against all losses
options.d: protect small and medium depositors and assist banks so as to engender public confidence

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance was set up to protect depositors, especially small and medium ones, and to give technical and financial assistance to banks so that the public trusts the banking system. Option C is wrong because shareholders are not protected, and option A is wrong because premiums go into an insurance fund, not government revenue. Option B is wrong because the NDIC works alongside the CBN rather than replacing it.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: When the NDIC began operations in 1989, banks paid a flat annual premium of 15/16 of 1 percent of total deposit liabilities. What premium would a bank with total deposit liabilities of N8 billion have paid?
questions.explanation: 15/16 of 1 percent is 0.9375 percent, and 0.9375% x N8 billion = N75 million. Option C applies 9.375 percent and option B applies 0.09375 percent, both decimal-point slips. Option A wrongly uses 1.5 percent.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In 2008 the NDIC moved from a flat-rate premium to a system in which each bank pays a base rate plus an add-on based on its riskiness. This system is known as ____.
questions.explanation: Under the Differential Premium Assessment System, the premium rate equals a base rate plus a risk-related add-on, so riskier banks pay more. Option C describes the old flat-rate approach it replaced, and option D is a supervision method, not a premium system. Option A is about insuring mobile money subscribers' pooled deposits.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Nigeria's deposit insurance arrangement is classified as an explicit guarantee mainly because ____.

options.a: the coverage level and limits are stipulated by statute
options.b: there is no fund set aside for paying depositors
options.c: depositors merely assume the government will rescue banks
options.d: the decision to pay is negotiated only after a bank fails

questions.explanation: An explicit guarantee rests on government declaration, with the level and limits of cover spelled out in legislation, as in the NDIC Act. Options B, C and D describe an implicit guarantee, which rests on public assumption with no rules, no fund and decisions made only when a failure occurs.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the stated policy objectives of Nigeria's deposit insurance scheme?

options.a: To facilitate the transition from blanket coverage to limited coverage
options.b: To finance government budget deficits with premiums
options.c: To replace bank supervision with deposit insurance
options.d: To provide blanket cover for all deposits without limit

questions.explanation: One objective of the NDIC scheme is to help the system move away from blanket guarantees towards limited, rule-based cover. Option D is the opposite of that objective, option C is wrong because supervision remains a separate safety-net function, and option B misuses premiums, which go into the insurance fund.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Nigeria, through the NDIC, is one of the founding members of which international body launched in Basel in 2002?
questions.explanation: The NDIC is a founding member of the International Association of Deposit Insurers, launched in Basel in May 2002. Option B is the body that monitors the global financial system, option D sets bank supervision standards, and option A is a regional European forum, none of which was founded in 2002 with the NDIC as a founder.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The establishment of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in the United States was a response mainly to ____.

options.a: the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s
options.b: the 1933 banking crisis and the Great Depression
options.d: the oil price shock of the 1970s

questions.explanation: The FDIC was created in 1933 after waves of bank failures during the Great Depression. Option C is the crisis behind Australia's Financial Claims Scheme, and options A and D happened decades after the FDIC was already in place.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The US Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created by the Banking Act of 1933. On what date did its deposit insurance cover actually begin?
questions.explanation: The Banking Act creating the FDIC was signed on 16 June 1933, but insurance of deposits began on 1 January 1934. Option D is the date the law was signed, not the start of cover. Options B and C do not match either event.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: FDIC cover began in January 1934 at US$2,500 per depositor, and the standard cover as at 2026 is US$250,000 per depositor. How many times larger is the 2026 limit?
questions.explanation: US$250,000 / US$2,500 = 100, so the limit is 100 times its 1934 level. Option D and option B are slips of one decimal place either way, and option A confuses the 25 in 250,000 with the answer.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Before the FDIC was created, which American state had already introduced an insurance scheme for bank obligations in 1829?
questions.explanation: New York introduced an insurance scheme for bank obligations in 1829, more than a century before the national FDIC. Options A, B and D are other states that did not start the 1829 scheme.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which US law expanded the role of the FDIC after the 2008 crisis, extending its resolution role to bank holding companies and non-bank systemically important financial institutions?
questions.explanation: The Dodd-Frank Act widened the FDIC's role, so its remit covers depository institutions, bank holding companies and non-bank SIFIs. Option B deals with corporate accounting and audit, option C (1999) allowed banks and insurers to combine, and option D created the US central bank in 1913.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In the United States, the FDIC collaborates mainly with which two federal agencies in its supervisory work?

options.a: The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund
options.b: The Securities and Exchange Commission and the Treasury
options.c: The Internal Revenue Service and the Federal Reserve
options.d: The Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

questions.explanation: The FDIC works alongside the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which also supervise US banks. Option B names a capital-market regulator and the finance ministry, option C pairs the tax authority with the Fed, and option A names international bodies rather than US agencies.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In which year did the European Union issue a directive requiring member states to establish deposit guarantee schemes?
questions.explanation: Directive 94/19/EC of 1994 required every EU member state to have a deposit guarantee scheme, so all EU states have had explicit schemes since then. Option B is the year of the later directive that revised the rules, not the first one. Options C and D do not match either directive.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under EU rules, a retail depositor has EUR 130,000 in one bank in an EU member state when it fails. How much of this is covered by the national deposit guarantee scheme?
questions.explanation: EU law protects deposits up to EUR 100,000 per depositor per bank, so EUR 100,000 is covered and EUR 30,000 is not. Option A ignores the limit and option D is the uncovered part, not the covered part. Option C confuses the euro limit with the old UK limit in pounds.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under the first EU deposit guarantee directive of 1994, depositors were usually paid within 3 months. Under Directive 2014/49/EU, the maximum payout period was phased down to how long from 2024?
questions.explanation: Directive 2014/49/EU phased the payout period down to 7 working days from 2024, matching the international benchmark for fast reimbursement. Option D was an interim target set during the 2008 crisis, and option B is roughly the old 3-month period. Option A is not the EU standard.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In 2012 the European Council agreed a roadmap for completing Economic and Monetary Union through a Banking Union with three pillars. Which option correctly matches the pillars?

options.a: SSM for deposit insurance, SRM for supervision, EDIS for resolution
options.b: SSM for supervision, SRM for resolution, EDIS for deposit insurance
options.c: SSM for resolution, SRM for supervision, EDIS for deposit insurance
options.d: SSM for supervision, SRM for deposit insurance, EDIS for resolution

questions.explanation: The first pillar is the Single Supervisory Mechanism (supervision), the second is the Single Resolution Mechanism (resolution) and the third is the European Deposit Insurance Scheme (deposit insurance). Options A, C and D each swap at least two of these functions; the names themselves tell you which job each pillar does.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Of the three pillars of the European Banking Union, which one had not yet been put in place when the first two were completed?
questions.explanation: The SSM and SRM were put in place, while the third pillar, a common European Deposit Insurance Scheme, remained a proposal. Options B and D are the two pillars already in operation. Option A is an institution that leads supervision, not a pillar awaiting adoption.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under the proposed European Deposit Insurance Scheme (EDIS), what would happen to the existing national deposit guarantee schemes?

options.b: They would be merged into the ECB
options.c: They would stop covering retail deposits
options.d: They would remain in place and form part of EDIS

questions.explanation: Under EDIS, national deposit guarantee schemes would remain and be part of the scheme, playing an important role in the early stages while a European Deposit Insurance Fund insures them. Options A, B and C wrongly suggest that national schemes would disappear or stop protecting depositors.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In the proposed European Deposit Insurance Scheme, what happens to depositor coverage during the 'co-insurance period'?

options.a: Coverage is shared between the European fund and the national scheme
options.b: Coverage is provided only by the ECB
options.c: Coverage is provided only by national schemes
options.d: Coverage is suspended until the fund is full

questions.explanation: In the co-insurance period, the cost of covering deposits is shared between the European Deposit Insurance Fund and the national deposit guarantee schemes. Option C is closer to the earlier re-insurance stage, when national schemes do most of the paying out. Options B and D do not describe EDIS.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Within the European Banking Union, which institution is the main prudential supervisory authority for banks in the euro area?
questions.explanation: Supervision in the Banking Union is built around the European Central Bank as the main prudential supervisor of euro-area banks. Option B is the main authority for bank resolution, while options A and D are political bodies involved in approving resolution decisions.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Within the European Banking Union, which body is the main authority that decides on bank resolution?
questions.explanation: The Single Resolution Board is the main authority for resolution decisions in the Banking Union. Option D determines whether a bank is failing and supervises banks, but does not take the main resolution decision. Options B and C are EU bodies with other jobs, such as development lending and rule-setting.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In the Banking Union's resolution procedure, decision-making typically involves all of the following EXCEPT ____.

options.b: the ECB, which determines bank failure

questions.explanation: Resolution decisions in the Banking Union involve the ECB (determining failure), the Single Resolution Board, the Commission and the Council, with national authorities implementing them. Options A, B and C are all part of that chain. The IMF is an international lender and adviser, not an EU resolution decision-maker.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Among EU stylised facts on deposit guarantee schemes (DGSs), which statement about administration is correct?

options.a: DGSs must always be administered by banking associations
options.b: DGSs can be administered privately, publicly or by a combination of both
options.c: DGSs must always be administered by the central bank
options.d: DGSs must always be administered by the European Commission

questions.explanation: EU deposit guarantee schemes may be run privately (for example by banking associations), publicly, or jointly. Options A, C and D each wrongly insist on a single type of administrator, which does not match the variety across member states.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: According to EU stylised facts on deposit guarantee schemes, how can such schemes be financed?

options.a: Ex ante or ex post, from public, private or both sources
options.b: Only ex post, from government budgets
options.c: Only from loans by the European Central Bank
options.d: Only ex ante, from depositors' fees

questions.explanation: EU schemes may be funded ex ante (building a fund in advance) or ex post (collecting after a failure), using public money, private money or both. Options B, C and D each restrict funding to a single method or a single type of funder, which is not the case.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which of the following is an EU stylised fact about deposit guarantee schemes?

options.a: Some countries, including Germany, have multiple schemes providing deposit protection
options.b: No EU scheme plays any role beyond paying out depositors
options.c: Implicit schemes are the norm in EU member states
options.d: Membership of every EU scheme is voluntary for banks

questions.explanation: Some countries, notably Germany, run more than one scheme to protect deposits. Option D is wrong because membership can be voluntary or compulsory, and option B is wrong because many schemes also help with resolution and restructuring. Option C is wrong because all EU states have had explicit schemes since 1994.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In the European Union, what is the most common way of organising a deposit guarantee scheme?

options.a: As a department of the national treasury
options.c: As a branch of the European Central Bank
options.d: As a unit inside each commercial bank

questions.explanation: Legally separate schemes are the most common form of organisation in the EU, although a scheme can also sit within a ministry, the central bank or another supervisor. Option A is a possible but less common arrangement. Options C and D are not how EU schemes are organised.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The Deposit Insurance Corporation of India (DICI) was established in which year?
questions.explanation: India's Deposit Insurance Corporation began operating on 1 January 1962. Option B is the year the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India was set up, and option A is the year the two merged. Option C is the year of Taiwan's deposit insurance law.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In 1978, the Deposit Insurance Corporation of India merged with the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India to form ____.

options.d: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC)

questions.explanation: The merger in 1978 created the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, which is wholly owned by the Reserve Bank of India. Options A, B and C are invented names that mix in terms from other countries' schemes.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Australia's deposit insurance arrangement, the Financial Claims Scheme (FCS), was set up in 2008 in response to ____.

options.c: the collapse of the Australian mining boom

questions.explanation: Australia created the Financial Claims Scheme in 2008 during the global financial crisis to protect depositors in authorised deposit-taking institutions. Option D was the crisis behind the US FDIC, and option B came about a decade earlier. Option C is not linked to the scheme's creation.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under Australia's Financial Claims Scheme, the institutions whose deposits are protected are called ____.
questions.explanation: Australia protects deposits held in authorised deposit-taking institutions, or ADIs. Option D and option A are Nigerian names for types of insured institutions, while option C refers to banks singled out for extra supervision, not the scheme's members.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: As at 2026, Australia's Financial Claims Scheme covers deposits up to what amount per account holder per authorised deposit-taking institution?
questions.explanation: Australia's Financial Claims Scheme covers up to A$250,000 per account holder per ADI and is administered by APRA once activated by the government. Options B, C and D do not match the scheme's limit; A$85,000 echoes an old UK limit.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Brazil's deposit insurance scheme, set up in 1995, is financed through ____.

options.a: loans from the International Monetary Fund
options.c: mandatory contributions from participating financial institutions
options.d: annual grants from the Brazilian federal budget

questions.explanation: Brazil's law does not support using government funds to rescue failing banks, so its scheme is funded by mandatory contributions from member institutions. Option D is the government money the law avoids, option A does not fund the scheme, and option B would not provide reliable funding.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: What is the name of the United Kingdom's deposit insurance scheme, set up in 2001?
questions.explanation: The UK's scheme is the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, set up in 2001. Option C is Australia's scheme, option D is not the name of the UK's compensation scheme, and option B is the UK bank regulator rather than the compensation scheme.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In January 2026, a UK resident had GBP150,000 in a single bank that failed. Under the FSCS deposit limit that took effect on 1 December 2025, how much of her deposit is protected?
questions.explanation: From 1 December 2025 the FSCS protects deposits up to GBP120,000 per depositor per bank, so GBP120,000 is covered and GBP30,000 is not. Option A was the limit before December 2025, option C ignores the limit, and option D confuses the UK limit with the EU's euro limit.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: As at 2026, the Kenya Deposit Insurance Corporation (KDIC) covers deposits up to what amount per depositor per member institution?
questions.explanation: As at 2026, KDIC covers up to KSh 500,000 per depositor per member institution. Options A, B and D do not match Kenya's limit; KSh 5,000,000 echoes the naira figure for Nigerian deposit money banks.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: China moved from implicit protection to an explicit deposit insurance scheme when it launched one on 1 May 2015. What was its coverage level?
questions.explanation: China launched its scheme on 1 May 2015 with cover of 500,000 yuan, which protected over 99 percent of depositors in full. Options A and D are out by a factor of ten either way, and option C confuses the yuan figure with the EU's euro limit.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: When China launched explicit deposit insurance in May 2015 with cover of 500,000 yuan, about what share of depositors were fully covered?
questions.explanation: The 500,000 yuan limit fully covered over 99 percent of Chinese depositors (about 99.6 percent), which matches the international aim of protecting the large majority of depositors. Options A, B and D greatly understate the share covered.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which of the following deposit insurers covers not only commercial banks but also insurance companies and securities companies?
questions.explanation: Korea's KDIC, set up in 1996, covers commercial banks, insurance companies, savings banks, securities companies and merchant banks. Option A covers deposit-taking institutions such as banks, microfinance banks and mortgage banks, not insurers or securities firms. Options B and C also focus on deposit-taking institutions.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Each of the following is correctly paired with its country's deposit insurer EXCEPT ____.
questions.explanation: The FSCS is the United Kingdom's scheme; Australia's is the Financial Claims Scheme. Options A, B and C are correct pairs: the NDIC in Nigeria, the FDIC in the US and the DICGC in India.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: According to the World Bank's deposit insurance database, how many of 189 countries had explicit deposit insurance by year-end 2013?
questions.explanation: By the end of 2013, 112 of 189 countries had explicit deposit insurance. Option A is the percentage (about 59 percent), not the number of countries. Option B is a different figure altogether (it matches the number of IADI Members reported in 2016), and option D would mean every country had a scheme.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: According to the World Bank's 2016 Bank Regulation and Supervision Survey, what proportion of high-income countries have some form of explicit deposit insurance?
questions.explanation: The 2016 survey found that over 80 percent of high-income countries have explicit deposit insurance, which shows that explicit schemes are standard in rich economies. Options A, C and D all understate how common explicit schemes are in that group.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: A deposit insurance scheme (DIS) is best defined as ____.

options.a: a financial guarantee to protect depositors in the event of bank failure
options.b: a fund that guarantees bank profits during recessions
options.c: a loan facility from the central bank to illiquid banks
options.d: an insurance policy that protects bank shareholders' capital

questions.explanation: A DIS is a financial guarantee that protects depositors when a bank fails and so gives the banking system a measure of safety. Option C describes the central bank's lender-of-last-resort role. Options B and D wrongly say the scheme protects owners or profits, when its focus is depositors.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Deposit insurance is designed particularly to protect small savers because they ____.

options.a: are required by law to keep all their savings in one bank
options.b: usually hold the largest share of a bank's total deposits
options.c: may not have adequate information on their banks' financial condition
options.d: are usually directors and shareholders of the banks

questions.explanation: Small savers often cannot judge the financial health of their banks because they lack adequate information, so they are least able to protect themselves. Option B is wrong because big depositors usually hold most of the value. Option A is not a legal rule, and option D describes insiders, whose deposits are often excluded from cover.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: What are the two broad options for implementing deposit protection in a country?

options.a: Ex ante and ex post funding

questions.explanation: Countries either have explicit deposit insurance, set out in law or contract, or rely on implicit protection, where there is no formal system. Option C lists mandate types within explicit schemes, option A lists funding methods, and option B lists ownership forms.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Under an implicit deposit insurance arrangement, ____.

options.a: there is no formal funding and no unambiguous government commitment to compensate depositors
options.b: banks pay risk-based premiums into a dedicated fund
options.c: a separate agency is set up by statute to reimburse depositors
options.d: depositors are covered up to a fixed limit set by law

questions.explanation: Implicit protection has no formal system: no formal funding and no clear government commitment to compensate depositors when a bank fails. Options B, C and D all describe features of an explicit scheme, which is set up by law with defined limits, funding and an agency.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: An explicit deposit insurance scheme is established by ____.

options.a: a decision taken only after a bank has failed
options.b: legislation or private contract that spells out its mandate, powers and governance
options.c: an informal promise made by bank managers to customers
options.d: public belief that government will rescue failing banks

questions.explanation: An explicit DIS is created by law or private contract that sets out its mandate, powers, governance, funding, coverage and reimbursement rules. Options A and D describe implicit protection, which rests on public belief and decisions made after failure. Option C has no legal force.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the novel deposit insurance practices implemented by the NDIC?

options.c: Unlimited blanket coverage of all deposits

questions.explanation: The NDIC has introduced risk-based supervision, continuous review of coverage, risk-based premiums, closed bank resolution and the bridge-bank model, which covers options A, B and D. Nigeria uses limited, explicit coverage rather than unlimited blanket cover.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Chinedu keeps savings in a microfinance bank in Lagos whose deposits are insured with the NDIC. Which element of a deposit insurance scheme does Chinedu represent?
questions.explanation: Chinedu is an insured depositor because he holds deposits in an institution covered by the NDIC. Option C is the microfinance bank itself, option B is the NDIC, and option D is a body such as the CBN.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: The NDIC in Nigeria, the FDIC in the United States and the FSCS in Britain are all examples of which element of a deposit insurance scheme?
questions.explanation: These are deposit insurance institutions: the bodies that give depositors cover when a bank fails. Option D refers to supervisors of the scheme, option C refers to the banks whose deposits are insured, and option A is the reinsurance-type backstop.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Among the basic elements of a deposit insurance scheme, the central bank is described as acting as a form of ____ because it guarantees the deposits of the deposit insurance institution.
questions.explanation: The central bank backs the deposit insurer, so it acts like a reinsurer standing behind the insurer. Option A means sharing a loss with the insured party, option C means bearing your own risk, and option B refers to unlimited cover of deposits, none of which fits this role.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: As a basic element of a deposit insurance scheme, what role can government play?

options.a: Acting only as a depositor in insured banks
options.b: Acting as an agency of the scheme or as an implicit or explicit guarantor
options.c: Acting only as a borrower from the insurance fund
options.d: Acting as the sole shareholder of every insured bank

questions.explanation: Government can be an agency of the deposit insurance scheme or stand behind it as an implicit or explicit guarantor. Options A, C and D describe narrow or incorrect roles that are not how government fits into a deposit insurance scheme.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In a deposit insurance scheme, the body that oversees the scheme, which may be a central bank, is called the ____.
questions.explanation: The supervisory institution oversees the deposit insurance scheme, and in many countries this is the central bank. Option A refers to the banks whose deposits are covered. Options C and D are not among the basic elements of a scheme.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: A guarantee promise to protect depositors can take which three forms?

options.c: Pay-box, loss minimiser and risk minimiser

questions.explanation: A guarantee promise for protecting deposits can be explicit, implicit or ambiguous. Option D mixes in coverage types, option B lists ownership structures, and option C lists mandate types of explicit schemes.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: A guarantee promise that is based on public assumption, with no rules on coverage, no funds set aside and decisions negotiated only when a bank fails, is called ____.
questions.explanation: An implicit guarantee rests only on the public's assumption that depositors will be protected, so there are no rules or funds and decisions are made at the time of failure. Option A is set out in law with clear limits, and option D is neither explicit nor implicit. Option B is a way of extending explicit cover to the customers behind a pooled account.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: A guarantee promise that is based on governmental declarations, with the level and limits of cover usually stipulated by legislation, is called ____.
questions.explanation: An explicit guarantee is formally declared by government and its level and limits are set in legislation, as with Nigeria's NDIC Act. Option B rests only on public assumption, and option D is neither explicit nor implicit. Option C covers deposits without the normal limits, usually only in a crisis.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which type of guarantee promise is neither explicit nor implicit, and is considered suitable mainly where the banking system is owned almost entirely by strong foreign financial institutions?
questions.explanation: An ambiguous guarantee is neither explicit nor implicit, and experts see it as workable mainly when strong foreign banks own nearly the whole banking system. Option A has statutory limits, and option C rests on public assumption of rescue. Option D is a crisis-time promise to protect all deposits.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: In the country of Zedland there is no deposit insurance law and no deposit insurance fund, but depositors widely believe the government will step in if a large bank fails. What type of guarantee promise does Zedland have?
questions.explanation: Zedland has an implicit guarantee because protection rests only on the public's belief in a rescue, with no law, fund or rules. Option D would need a statute setting coverage and limits. Option B is a guarantee that is neither explicit nor implicit, and here the public clearly assumes a rescue. Option A is a feature of explicit schemes.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: A country passes a law creating a deposit insurer, requiring all banks to pay premiums into a fund and stating that each depositor is covered up to a fixed amount. Which type of guarantee promise has it adopted?
questions.explanation: A law that sets up an insurer, a fund and a stated coverage limit is an explicit guarantee. Option B has no rules or funds, and option C is neither explicit nor implicit. Option A would protect deposits without any limit, but this law sets a fixed maximum.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which feature best distinguishes an explicit deposit guarantee from an implicit one?

options.a: Explicit cover protects shareholders; implicit cover protects depositors
options.b: Explicit cover applies only to foreign banks; implicit cover applies only to local banks
options.c: Explicit cover has limits and funding set in advance by law; implicit cover is decided only after failure
options.d: Explicit cover is always run privately; implicit cover is always run by government

questions.explanation: The key difference is certainty: explicit cover has its limits, funding and rules fixed in law before any failure, while implicit cover depends on decisions made after a bank fails. Option A is wrong because neither form is meant to protect shareholders. Options B and D invent ownership and bank-nationality rules that do not define either type.

questions.topic: Overview of Deposit Insurance in Nigeria and Globally
questions.question: Which type of deposit insurance arrangement is described as the preferred arrangement in global practice?
questions.explanation: Explicit deposit insurance is the preferred arrangement because clear rules, funding and limits give depositors certainty and reduce panic. Options B and D leave depositors unsure of what they will get, which can trigger runs. Option A gives depositors no protection at all.

questions.question: Which of the following countries operates both a statutory (public) deposit protection scheme and private, bank-association-run protection funds?
questions.explanation: Germany is the classic example of a country with multiple deposit protection schemes: a statutory scheme exists alongside private protection funds run by banking associations. Option D is wrong because Nigeria has a single, publicly owned insurer, the NDIC. Switzerland's scheme is a self-regulatory arrangement run by the banks themselves, and Slovakia relies on a single national fund, so neither combines public and private schemes the way Germany does.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised mandate type of a deposit insurer?
questions.explanation: Deposit insurers are grouped by mandate as pay box, pay box plus, loss minimiser and risk minimiser, so a "cost maximiser" does not exist; no deposit insurer aims to make failures more expensive. A pay box only collects premiums and reimburses depositors, a loss minimiser actively picks least-cost resolution strategies, and a risk minimiser like the NDIC adds supervision and early intervention powers. Those three are all real mandate types.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an ownership structure of deposit insurance schemes?
questions.explanation: Deposit insurance schemes are owned or administered publicly by government, privately by banks or banking associations, or jointly by both. "Sole" is not one of these categories. The NDIC, for example, is publicly owned by the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance, while some countries use private or joint arrangements, so options A, B and D are all real structures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a requirement of a well-designed deposit insurance scheme?

options.c: Exemption of weak banks from membership

questions.explanation: Incentive compatibility means the scheme is designed so that banks and depositors are not encouraged to take more risk just because deposits are insured, which is how moral hazard is kept in check. Option D is wrong because good practice is limited coverage, leaving large depositors with a reason to monitor their banks. Letting weak banks opt out would undermine the fund, and deregulation of power is not a design requirement at all.

questions.question: A deposit insurer that, in addition to paying depositors and resolving failed banks, has powers to supervise insured institutions and intervene early to protect insured deposits is called a ____
questions.explanation: A risk minimiser has the widest mandate: risk assessment, supervision, early intervention and a full set of resolution powers, and the NDIC is an example. Option D is the closest distractor, since a loss minimiser chooses least-cost resolution methods but usually has no supervisory powers. A pay box only reimburses depositors, and a pay box plus adds just some resolution functions.

questions.question: Which of the following types of deposit guarantee is operated by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation?
questions.explanation: An explicit scheme is one where the guarantee is written into law, with clear rules on coverage, funding, membership and payout, and that is exactly how the NDIC operates. Option A, an implicit guarantee, rests only on the public's belief that government will not let banks fail, with no formal commitment or fund behind it. Options C and D are not recognised types of deposit insurance.

questions.question: In deposit insurance, what does the abbreviation DIS commonly stand for?
questions.explanation: DIS stands for Deposit Insurance Scheme, the arrangement that protects depositors up to a set limit if their bank fails; it is also often expanded as Deposit Insurance System, which means the same thing. Option C confuses the abbreviation with the scope of cover, option D wrongly turns it into an investment product, and option B describes supervision of insurers rather than protection of depositors.

questions.question: A financial guarantee that protects depositors in the event of bank failure and also offers a measure of safety for the banking system is called a
questions.explanation: A deposit insurance scheme guarantees depositors that they will be repaid, up to a limit, if their bank fails, and in doing so it adds a layer of safety to the whole banking system. Option A is the central bank lending to banks with temporary liquidity problems, not a guarantee to depositors. Options C and D are about rules for banks and injecting capital into banks, not about protecting depositors' funds.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a deposit insurance scheme?

options.a: A facility through which the central bank lends to banks short of liquidity
options.b: A policy that insures a bank's loan book against borrower default
options.c: A guarantee that reimburses depositors, up to set limits, when an insured bank fails
options.d: A fund that compensates shareholders when a bank's share price falls

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance protects depositors: if an insured bank fails, depositors are paid back up to the coverage limit. Option A describes the lender of last resort role of a central bank. Option B is credit insurance for lenders, and option D is wrong because deposit insurance never protects shareholders' investment.

questions.question: A deposit insurance scheme is designed to save particularly which group of people?

options.a: Large corporate depositors with access to detailed bank data
options.b: Foreign investors who hold shares in local banks
options.c: Small savers who may lack adequate information on their banks' financial condition
options.d: Banks that lend to one another in the interbank market

questions.explanation: Small savers usually cannot study a bank's accounts or judge its soundness, so deposit insurance is built mainly to protect them. Option A describes sophisticated depositors who can monitor banks themselves and are the group usually left partly exposed. Options B and D are investors and banks, not the small depositors the scheme targets.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of a deposit insurance scheme?

options.a: It protects depositors against full or partial loss of their savings
options.b: It reduces bank runs and contributes to financial stability
options.c: It creates a formal mechanism for addressing bank failure
options.d: It guarantees that no insured bank will ever fail

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance does not stop banks from failing; it makes sure that when a bank does fail, insured depositors are protected and the failure is handled in an orderly way. Options A, B and C are all genuine benefits of a deposit insurance scheme.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of a deposit insurance scheme?

options.a: It removes the need for banks to be supervised
options.b: It guarantees every deposit in full, whatever its size
options.c: It ensures shareholders of failed banks are repaid in full
options.d: It can limit the government's fiscal and political exposure when banks fail

questions.explanation: With a formal, pre-funded scheme, the cost of protecting depositors is not left to the government's budget and political pressure each time a bank fails. Option A is wrong because supervision is still needed and even helps contain the risks deposit insurance creates. Option B is wrong because cover is limited, and option C is wrong because shareholders are never protected by deposit insurance.

questions.question: Before Country K set up deposit insurance, its government used tax money to rescue every failing bank. It then created an explicit scheme funded by premiums from banks. Which deposit insurance objective does this change mainly serve?

options.b: Contributing to an orderly payment system mechanism
options.c: Redistributing the cost of bank failure away from taxpayers
options.d: Facilitating the move from limited to blanket coverage

questions.explanation: When banks pay premiums into a fund, the cost of failures is shared by the banking industry instead of falling on taxpayers, which is the objective of redistributing the cost of failure. Options A and B are genuine objectives but are not what this change is about. Option D reverses a real objective: the aim is to move from blanket coverage to limited coverage, not the other way round.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a policy objective of the deposit insurance scheme in Nigeria?

options.a: To promote competition amongst deposit-taking financial institutions
options.b: To guarantee the profits of insured banks
options.c: To facilitate transitioning from blanket coverage to limited coverage
options.d: To contribute to an orderly payment system mechanism

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance protects depositors and the stability of the system; it does not protect a bank's profits, which are the owners' business risk. Options A, C and D are all listed policy objectives of Nigeria's scheme, alongside protecting small depositors, supporting financial stability, providing a failure-resolution mechanism and redistributing the cost of failure.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the public policy objectives of deposit insurance in Nigeria include all of the following EXCEPT

options.a: fixing the interest rates banks pay on savings deposits
options.b: protecting depositors, especially small and less-informed ones, through an orderly means of compensation
options.c: contributing to the stability of the financial system
options.d: providing a framework for the resolution and orderly exit of failing and failed institutions

questions.explanation: Section 2 of the NDIC Act 2023 sets out three public policy objectives: protecting depositors (especially small, less-informed ones), contributing to financial system stability, and providing a framework for resolving and closing failing and failed institutions in an orderly way. Options B, C and D are those objectives. Setting interest rates is a monetary policy matter for the central bank, not a deposit insurance objective.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, which statement about the public policy objectives of Nigeria's deposit insurance scheme was correct?

options.a: They were stated in Section 2 of the 2006 Act
options.b: They were not stated in the Act; they were later spelt out in the NDIC Act 2023
options.c: They were fixed each year by a CBN circular
options.d: They were set by IADI rules that bound Nigeria directly

questions.explanation: The 2006 Act gave the NDIC its powers but did not state the public policy objectives of the scheme, which was a gap compared with international practice; the NDIC Act 2023 filled it in Section 2. Option A confuses the two Acts. Options C and D are wrong because objectives of a statutory scheme belong in the law itself, and IADI guidance is not binding law in Nigeria.

questions.question: A small new bank in Ibadan is able to attract savings because customers know their deposits are protected up to the same limit as deposits in the biggest banks. Which deposit insurance objective does this illustrate?

options.b: Redistributing the cost of bank failure
options.d: Providing a formal mechanism for failure resolution

questions.explanation: Because every insured bank's depositors enjoy the same protection, small banks can compete for deposits with big ones, which promotes competition. Options B, C and D are real objectives or benefits of deposit insurance, but none of them explains why savers are willing to use a small bank.

questions.question: A deposit insurance system established by legislation or private contract that spells out its mandate, powers, governance, funding, coverage limits and reimbursement rules is
questions.explanation: An explicit scheme is written down in law or contract, so its mandate, funding, coverage and rules are known in advance. Option A has no formal rules or funding. Option C is a declaration protecting deposits beyond normal limited cover, and option D is protection that is neither clearly explicit nor implicit.

questions.question: Where there is no formal deposit protection system, no formal means of funding and no clear government commitment to compensate depositors, but people believe the government will step in when banks fail, deposit protection is
questions.explanation: Implicit protection rests only on the expectation that the government will not let depositors lose their money, without any law, fund or set limits. Option A is the opposite, a scheme written in law. Options B and D describe features of formal explicit schemes, namely a mandate type and a funding method.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of implicit deposit protection?

options.a: Coverage limits are set out in a statute
options.b: Premiums are collected from banks before any failure
options.c: Membership is made compulsory by law
options.d: Whether and how depositors are compensated is decided only when a bank fails

questions.explanation: Under implicit protection there are no rules on coverage and no fund set aside, so decisions about compensating depositors are negotiated at the time of failure. Options A, B and C are all features of an explicit scheme, which fixes coverage, funding and membership in advance.

questions.question: Which of the following would NOT normally be spelt out in the law that sets up an explicit deposit insurance scheme?

options.c: Rules guiding participation by insured institutions
options.d: The dividend each insured bank must pay its shareholders

questions.explanation: The law for an explicit scheme sets out its mandate, powers, governance, membership rules, funding, coverage limits, failure resolution and reimbursement of depositors. Options A, B and C are all such provisions. A bank's dividend policy is decided by its board and shareholders within banking rules, not by the deposit insurance law.

questions.question: Nigeria's deposit insurance system is classified as explicit mainly because

options.a: the government has informally promised to rescue large banks
options.b: the CBN decides case by case whether to repay depositors
options.c: banks signed a voluntary private pact to help each other
options.d: its mandate, coverage, funding and membership are set out in the NDIC Act

questions.explanation: Nigeria's scheme is created and governed by statute, the NDIC Act, which fixes who is insured, how much is covered and how the scheme is funded, so it is explicit. Options A and B describe implicit or discretionary protection. Option C is wrong because membership in Nigeria is compulsory by law, not a voluntary pact.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts explicit and implicit deposit protection?

options.a: Implicit schemes have pre-set coverage limits; explicit schemes rely on government discretion
options.b: Explicit schemes cover all deposits without limit; implicit schemes cover only small deposits
options.c: Both have formal funding and differ only in who owns the insurer
options.d: Explicit schemes have pre-set coverage and funding rules; implicit protection rests on the expectation of government support

questions.explanation: The difference is formality: an explicit scheme sets coverage, funding and rules in law before any failure, while implicit protection relies only on the belief that government will step in. Option A reverses the two. Option B is wrong because explicit schemes normally have limited cover, and option C is wrong because implicit protection has no formal funding at all.

questions.question: China introduced deposit insurance on 1 May 2015 with cover of 500,000 yuan per depositor. This is best described as

options.a: a move from explicit to implicit deposit protection
options.b: a move from implicit to explicit deposit protection
options.c: a switch from a risk minimiser to a paybox mandate
options.d: the introduction of a blanket guarantee on all deposits

questions.explanation: Before 2015 Chinese depositors relied on an implied state guarantee; the 2015 scheme put a formal, limited cover into law, which is a move to explicit protection. Option A reverses the direction. Option D is wrong because a fixed 500,000 yuan limit is limited cover, not a blanket guarantee, and option C confuses this with a change of mandate.

questions.question: A declaration by the authorities that, in addition to the protection provided by limited deposit insurance coverage, certain deposits and possibly other financial instruments will be protected is called
questions.explanation: A blanket guarantee goes beyond the normal limited cover, usually announced in a crisis to stop panic. Option A makes depositors bear part of the loss, which is the opposite. Option B extends cover to the beneficial owners of pooled accounts, and option C is the act of paying out insured deposits after a bank closes.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four deposit insurance mandates identified by IADI?
questions.explanation: IADI groups deposit insurer mandates into paybox, paybox plus, loss minimiser and risk minimiser, from the narrowest to the broadest set of powers. Options A, B and C are three of those four. A deposit insurer is a public-interest body, so 'profit maximiser' is not a mandate type.

questions.question: A deposit insurer that is responsible only for reimbursing insured deposits when a bank fails operates which mandate?
questions.explanation: The paybox is the narrowest mandate: the insurer simply pays insured depositors. Option B adds certain resolution functions, option C actively chooses least-cost resolution strategies, and option D adds supervision and early intervention powers.

questions.question: The role of a paybox deposit insurer is limited to

options.a: supervising banks and enforcing prompt corrective action
options.b: choosing the least-cost resolution option for failing banks
options.c: collecting premiums, managing the insurance fund and reimbursing insured depositors
options.d: setting prudential regulations for all deposit-taking banks

questions.explanation: A paybox collects premiums, looks after the fund and pays depositors when a bank fails, and nothing more. Options A and D describe powers of a risk minimiser. Option B describes a loss minimiser.

questions.question: To reimburse depositors in a timely and efficient way when banks fail, a paybox system needs

options.a: appropriate authority, access to deposit information and adequate funding
options.b: the power to license and revoke bank licences
options.c: the power to set the monetary policy rate
options.d: ownership of the banks whose deposits it insures

questions.explanation: Even a paybox cannot pay quickly unless the law gives it authority, it can get accurate depositor records, and it has money ready. Option B belongs to the bank licensing authority, usually the central bank. Options C and D are not needed to reimburse depositors at all.

questions.question: A deposit insurer that reimburses depositors and also has certain limited resolution functions, such as giving financial support to a failing bank, but does not actively choose among least-cost strategies or supervise banks, has which mandate?
questions.explanation: Paybox plus is a paybox with some extra resolution responsibilities, such as financial support. Option A only pays depositors. Option B actively selects from a range of least-cost resolution strategies, and option C also has supervision and early intervention powers.

questions.question: A deposit insurer that actively engages in selecting from a range of least-cost resolution strategies has which mandate?
questions.explanation: The loss minimiser's defining feature is choosing the resolution method that costs the fund least. Option A only pays depositors and option B has only certain limited resolution functions. Option D goes further still, adding risk assessment, early intervention and, in some cases, prudential oversight.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a loss minimiser deposit insurer?

options.a: It has full prudential oversight and sets regulations for banks
options.b: It determines resolution and receivership strategies and optimises recoveries, but in most cases has no supervisory powers
options.c: It only collects premiums and reimburses insured depositors
options.d: It licenses new banks and acts as lender of last resort

questions.explanation: A loss minimiser has wide resolution tools, decides how failed banks are handled, manages claims and maximises recoveries, but usually does not supervise banks. Option A describes a risk minimiser and option C a paybox. Option D describes central bank functions, not a deposit insurer.

questions.question: Which deposit insurance mandate has the widest set of powers and is therefore best placed to contribute to financial stability?
questions.explanation: A risk minimiser can supervise, intervene early, enforce corrective action and resolve failing banks, so it can act before losses arise. Options A and B mainly pay depositors after failure. Option D has wide resolution tools but in most cases no supervisory powers.

questions.question: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) operates which type of deposit insurance mandate?
questions.explanation: The NDIC guarantees deposits, supervises insured institutions with the CBN, resolves failing banks and liquidates failed ones, which makes it a risk minimiser. Option A would only pay depositors. Options B and D lack the supervisory powers the NDIC has.

questions.question: The NDIC Act makes the NDIC a risk minimiser rather than a paybox mainly by

options.a: giving it powers to supervise insured institutions
options.b: limiting it to collecting premiums from banks
options.c: making it privately owned by the insured banks
options.d: removing its power to liquidate failed banks

questions.explanation: Supervisory power is what moves a deposit insurer from merely paying depositors to actively reducing risk in the banks it insures. Option B describes a paybox. Option C is wrong because the NDIC is publicly owned, and option D is wrong because the NDIC is the liquidator of failed insured institutions.

questions.question: The deposit insurer of Country A collects premiums and pays insured depositors whenever the central bank closes a bank. It plays no part in supervising banks or deciding how failed banks are resolved. Its mandate is
questions.explanation: An insurer that only collects premiums and pays depositors is a paybox. Option A would also have some resolution functions. Option B would choose the least-cost resolution method, and option C would supervise banks as well.

questions.question: The deposit insurer of Country B does not supervise banks, but when a bank fails it compares purchase and assumption, a bridge bank and a deposit payoff, and chooses whichever costs its fund the least. Its mandate is
questions.explanation: Actively choosing the least-cost resolution option, without supervisory powers, is the mark of a loss minimiser. Option A would simply pay depositors. Option B has only certain limited resolution functions, and option C would also supervise banks.

questions.question: The deposit insurer of Country C examines banks on-site, analyses their returns off-site, issues directives to correct unsafe practices and resolves failing banks. Its mandate is
questions.explanation: Supervision, enforcement and prompt corrective action on top of resolution powers make this a risk minimiser, like the NDIC. Option A usually has no supervisory powers. Options C and D are focused on paying depositors with, at most, limited resolution roles.

questions.question: The deposit insurer of Country D pays insured depositors and can also provide financial support to a failing bank and act as liquidator, but it does not supervise banks or select among least-cost strategies. Its mandate is
questions.explanation: Paybox plus means paying depositors plus certain resolution functions such as financial support and liquidation. Option A would only pay depositors. Option B would actively choose least-cost resolution strategies, and option D would also supervise banks.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a paybox from a risk minimiser?

options.a: A paybox supervises banks; a risk minimiser only reimburses insured depositors
options.b: A paybox only reimburses insured depositors; a risk minimiser also has supervisory, early intervention and resolution powers
options.c: Both supervise banks, but only a risk minimiser collects premiums
options.d: A risk minimiser cannot pay depositors; it can only supervise banks

questions.explanation: The two sit at opposite ends of the range: the paybox only pays depositors, while the risk minimiser also supervises, intervenes early and resolves failing banks. Option A reverses them. Option C is wrong because a paybox does not supervise and also collects premiums, and option D is wrong because a risk minimiser still guarantees and pays insured deposits.

questions.question: What mainly distinguishes a risk minimiser from a loss minimiser?

options.a: The loss minimiser supervises banks, which a risk minimiser cannot do
options.b: The risk minimiser cannot take part in resolving failed banks
options.c: The risk minimiser has supervisory and prudential oversight powers, which a loss minimiser in most cases lacks
options.d: The loss minimiser only reimburses depositors and has no resolution role

questions.explanation: Both have strong resolution roles, but the risk minimiser adds supervision, enforcement and prompt corrective action to reduce risk before failure. Option A reverses the two. Option B is wrong because a risk minimiser has a full suite of resolution powers, and option D describes a paybox.

questions.question: Lessons from the global financial crisis led many deposit insurance systems to migrate

options.a: from risk minimiser mandates back to the pure paybox model
options.b: from explicit schemes to implicit protection
options.c: from compulsory membership to voluntary membership
options.d: from the paybox model towards mandates involving more supervision and resolution

questions.explanation: As financial stability became a central goal, many insurers were given wider roles in supervision and resolution instead of only paying depositors. Option A reverses this trend. Options B and C go against the post-crisis push for explicit schemes with compulsory membership.

questions.question: After the global financial crisis, the main goal of deposit insurance shifted from primarily protecting small depositors towards

options.c: protecting the shareholders of failing banks

questions.explanation: The crisis showed that depositor panic can threaten the whole system, so deposit insurers came to see financial stability as a major objective alongside depositor protection. Option B is not a policy goal. Option C is wrong because deposit insurance does not protect shareholders, and option D is a fiscal matter.

questions.question: A deposit insurance scheme run by a banking association and financed by its member banks, with no government ownership, is
questions.explanation: When the banking industry itself owns and runs the scheme, it is privately administered. Option A would be owned or run by government or the central bank, and option B would combine public and private bodies. Option D is wrong because a scheme run under formal arrangements by an association is explicit, not implicit.

questions.question: The NDIC's paid-up capital was contributed 60 percent by the Central Bank of Nigeria and 40 percent by the Federal Ministry of Finance. Its ownership is therefore best described as
questions.explanation: Both owners, the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance, are government bodies, so the NDIC is publicly owned. Option C is tempting because there are two owners, but a mixed structure needs a private-sector owner such as the banks. Options B and D are wrong because insured banks pay premiums but do not own the NDIC.

questions.question: India's Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is wholly owned by the Reserve Bank of India. It is therefore an example of
questions.explanation: A deposit insurer owned entirely by the central bank is publicly owned. Options A and B would need private-sector ownership. Option D is wrong because the DICGC is a formal statutory insurer, which makes India's protection explicit.

questions.question: Which of the following deposit insurers is privately run?
questions.explanation: Brazil's FGC is a private non-profit body funded by contributions from its member institutions. Option A is owned by the Reserve Bank of India, option C by the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance, and option D by Taiwan's government through its finance ministry and central bank, so all three are public.

questions.question: Switzerland's esisuisse is a self-regulatory organisation formed by banks and securities firms to protect depositors. Its administration is best described as
questions.explanation: A scheme set up and run by the banks and securities firms themselves is privately administered. Options B and C would need the state or central bank to run it. Option D is wrong because esisuisse is a formal arrangement with set rules, so the protection is explicit.

questions.question: Taiwan's Central Deposit Insurance Corporation is government-owned, with capital provided jointly by the Ministry of Finance and the central bank. Its ownership is
questions.explanation: Both owners are state bodies, so the corporation is publicly owned, just like the NDIC. Option C is a trap: having two owners does not make ownership mixed unless one of them is private. Options B and D are wrong because banks and private investors do not own it.

questions.question: A deposit insurance scheme set up and run jointly by public authorities and the private banking industry is said to have
questions.explanation: When government bodies and the banking industry share in running the scheme, administration is mixed. Option A is run by government alone and option C by the industry alone. Option D is not an administration type; implicit protection has no formal scheme to administer.

questions.question: Which statement about how deposit guarantee schemes can be organised is correct?

options.a: A scheme must always be a separate privately owned company
options.b: A scheme must always be a department of the ministry of finance
options.c: A scheme can only operate as a unit inside a commercial bank
