questions.topic: Functions, Membership and Guarantee Limit of the NDIC
questions.question: When the NDIC Act 2006 replaced the 1988 Decree, the maximum cover for depositors of licensed banks moved from:
questions.explanation: The 1988 Decree covered up to N50,000 per depositor, and the 2006 Act raised the cover for licensed banks to N200,000. Option D confuses the new N100,000 limit for other deposit-taking institutions, option A is the later MFB/PMB increase, and option B is the later DMB increase.

questions.question: The "E" in CAMEL stands for ____
questions.explanation: CAMEL is the rating framework examiners use to judge a bank's health: Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings and Liquidity. Earnings measures how profitable the bank is and whether its income can absorb losses and build capital. Options A and B are tempting because they sound like income-statement items, but expenses are only one part of the earnings picture and are not what the letter stands for.

questions.question: Supervision based on the entire banking group, including its subsidiaries and related entities, is known as ____ supervision.
questions.explanation: Consolidated supervision looks at a banking group as a whole, so risks in subsidiaries, including foreign ones, are captured along with the parent bank. Option C, risk-based supervision, focuses on how risky a bank's activities are rather than on the group structure. On-site supervision in option D simply means examiners visiting the bank, and transaction-based checking looks at individual deals.

questions.question: The Financial Stability Board (FSB) describes G-SIFIs as financial institutions whose distress or disorderly failure would cause significant disruption to ____

options.b: Both the wider financial system and economic activity
options.d: Neither the financial system nor economic activity

questions.explanation: The FSB defines global systemically important financial institutions as those whose distress or disorderly failure, because of their size, complexity and interconnectedness, would significantly disrupt both the wider financial system and economic activity. Options A and C are each only half of that definition, and option D contradicts the very idea of being systemically important.

questions.question: A Systemically Important Financial Institution (SIFI) could be:

options.c: a bank, an insurance company or any other financial institution

questions.explanation: A SIFI is defined by how much damage its failure would do to the wider financial system, not by the type of licence it holds, so it can be a bank, an insurer or any other large, interconnected financial institution. Option B and option D each pick out just one type of institution, which is too narrow. Option A is wrong because ownership does not decide systemic importance; size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity do.

questions.question: The Basel Committee has identified factors for assessing the systemic importance of a financial institution, such as:
questions.explanation: The Basel Committee looks at several indicators when judging how systemically important a bank is: its size, interconnectedness, substitutability, complexity and cross-jurisdictional activity. Interconnectedness (A) captures links with other institutions, substitutability (B) asks how easily others could take over its services, and cross-jurisdictional activity (C) measures its reach across countries. Since all three are on the list, D is the best answer.

questions.question: In Nigeria, because banks dominate the financial system, the CBN and NDIC focus enhanced supervision on:
questions.explanation: Banks hold most of the assets in Nigeria's financial system, so the CBN and NDIC framework concentrates on Systemically Important Banks, whose failure could destabilise the whole system. SIBs face more frequent and intensive on-site and off-site supervision. Options D, C and A are small institutions whose individual failure would not threaten the system in the same way.

questions.question: Methodologies suggested by the Basel Committee for identifying systemically important banks include:
questions.explanation: The Basel Committee's methodology combines an indicator-based measurement approach (scoring banks on indicators such as size and interconnectedness), a bucketing approach (grouping banks by score to set extra capital charges) and supervisory judgement to adjust the results. Each of A, B and C is part of that methodology, so D is correct.

questions.question: In determining Systemically Important Banks (SIBs) in Nigeria, the CBN/NDIC framework used:

options.a: the indicator-based measurement approach together with supervisory judgement
options.c: the indicator-based approach only, with no supervisory judgement
options.d: the age of each bank and its number of branches only

questions.explanation: Nigeria's SIB framework scored banks with an indicator-based measurement approach (size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity) and then applied supervisory judgement to arrive at the final list. Option C leaves out the judgement step, which the regulators did use. Option B is one of the Basel methods, but Nigeria did not adopt it to identify SIBs, and option D is not a recognised method at all.

questions.question: A statutory function in which a specialised agency monitors banks for compliance with written rules on acceptable conduct, so that their activities promote a safe, sound and stable financial system, is called
questions.explanation: Bank supervision is the ongoing monitoring of banks against rules of acceptable behaviour, with the aim of keeping the financial system safe, sound and stable. Option A is the winding up of a bank that has already failed, and option C is the promise to pay insured depositors. Option B deals with banks that are already failing, not routine monitoring of all banks.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an aim of banking supervision?

options.a: Guaranteeing shareholders a minimum return on their investment
options.b: Safeguarding the financial system against disruption and mass bank failure
options.c: Minimising money laundering in the financial system
options.d: Reducing the risk to which depositors and creditors are exposed

questions.explanation: Supervision protects the system and its depositors and creditors; it does not promise shareholders any return, since owners carry the risk of the business. Options B, C and D are all genuine aims of supervision, alongside improving efficiency and channelling resources to priority sectors.

questions.question: The NDIC examines the books and affairs of every licensed insured institution through two forms of supervision. These are
questions.explanation: The two forms of supervision are off-site surveillance (analysing returns away from the bank) and on-site examination (inspecting the bank on its premises). Option B describes the scope of supervision and option C describes methodologies of supervision. Option D names the two categories of returns, which feed off-site surveillance.

questions.question: The receipt and analysis of returns sent periodically by insured banks, to check their compliance with prudential regulations, is known as
questions.explanation: Off-site surveillance is done from the supervisor's office by analysing the periodic returns banks submit. Option C requires examiners to visit the bank's premises, and option A is a type of on-site visit called for a particular concern. Option B concerns supervising a whole banking group, not the method of analysing returns.

questions.question: Examining a bank's reports and documents within its premises and reconciling them with physical realities such as cash and other inventories is called
questions.explanation: On-site examination takes place inside the bank, where examiners check documents against physical assets like cash. Option A is carried out away from the bank using returns. Option B refers to the scope of supervision (one bank on its own), and option D is a step within risk-based supervision rather than a form of supervision.

questions.question: NDIC examiners visit a branch of Ikeja Trust Bank in Lagos, count the cash in the vault and compare the total with the cash figure in the bank's last monthly return. This activity is part of
questions.explanation: Checking a bank's returns against the physical cash on its premises is the heart of on-site examination. Option D only analyses the returns without visiting the bank. Option C looks at a whole banking group, and option B is paying insured depositors after a bank fails.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the things an on-site examination seeks to determine?

options.a: How much each insured depositor should be paid after the bank closes
options.b: Whether the returns sent by the bank match the physical realities in the bank
options.c: Whether the bank complies with banking regulations
options.d: Whether the findings of off-site analysis truly describe the bank's financial risk performance

questions.explanation: Calculating payments to insured depositors happens after a bank has failed and its licence is revoked; it is part of deposit payout, not examination. Options C, B and D are exactly the three things an on-site examination checks: regulatory compliance, the accuracy of returns, and whether off-site findings are correct.

questions.question: After an examination, exceptions are reported and recommendations made to the bank. How is the bank's implementation of those recommendations monitored?

options.a: Through the bank's annual general meeting of shareholders
options.b: Through the appointment of a liquidator for the bank
options.c: Through the yearly assessment of deposit insurance premium
options.d: Through scheduled post-examination visits to the bank

questions.explanation: Supervisors follow up with scheduled post-examination visits to confirm that the lapses they found are being corrected. Option A is a shareholders' forum, not a supervisory tool, and option C is a funding exercise. Option B happens only when a bank has failed, not as follow-up to an examination.

questions.question: Requirements made by regulatory or supervisory authorities on banks, submitted on a set periodic basis to help ensure the banks conform to desired operating rules, are called
questions.explanation: Returns are the periodic reports banks must send to supervisors, and they are the raw input of off-site surveillance. Option B is what banks pay for deposit insurance, and option C is what creditors of a failed bank receive as its assets are sold. Option A refers to restrictions placed on distressed banks.

questions.question: Statutory returns are best described as returns that

options.a: supervisors request from time to time through circulars or questionnaires
options.b: must be made by banks as provided for in the Acts governing banking business
options.c: banks submit voluntarily to attract more depositors
options.d: are prepared by the NDIC for publication in its annual report

questions.explanation: Statutory returns are required by law, that is, by the Acts that govern banking business. Option A describes non-statutory returns, which are called for in day-to-day supervision. Options C and D are not regulatory returns at all, since returns are mandatory submissions from banks to supervisors.

questions.question: Non-statutory returns are usually called for by supervisors by means of
questions.explanation: Non-statutory returns are requested in the course of day-to-day supervision, so they are typically demanded through circulars or questionnaires. Option B is how statutory returns arise, since those are set by law. Options D and A are not ways supervisors request information from banks.

questions.question: The NDIC sends a questionnaire to all deposit money banks asking for details of their loans to the aviation sector. No Act specifically requires this report. The information the banks send back is an example of
questions.explanation: A return requested by the supervisor through a questionnaire, without a specific legal requirement, is a non-statutory return. Option A would be one required by the Acts governing banking. Option C is prepared by examiners after visiting a bank, and option B relates to failed banks in liquidation.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes off-site surveillance from on-site examination?

options.a: Off-site surveillance is done only after a bank fails, while on-site examination is done before failure
options.b: Off-site surveillance analyses banks' periodic returns away from the bank, while on-site examination verifies the bank's records on its premises
options.c: Off-site surveillance covers only microfinance banks, while on-site examination covers only deposit money banks
options.d: Off-site surveillance is done by the CBN alone, while on-site examination is done by the NDIC alone

questions.explanation: The difference is about where and how the work is done: off-site work analyses returns at the supervisor's office, while on-site work checks records and assets inside the bank. Option A is wrong because both are used on going-concern banks. Options D and C are wrong because both CBN and NDIC use both forms, across all types of insured institutions.

questions.question: A method of examination that involves checking for and enforcing compliance with the legislation, regulations or policies that apply to a bank is known as
questions.explanation: Compliance-based supervision is rule-checking: examiners test whether the bank obeyed the applicable laws and regulations. Option C focuses instead on identifying and assessing each bank's most critical risks. Options D and B describe the scope of supervision (a group, or operations across countries), not a rule-checking method.

questions.question: A major weakness of compliance-based supervision is that it is

options.b: too forward-looking and focused on future risks
options.c: reactive and static, and less useful in a constantly changing environment
options.d: applied only to groups of banks rather than single banks

questions.explanation: Compliance-based supervision checks past behaviour against rules, so it reacts after problems occur and does not adapt well to a dynamic financial world. Option B describes risk-based supervision, which is forward-looking. Option D confuses it with consolidated supervision, and option A is the opposite of what compliance checking does.

questions.question: A structured process that identifies the most critical risks facing each bank and, through a focused review, assesses the bank's management of those risks and its financial vulnerability to adverse experience is called
questions.explanation: Risk-based supervision (RBS) starts from each bank's key risks and then judges how well the bank manages them. Option D only checks obedience to rules, and option C refers to supervising a single bank on its own. Option A is a form of supervision based on analysing returns, which can be used under either methodology.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of risk-based supervision?

options.a: It assesses inherent risks separately from risk management processes
options.b: It applies the same examination intensity to every bank regardless of its risk profile
options.c: It allows supervisors to channel more resources to banks with higher risk profiles
options.d: It is a dynamic, forward-looking process that seeks early identification of emerging risks

questions.explanation: RBS deliberately treats banks differently, putting more supervisory effort where the risks are greatest, so a one-size-fits-all intensity is not one of its features. Options D, A and C are genuine features: RBS is forward-looking, separates inherent risks from risk management, and prioritises higher-risk banks.

questions.question: Under risk-based supervision, which of the following is NOT a Risk Management Control Function (RMCF)?
questions.explanation: Credit risk is an inherent risk that a bank faces; the RMCFs are the functions that manage such risks. Options B, D and A are all RMCFs, together with the board, risk management and financial analysis.

questions.question: Under risk-based supervision, which of the following is classified as an inherent risk of a bank?
questions.explanation: Inherent risks are the risks that come with the business of banking, such as credit, operational, liquidity and market risk. Options B, D and A are Risk Management Control Functions, which exist to manage those inherent risks.

questions.question: After profiling all insured banks, a supervisor decides to send more examiners to Bank Q, which has a high risk profile, and fewer to Bank R, which has a low risk profile. This approach is typical of
questions.explanation: Allocating supervisory resources in line with each bank's risk profile is a defining feature of risk-based supervision. Option A focuses on checking rules and is not driven by risk profiles. Option B is about supervising single entities rather than allocating resources, and option C is paying depositors of a failed bank.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares risk-based supervision (RBS) with compliance-based supervision?

options.a: RBS ignores how a bank manages its risks, while compliance-based supervision focuses on it
options.b: RBS is proactive and forward-looking, while compliance-based supervision is reactive
options.c: RBS is reactive, while compliance-based supervision is forward-looking
options.d: RBS checks only past compliance with rules, while compliance-based supervision profiles risks

questions.explanation: RBS looks ahead to emerging risks and how well they are managed, whereas compliance-based supervision checks after the fact whether rules were followed. Option C reverses the two. Options A and D also swap the defining features of the two methods.

questions.question: Which supervisory approach is described as gradually becoming the dominant approach to the supervision of financial institutions around the world?
questions.explanation: Risk-based supervision is spreading worldwide because it focuses supervisory effort on the biggest risks. Options A and B are the same older rule-checking approach under two names. Option D describes the scope of supervision, not the dominant methodology.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the scopes of bank supervision?
questions.explanation: Risk-based supervision is a methodology of supervision, not a scope. The scope of supervision covers how widely the supervisor looks: a single bank (option C), the whole group (option B), or operations across national borders (option A).

questions.question: Supervision that focuses on a single bank, its distinct individual operations, risk profile and management is called
questions.explanation: Solo-based supervision looks at one entity on its own, under the capital rules of its own regulator. Option D assesses the whole business group, and option B covers operations in other countries. Option C describes who carries out supervision (for example CBN and NDIC together), not its scope.

questions.question: A qualitative and quantitative assessment of the strength of business groups that contain banks, in order to identify and evaluate all the risks to which the banks are exposed, is known as
questions.explanation: Consolidated supervision looks at the group as a whole, including a group-wide assessment of capital adequacy. Option D looks only at a single entity. Option A is a rule-checking methodology, and option B is a form of supervision based on returns.

questions.question: The adoption of which banking model in Nigeria in 2001 increased the need for consolidated supervision, because many banks began to operate through subsidiaries and affiliates?
questions.explanation: Universal banking (2001) let banks carry on many activities through subsidiaries, so supervisors had to look at whole groups. Option D was the later recapitalisation exercise that cut the number of banks, and option A is a type of banking based on non-interest principles. Option B was the 1986 reform that liberalised bank licensing.

questions.question: Consolidated supervision helps prevent the over-leveraging of capital within a group, where the same capital is counted more than once by different group entities. This problem is known as
questions.explanation: Double gearing happens when capital is used to support risks in more than one entity of a group, overstating the group's true capital; consolidated supervision checks for it. Option C is the incentive to take more risk when others bear the cost. Option D is funding long-term assets with short-term liabilities, and option A is about attracting riskier customers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of consolidated supervision?

options.a: Evaluating the strength of the group's consolidated financial resources
options.b: Preventing the over-leveraging of capital (double gearing)
options.c: Supporting the principle that no business segment's risk escapes supervision
options.d: Supervising each group entity only by its own regulator's capital rules without looking at the group

questions.explanation: Looking at each entity only on its own is solo-based supervision, which is exactly the gap consolidated supervision is meant to close. Options C, B and A are the stated objectives of consolidated supervision.

questions.question: Consolidated supervision is regarded as an essential element of
questions.explanation: Because group links can expose a bank to risks from its parent or affiliates, a full risk-based view requires looking at the whole group. Option B focuses on rule-checking rather than risk. Options C and D are post-failure activities, not supervision.

questions.question: Afro Holdings Plc owns a deposit money bank, an insurance company and a stockbroking firm. Supervisors assess the risks and the capital adequacy of the whole group, not just the bank. This is
questions.explanation: Assessing a whole business group, including a group-wide view of capital, is consolidated supervision. Option A would look at the bank alone. Option B is a rule-checking method, and option D is the first examination of a newly licensed bank.

questions.question: A Nigerian bank has subsidiaries in Ghana, Sierra Leone and The Gambia. Supervising the risks that arise from its operations in these other countries falls under
questions.explanation: Supervising a bank's operations outside its home country is the cross-border scope of supervision. Option C focuses on one entity in isolation. Option A is a form of supervision, not a scope, and option B is a rule-checking methodology.

questions.question: The global financial meltdown showed that some events could have been foreseen if supervisors had adopted a holistic approach rather than a solo perspective. This lesson strengthens the case for
questions.explanation: A holistic approach looks at the whole group and its connections, which is what consolidated supervision does. Option D is narrow rule-checking. Options A and B concern deposit protection design and premium setting, not the scope of supervision.

questions.question: Because the law confers on the NDIC powers to supervise all insured institutions, the NDIC is classified as a
questions.explanation: A deposit insurer with supervisory powers, enforcement and prompt corrective action is a risk minimiser, and the NDIC is one. Option A only reimburses insured deposits. Option C adds some resolution functions, and option B actively chooses least-cost resolutions but in most cases has no supervisory powers.

questions.question: Why does a deposit insurer such as the NDIC supervise banks instead of only paying depositors after a bank fails?

options.a: To replace the CBN as the licensing authority for banks
options.b: To detect problems early and reduce the likelihood and cost of failures that its fund would have to bear
options.c: To earn examination fees that pay for its operating expenses
options.d: To guarantee all deposits in full regardless of size

questions.explanation: A deposit insurer that supervises can spot unsafe practices early and act before failure, which protects depositors and the insurance fund. Option C is wrong because supervision is a statutory function, not a fee business. Option A is wrong because the CBN remains the licensing authority, and option D confuses supervision with a blanket guarantee.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the 'nature of banking business' that justifies bank regulation and supervision?

options.b: Banks perform the financial intermediation function
options.c: Banks are funded mainly by their owners' equity rather than by deposits
options.d: Banks have a large fiduciary responsibility over cash assets in the economy

questions.explanation: Banks trade largely on other people's money, mainly deposits, not on their owners' equity, which is precisely why they are supervised. Options D, B and A are genuine features of banking that make supervision necessary.

questions.question: Banks are said to trade largely on 'OPM'. This means that

options.a: banks invest only in options and other derivative products
options.b: banks are owned mostly by the government
options.c: most of the funds banks use belong to people other than the bank's owners, mainly depositors
options.d: banks borrow only from the central bank

questions.explanation: OPM stands for other people's money: most of the funds a bank controls belong to depositors rather than its shareholders, which is a key reason for supervision. Options A, B and D do not describe this feature of banking.

questions.question: The Structural Adjustment Programme of 1986 liberalised bank licensing and was expected to sharply increase the number of banks. How was an explicit deposit insurer with supervisory powers expected to help?

options.a: By complementing the supervisory efforts of the CBN over the larger number of banks
options.b: By issuing banking licences in place of the CBN
options.c: By taking over the CBN's role as lender of last resort
options.d: By guaranteeing that no bank would ever fail

questions.explanation: With many more banks to watch, an insurer with supervisory powers was meant to add to, not replace, the CBN's supervision. Options C and B are wrong because lender of last resort and licensing remain CBN functions. Option D is wrong because deposit insurance protects depositors when banks fail; it does not prevent all failures.

questions.question: Since the NDIC began operations in 1989, what has been one practical benefit of having both the CBN and the NDIC supervise banks?

options.a: On-site examinations were abolished in favour of off-site surveillance
options.b: Routine and special examinations of banks could be carried out more frequently despite the increase in the number of banks
options.c: Banks no longer needed to send returns to the CBN
options.d: Banks stopped paying deposit insurance premiums

questions.explanation: Two supervisors sharing the work made it possible to examine banks more often, even as bank numbers grew. Option C is wrong because returns remain central to off-site work. Options A and D are wrong because on-site examination continued and banks still pay premiums.

questions.question: Many new banks enter the market and compete fiercely for deposits. Some start making very risky loans with depositors' money to grow quickly. Which rationale for supervision and deposit insurance does this illustrate?

options.a: Increased competition among banks can encourage excessive risk-taking with depositors' funds
options.b: Lessons from the founding of the IADI
options.d: Change in government bank support policy

questions.explanation: Competition is generally good, but it can push banks to take excessive risks with depositors' funds, so depositors, especially small ones, need protection. Option D is about government shifting from propping up weak banks to protecting deposits. Options C and B are not the rationale shown in this scenario.

questions.question: Within Nigeria's financial safety net, which function is carried out jointly by the CBN and the NDIC?
questions.explanation: Supervision of banks is done jointly by the CBN and NDIC. Option A is a CBN function, and option D is the NDIC's own function. Option C also belongs to the CBN, which grants and revokes licences.

questions.question: When supervision shows that an insured bank's licence should be revoked, which institution actually revokes the licence?

options.a: The Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee

questions.explanation: Licensing and licence revocation belong to the CBN; the NDIC can recommend revocation but then acts as liquidator after the CBN revokes. Option C is the tempting wrong answer because the NDIC makes the recommendation. Options D and A do not revoke banking licences.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, when an examination shows that an insured institution needs action that lies outside the NDIC's own powers, the Act provides for the NDIC to

options.c: refer the matter to the IADI for a decision
options.d: sell the institution to AMCON on its own authority

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act has a provision for the NDIC to make recommendations to the CBN after examination, consistent with the CBN being the licensing authority. Option A is wrong because licence revocation is a CBN power. Options D and C are not how supervisory findings are acted on; the IADI is an international association, not a Nigerian regulator.

questions.question: eFASS, an electronic platform used for the rendering and analysis of banks' returns, was developed by the NDIC in collaboration with

options.d: the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria

questions.explanation: eFASS was developed jointly by the CBN and NDIC to support off-site surveillance of banks. Options B, A and D are other institutions that were not partners in developing this joint supervisory platform.

questions.question: Risk-based supervision of insured banks in Nigeria was adopted by the NDIC

options.a: at the direction of the Securities and Exchange Commission
options.c: in place of any form of on-site examination

questions.explanation: The NDIC adopted risk-based supervision together with the CBN, and the two use a jointly developed RBS framework. Option C is wrong because on-site examinations continue under RBS. Options D and A are wrong because RBS covers deposit money banks too and was not directed by the SEC.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, a 'failing insured institution' was defined as one whose

options.a: shareholders have voted to wind it up
options.b: licence has been withdrawn by the CBN
options.c: deposits have all been paid out by the NDIC
options.d: capital adequacy ratio is below the minimum prescribed by the CBN

questions.explanation: A failing institution was one whose capital adequacy (capital to risk-weighted assets) had fallen below the CBN minimum, while it still held a licence. Option B is the definition of a failed insured institution. Options C and A describe later stages or voluntary winding up, not the statutory test.

questions.question: The first examination conducted on a newly licensed bank, to assess its safety, soundness and compliance with banking laws, is called a
questions.explanation: A maiden examination is the first examination of a new bank. Option B is the regular, scheduled examination of an existing bank. Option D is called because of a particular concern, and option C focuses on one specific area of a bank's operations.

questions.question: A regular, scheduled examination carried out on every insured bank as part of the normal supervisory cycle is a
questions.explanation: Routine examinations are the periodic examinations every bank receives in the normal cycle. Option B is unscheduled and triggered by specific concerns. Option C is only for newly licensed banks, and option A concentrates on a particular area rather than the whole bank.

questions.question: In 2009, the CBN and NDIC jointly examined 24 banks, outside the normal cycle, because of concerns about their condition. This kind of unscheduled examination triggered by specific concerns is a
questions.explanation: An examination called outside the normal cycle because of particular concerns is a special examination, and the 2009 CBN/NDIC exercise is a well-known example. Option D is for newly licensed banks, and option B is the normal scheduled examination. Option C only follows up on earlier recommendations.

questions.question: Examiners visit Coastal Bank Plc to review only its foreign exchange operations, without examining the rest of the bank. This is best described as a
questions.explanation: A target examination concentrates on a specific area of a bank's business, such as foreign exchange or risk assets. Option A is the first examination of a new bank, and option B covers a whole group. Option D is the regular full-scope examination in the normal cycle.

questions.question: In 2018, the NDIC and CBN together conducted a Risk Assets Examination of deposit money banks to assess asset quality and loan loss provisions. This exercise is an example of

options.c: solo examination by the NDIC alone

questions.explanation: Because both supervisors carried out the exercise together, it is a joint CBN/NDIC examination. Option B applies only to newly licensed banks, and option D does not involve visiting banks. Option C is wrong because the CBN took part.

questions.question: Which of the following is a type of bank examination rather than a failure resolution option?
questions.explanation: A target examination is a supervisory tool used on going-concern banks to look at a specific area. Options C, D and B are ways of dealing with banks that are failing or have failed.

questions.question: In the CAMEL rating framework, the component measured mainly by a bank's ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets is
questions.explanation: The capital to risk-weighted assets ratio measures how much capital cushion a bank has, which is the C (capital adequacy) in CAMEL. Option B is about the quality of loans and other assets. Options A and D measure profitability and the ability to meet withdrawals.

questions.question: Unity Star Bank's ratio of non-performing loans to total loans rose from 4% to 22% within a year. Which CAMEL component is most directly weakened?
questions.explanation: Non-performing loans are bad assets, so a sharp rise in the NPL ratio mainly hurts asset quality, the A in CAMEL. Option C may suffer later as losses eat into capital, but the direct measure here is asset quality. Options A and B measure governance and the ability to meet withdrawals.

questions.question: Examiners find that the directors of a bank are constantly quarrelling, internal controls are weak and insiders are granted loans without proper approval. In the CAMEL framework, these findings mainly affect the rating for
questions.explanation: Board conflicts, weak controls and insider abuse are signs of poor management, the M in CAMEL. Options A and D measure profitability and liquidity position. Option B measures exposure to changes in interest rates, exchange rates and prices.

questions.question: Prime Savings Bank repeatedly borrows overnight from other banks at very high rates just to meet customers' daily withdrawals. The CAMEL component that best captures this problem is
questions.explanation: Struggling to meet withdrawals and relying on expensive short-term borrowing shows a liquidity problem, the L in CAMEL. Option B concerns the capital cushion. Options C and D concern the quality of loans and profitability, though both may suffer if the liquidity problem persists.

questions.question: When CAMEL is extended to CAMELS, the added 'S' stands for
questions.explanation: The S in CAMELS stands for sensitivity to market risk, meaning how changes in interest rates, exchange rates and prices could affect the bank. Options B and C are not CAMELS components. Option A is one of the three pillars of Basel II, not part of CAMELS.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the CAMEL rating framework?
questions.explanation: CAMEL stands for Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings and Liquidity; market share is not one of them. Options A, B and D are all genuine CAMEL components.

questions.question: On the standard CAMEL(S) composite rating scale of 1 to 5, a bank rated 1 is

options.a: the weakest, with a high risk of failure
options.b: the soundest, with the least supervisory concern
options.d: one whose licence has already been revoked

questions.explanation: The scale runs from 1 (strongest, least concern) to 5 (weakest, highest risk of failure). Option A describes a rating of 5, and option C describes the middle of the scale. Option D is wrong because CAMEL ratings apply to operating banks.

questions.question: A set of indicators, mostly drawn from banks' periodic returns, that supervisors use to detect banks heading towards distress early enough to intervene before they fail is called
questions.explanation: An early warning system flags deteriorating banks from their ratios and trends so supervisors can act in time. Option D is how risk-based premiums are set. Options A and C are used after a bank fails, not to detect distress early.

questions.question: Under the 2014 IADI Core Principles, which principle requires the deposit insurer to be part of a framework for early detection and timely intervention, acting before a bank becomes non-viable?
questions.explanation: Core Principle 13 of the 2014 set deals with early detection and timely intervention. Option C covers coverage limits, option B covers public awareness, and option D covers reimbursing depositors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an early warning signal of bank distress?

options.a: A rising ratio of non-performing loans
options.b: Persistent heavy borrowing in the interbank market at high rates
options.c: Steady growth in retained earnings alongside improving liquidity
options.d: Late or inaccurate rendition of returns to supervisors

questions.explanation: Growing retained earnings and better liquidity are signs of strength, not distress. Options B, A and D are classic warning signals that a bank may be heading for trouble.

questions.question: Mrs Okafor notices that her bank suddenly offers deposit rates far above what other banks pay and keeps phoning customers to bring in cash, while supervisors note it is borrowing heavily from other banks. To a supervisor, this pattern is best read as

options.a: a sign the bank has just passed a maiden examination
options.c: proof that the bank is a systemically important bank
options.d: an early warning signal of liquidity distress

questions.explanation: Paying unusually high rates and borrowing desperately for funds usually means a bank is short of liquidity, a common early warning signal. Option B is unrelated, since deposit-chasing says nothing good about loan quality. Options A and C are not shown by this pattern.

questions.question: Analysing the periodic returns of all insured banks to flag those whose key ratios are deteriorating is mainly carried out through
questions.explanation: Off-site surveillance analyses returns from all banks and is the natural home of ratio-based early warning. Option D is a physical on-site check of one bank. Options C and B deal with banks that have already failed.

questions.question: The risk-weighted capital ratio (capital adequacy ratio) of a bank is calculated as

options.a: liquid assets divided by total deposits
options.c: total deposits divided by total loans

questions.explanation: The capital adequacy ratio is capital divided by risk-weighted assets (RWA). Option D inverts the formula. Option C is a loan-to-deposit type measure, and option A is a liquidity ratio.

questions.question: Under the original Basel I Accord, which of the following was NOT one of the credit risk weights applied to assets?
questions.explanation: Basel I used a simple set of risk weights: 0%, 10%, 20%, 50% and 100%; 75% was not among them. Options C, B and A are genuine Basel I risk weights.

questions.question: Under Basel I risk weights, a bank holds cash of N20m (0%), claims on other banks of N30m (20%), residential mortgages of N40m (50%) and corporate loans of N60m (100%). What are its total risk-weighted assets?
questions.explanation: Multiply each exposure by its weight and add: 0 + 6 + 20 + 60 = N86m. Option B simply adds the exposures without weighting. Option D leaves out the N6m from interbank claims, and option A wrongly weights cash at 100%.

questions.question: A Nigerian bank required to keep a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 10% has risk-weighted assets of N500m. What is the minimum capital it must hold?
questions.explanation: Minimum capital = RWA x required ratio = N500m x 10% = N50m. Option C uses the 8% Basel I international minimum instead of the 10% given. Option A uses 15%, and option B misplaces the decimal point.

questions.question: A bank has qualifying capital of N12bn and risk-weighted assets of N80bn. What is its capital adequacy ratio?
questions.explanation: Capital adequacy ratio = capital / RWA = 12 / 80 = 0.15, or 15%. Option D divides RWA by capital the wrong way round and misplaces the decimal. Option B assumes RWA of N100bn, and option C is simply the Basel I minimum, not this bank's ratio.

questions.question: The original 1988 Basel I Accord set minimum capital requirements mainly to cover which risk?
questions.explanation: Basel I's capital requirements were built around credit risk, with an inherent buffer for other risks. Option B was brought into explicit capital requirements under Basel II. Options C and D were not the basis of Basel I's capital charge.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of Basel II?
questions.explanation: Basel II rests on three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline. Deposit insurance is part of the financial safety net, not a Basel II pillar. Options D, C and A are the genuine pillars.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a weakness of Basel I?

options.a: Its capital requirements did not always reflect economic risk
options.b: It created arbitrage opportunities, for example through securitisation
options.c: It gave little recognition to credit risk mitigants
options.d: It created an internationally recognised capital standard

questions.explanation: Creating an internationally recognised standard is an advantage of Basel I, not a weakness. Options A, B and C are recognised weaknesses that Basel II tried to fix.

questions.question: Basel II requires banks to measure the riskiness of their assets with respect to which three risks?

options.a: Market, country and interest rate risks only

questions.explanation: Basel II aligns capital more closely with risk by covering credit, market and operational risks. Options C, B and A mix in risks that are not the three named in the Basel II capital framework.

questions.question: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), now part of the banking supervision environment, are developed and published by the
questions.explanation: IFRS are a single set of global accounting standards issued by the IASB. Option D sets bank capital standards such as Basel I-III, and option A sets deposit insurance principles. Option B monitors the global financial system but does not write accounting standards.

questions.question: Banks whose failure would generate severe undesirable externalities, including disruption of the financial system and the real economy, are called
questions.explanation: SIFIs are institutions whose size, complexity and interconnectedness mean their failure would seriously disrupt the wider system and economy. Option A is a temporary bank set up to take over a failed bank. Options C and B are categories of institution that are not defined by systemic impact.

questions.question: In the CBN/NDIC framework for domestic systemically important banks issued in 2014, which two indicators carry the highest weight (30% each) in assessing systemic importance?
questions.explanation: The 2014 framework weights size (total assets) at 30%, substitutability at 30%, complexity at 25% and interconnectedness at 15%. Options C, A and B each include complexity or interconnectedness, which carry lower weights.

questions.question: Under the CBN/NDIC framework for systemically important banks (2014), the minimum capital adequacy ratio for a bank designated as a SIB is
questions.explanation: SIBs must keep a minimum CAR of 15%, higher than ordinary national banks, plus a 1% higher loss absorbency surcharge. Option A is the Basel I international minimum, and option B is the general Nigerian minimum for many non-SIB banks. Option C is not the framework's minimum.

questions.question: Under the 2014 CBN/NDIC framework for systemically important banks, the additional 1% Higher Loss Absorbency surcharge must be met with
questions.explanation: The 1% HLA surcharge must be met with CET1, the highest-quality capital, so SIBs can absorb losses as going concerns. Option D is lower-quality capital that is already limited to 25% of qualifying capital. Options C and A are liabilities or payments, not capital.

questions.question: Under the 2014 CBN/NDIC SIB framework, Tier 2 capital may not exceed 25% of a SIB's qualifying capital. If a SIB has qualifying capital of N400bn, what is the maximum amount of Tier 2 capital it can count?
questions.explanation: Maximum Tier 2 = 25% x N400bn = N100bn, which means Tier 1 must be at least N300bn (75%). Option B is the minimum Tier 1 amount, not the Tier 2 cap. Option D applies 15% (the minimum CAR) by mistake, and option C treats 25% as N25bn.

questions.question: Under the 2014 CBN/NDIC framework, systemically important banks must submit a specific recovery plan to the CBN and NDIC

options.a: only after their licence is revoked
options.c: only when they record a loss

questions.explanation: SIBs must prepare and submit a recovery plan to both the CBN and NDIC by 1 January each year, so authorities are ready before trouble comes. Option A is wrong because recovery planning is for going-concern banks. Options D and C do not match the annual requirement.

questions.question: Under the 2014 CBN/NDIC framework, how often must systemically important banks carry out stress tests of their capital and liquidity?
questions.explanation: SIBs must run capital and liquidity stress tests every quarter, with results reviewed by the CBN. Option A is the frequency of the CBN's monitoring of SIB key performance indicators, not of stress tests. Options C and B are not what the framework requires.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, which of the following was NOT one of the NDIC's enforcement powers over insured institutions?

options.a: Terminating the insured status of an insured institution
options.b: Setting the monetary policy rate for the banking system
options.c: Issuing specific directives to address unsafe and unsound practices after an examination
options.d: Taking over the control and management of an insured institution

questions.explanation: Setting the monetary policy rate is a CBN monetary policy function, not an NDIC enforcement power. Options C, D and A were among the NDIC's enforcement powers, along with recommending licence revocation and prosecuting directors for malpractice.

questions.question: After examining Eko Commerce Bank, the NDIC directs it to stop granting new loans to its directors and to raise fresh capital within six months. Directives like this, issued promptly after an examination to correct unsafe practices, are known as
questions.explanation: Prompt corrective action means supervisors quickly order a bank to fix unsafe or unsound practices while it is still operating. Options A, D and C are ways of dealing with a bank that has failed or is being closed, not corrective orders to an operating bank.

questions.question: Holding actions belong to which group of bank failure resolution options?
questions.explanation: Holding actions are applied while the bank is still open and operating, so they fall under open bank assistance, together with financial assistance and takeover of management. Options A, B and D all involve a bank that has been closed or had its licence revoked.

questions.question: The CBN and NDIC bar a distressed bank from opening new branches and granting fresh loans until it restructures and recapitalises, but allow it to keep operating. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Restricting a distressed but still-open bank's operations while it restructures is a holding action. Option D would require a failed bank's business to be moved into a new temporary bank. Options C and B happen only after the bank is closed.

questions.question: The NDIC has expressed serious concern about the integrity of data supplied by insured banks. Which problem most clearly shows this?

options.a: Depositors filing claims too quickly after a bank closes
options.b: Significant disparity between data from on-site examination and data from off-site returns
options.c: Banks paying premiums before the due date
options.d: Too many banks applying for deposit insurance

questions.explanation: When figures found on-site differ widely from what banks reported in their returns, off-site analysis becomes unreliable; this is the data integrity problem. Options D, A and C are not data integrity issues, and early premium payment is not a problem at all.

questions.question: How does deposit insurance differ from conventional insurance such as fire or motor insurance?

options.a: Deposit insurance involves only two parties, the insurer and the depositor
options.b: Deposit insurance never pays out because banks cannot fail
options.c: Deposit insurance involves three parties and actively seeks to reduce the insured risk through supervision
options.d: In deposit insurance the depositor pays the premium directly

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance has three parties (the insurer, the depositor who pays no premium, and the bank that pays the premium), and the insurer works to reduce the risk through supervision. Option A describes conventional insurance. Option D is wrong because the bank, not the depositor, pays, and option B is wrong because banks do fail.

questions.question: Both the depositor and the bank benefit from deposit insurance. How does the bank benefit?

options.a: Its shareholders are guaranteed against loss
options.b: It receives the premiums paid by depositors
options.c: It is exempted from all prudential regulations
options.d: It is supervised and assisted in times of problems

questions.explanation: While the depositor is protected, the bank gains from being supervised and assisted when it runs into problems. Option C is wrong because insured banks remain fully regulated. Option B is wrong because depositors pay no premium, and option A is wrong because deposit insurance protects depositors, not shareholders.

questions.question: Why does the NDIC see emerging distress in microfinance banks and primary mortgage institutions as a supervisory concern even when deposit money banks are sound?

options.a: Because their depositors are never insured
options.b: Because they are supervised by the SEC
options.c: Because these segments are interdependent with the mainstream insured banks
options.d: Because they pay no deposit insurance premiums at all

questions.explanation: Distress in MFBs and PMBs can spill over to deposit money banks because the segments are linked. Option D is wrong because MFBs pay premiums (at a flat rate). Options B and A are wrong because these institutions are supervised by the CBN and NDIC and their depositors are insured up to set limits.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, from which of the following must the NDIC NOT meet its day-to-day operating expenses?

options.c: The deposit insurance funds held in trust for depositors

questions.explanation: The insurance funds are held in trust for depositors, so running costs come from a separate Operating Fund financed by capital, investment income, approved borrowing and other approved sources. Options A, D and B are all permitted ways of financing operating costs.

questions.question: Which of the following banks did NOT have its licence revoked on 16 January 1998, when the CBN closed 26 banks with the NDIC as liquidator?
questions.explanation: Allstates Trust Bank survived the 1998 closures and only lost its licence in January 2006, when it was one of the banks that failed to meet the N25 billion consolidation requirement. Allied Bank, Amicable Bank and Pan African Bank in options A, B and D were among the 26 banks whose licences were revoked at once in January 1998, the largest single closure in Nigerian banking history.

questions.question: Which of the following is a symptom of bank distress?
questions.explanation: All three are warning signs that a bank is in trouble. Boardroom squabbles point to weak governance, window dressing means making the accounts look healthier than they are, and desperate borrowing, often at high rates in the interbank market, shows the bank is struggling for liquidity. Because options A, B and C are each a symptom, D is the best answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of bank distress?
questions.explanation: Strong management helps a bank avoid distress, so it is not a cause. Macroeconomic instability is an external cause that hurts borrowers and asset values, political interference can push banks into bad lending, and fraud drains a bank's resources directly. That makes options A, B and C genuine causes of distress.

questions.question: At the end of the 2004-2005 banking consolidation exercise, the number of banks in Nigeria fell from 89 to ____
questions.explanation: In July 2004 the CBN required every bank to have at least N25 billion in capital by 31 December 2005, and through mergers and acquisitions the 89 banks were reduced to 25. Option C is close to the number of banks that failed to meet the deadline and lost their licences in January 2006, not the number that remained. The other figures do not match the outcome of the exercise.

questions.question: On 16 January 1998, the Central Bank of Nigeria revoked the licences of ____ banks.
questions.explanation: On 16 January 1998 the CBN revoked the licences of 26 distressed banks in one go, the largest single closure of the 1990s distress era, with the NDIC appointed as liquidator. The other figures are distractors and do not match that closure.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, an insured institution whose capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio had fallen below the minimum prescribed by the CBN was defined as a:
questions.explanation: The 2006 Act used capital adequacy below the CBN minimum as the test for a failing insured institution: it is in trouble but still holds its licence. Option D is wrong because a failed institution is one whose licence has already been withdrawn. A bridge bank (C) is a temporary bank that takes over a failed bank, and a systemically important bank (B) is identified by size and interconnectedness, not weak capital.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, a 'failed insured institution' was one whose:

options.a: Capital adequacy ratio was below the CBN minimum
options.c: Management had been changed by the CBN
options.d: Deposits had fallen for two consecutive years

questions.explanation: A failed insured institution is one whose licence has been withdrawn, so it can no longer operate as a bank. Option A describes a failing institution, which is still licensed but undercapitalised. Options C and D may happen to troubled banks but were not the legal test of failure.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, what was the key difference between a failing and a failed insured institution?

options.a: A failing institution was a microfinance bank; a failed institution was a deposit money bank
options.b: A failing institution had lost its licence; a failed institution was only undercapitalised
options.c: A failing institution was still licensed but undercapitalised; a failed institution had lost its licence
options.d: A failing institution was under CBN control; a failed institution was under NDIC control

questions.explanation: Distress comes before failure: a failing bank has capital below the CBN minimum but still operates, while a failed bank has had its licence withdrawn. Option B simply reverses the two definitions. Options A and D are wrong because the terms depend on capital and licence status, not on the type of bank or which regulator is involved.

questions.question: Effective bank resolution is described as a series of systematic actions designed to end a bank's distressed condition with minimal disruption and:

options.a: By guaranteeing all deposits without any limit
options.c: By keeping the failed bank's management in place
options.d: By passing all losses to insured depositors

questions.explanation: Good resolution ends a bank's distress smoothly while keeping the cost off taxpayers, so losses fall on shareholders and uninsured creditors instead. Option A describes a blanket guarantee, which is costly and encourages moral hazard. Options D and C are the opposite of what resolution tries to do, since insured depositors are protected and the managers who caused the problem are usually removed.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of bank resolution in Nigeria?

options.a: Ensuring continuity of basic banking functions
options.c: Minimising reliance on public sector support
options.d: Protecting the investment of the failed bank's shareholders

questions.explanation: Resolution aims to protect depositors, keep essential banking services running, protect client funds, limit harm to financial stability and reduce reliance on public money. Shareholders are not protected; they are expected to bear losses first. Options A, C and B are all genuine objectives of resolution.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the failure of a bank has a greater impact than the failure of an ordinary commercial business?

options.a: Banks have a low capital-to-assets ratio (high leverage)
options.b: Banks keep most of their assets in cash, so they rarely need to sell assets
options.c: Banks fund themselves heavily with demand deposits
options.d: Banks are closely linked through interbank lending and the payments system

questions.explanation: Banks actually keep only a small share of assets in cash (fractional reserve banking), which is why they may have to sell earning assets to meet withdrawals. Options A, D and C are genuine reasons: high leverage leaves little room for losses, interconnection spreads failure to other banks, and demand deposits create the risk of runs.

questions.question: Because banks lend to and borrow from one another, hold deposits with one another and share the payments clearing system, the failure of one bank can spill over and threaten the whole banking system. This danger is known as:
questions.explanation: Systemic risk is the risk that trouble at one institution spreads through its links with others and endangers the whole system. Credit risk (A) is the risk that a particular borrower will not repay. Moral hazard (D) is the incentive to take more risk when others bear the cost, and interest rate risk (C) comes from changes in interest rates.

questions.question: After rumours of trouble, depositors rush to withdraw from Gamma Bank. With little cash on hand, the bank must sell loans and other hard-to-value assets quickly at heavy discounts to pay them. The losses from such forced sales are called:
questions.explanation: Fire-sale losses arise when a bank must sell opaque or illiquid assets in a hurry for much less than their true value, which can turn a liquidity problem into insolvency. Liquidation dividends (A) are payments made to uninsured depositors and creditors after a bank is closed. Premium rebates (B) are refunds of deposit insurance premiums, and provisioning gains (C) are not the result of forced sales.

questions.question: Why does a low capital-to-assets ratio make a bank more likely to fail when it suffers losses?

options.a: It leaves only a thin cushion of owners' funds to absorb losses before depositors' money is affected
options.b: It forces the bank to hold too much idle cash
options.c: It means the bank has too few depositors to lend to
options.d: It reduces the bank's deposit insurance premium to zero

questions.explanation: Capital is the buffer that absorbs losses; when it is small relative to assets (high leverage), even modest loan losses can wipe it out and leave the bank insolvent. Option B confuses capital with cash holdings. Options C and D have nothing to do with leverage.

questions.question: Causes of bank failure that arise from within the bank itself, such as weak credit policies, insider loans and frauds, are classified as:
questions.explanation: Endogenous causes come from inside the bank: its policies, its operations and the way it is managed. Exogenous causes (C) come from outside the bank, such as the economy or regulation. Options B and A describe problems in the wider system or economy, not internal weaknesses.

questions.question: Which of the following is an endogenous (internal) cause of bank failure?

options.b: Rapid rise in asset prices (boom and burst)

questions.explanation: Connected lending and insider loans are decisions made inside the bank, where directors or related parties borrow on soft terms and often fail to repay. Options B, C and D are exogenous causes because they come from markets, the regulator or the supervisory system rather than from the bank itself.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an endogenous cause of bank failure?
questions.explanation: The macroeconomic environment is outside any single bank's control, so it is an exogenous cause. Frauds and forgeries (D) and ineffective audit (B) are failures in the bank's operations, while credit concentration (A) is a failure of the bank's lending policy.

questions.question: The directors of Delta Bank approve large loans on soft terms, with little collateral, to companies they own. Most of the loans are never repaid. Which cause of distress does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Lending to directors or their related companies on favourable terms is connected (insider) lending, a classic cause of bank distress in Nigeria. Credit concentration (C) means lending too much to one borrower group or sector, whether insiders or not. A loan/deposit mismatch (B) is about maturities, and regulatory change (D) is an external cause.

questions.question: Epsilon Bank lends about 70 percent of its loan book to a handful of oil-marketing companies. When the sector runs into trouble, most of the loans go bad at the same time. Which internal cause of failure does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Credit concentration means putting too large a share of loans into one borrower, group or sector, so a single shock damages much of the portfolio at once. Insider loans (B) involve lending to directors or related parties, which is not stated here. Options D and C are operational and accounting weaknesses unrelated to how the loan book is spread.

questions.question: Zeta Bank funds 10-year mortgage loans mainly with customers' demand deposits that can be withdrawn at any time. When many depositors withdraw together, it cannot pay them. This weakness is called:
questions.explanation: A loan/deposit (maturity) mismatch occurs when long-term loans are financed with short-term or demand funds, so the bank cannot meet withdrawals even if the loans are good. Credit concentration (C) is about lending too much to one sector, frauds (A) involve dishonest acts, and ineffective recovery (B) is failure to collect bad debts.

questions.question: For several years Eta Bank's internal auditors failed to detect that some staff were diverting customers' deposits, and the losses grew until the bank became distressed. Which internal causes of failure are shown?

options.a: Credit concentration combined with loan/deposit mismatch
options.b: Frauds and forgeries combined with ineffective audit
options.c: Major regulatory change combined with weak supervision
options.d: Boom and burst in asset prices combined with external shocks

questions.explanation: Staff diverting deposits is fraud, and the auditors' failure to catch it points to ineffective audit; both are failures in the bank's operations. Option A concerns lending and funding structure, not theft. Options C and D are exogenous causes that come from outside the bank.

questions.question: Theta Bank knows that N8 billion of its loans are unlikely to be repaid, but sets aside only N2 billion against them so that its profit looks higher. This practice is:
questions.explanation: Setting aside less than the expected loan losses is under-provisioning; it inflates profit and capital and hides the bank's true condition. Dipping into reserves (A) means using past retained profits, and postponing accruals (D) means delaying the recording of expenses such as salaries. Credit concentration (C) is about how loans are spread, not how losses are provided for.

questions.question: Kappa Bank continues to book interest as income on loans that have not been serviced for over a year. Apart from overstating profit, why does this practice worsen the bank's condition?

options.a: It automatically cancels the bank's deposit insurance cover
options.b: It forces the CBN to revoke the licence immediately
options.c: It attracts additional tax on income the bank will never receive
options.d: It turns the bad loans into insured deposits

questions.explanation: Recognising uncollectable interest as income makes profit look larger than it is, and the bank then pays tax on money it will never collect, draining real cash. Option A is wrong because insurance cover does not lapse because of an accounting practice. Options D and B are not consequences of this practice.

questions.question: Iota Bank delays recording expenses it has already incurred, such as staff costs and rent, until the next financial year so that this year's results look better. Which cause of bank failure is this?
questions.explanation: Expenses should be recorded in the period in which they are incurred; delaying them overstates current profit and hides weakness. Under-provisioning (D) relates specifically to provisions for bad loans. Laissez-faire credit review (B) and loan/deposit mismatch (C) are lending and funding problems, not expense recording.

questions.question: Under-provisioning for bad loans, booking uncollectable interest as income and postponing expenses all make a distressed bank's accounts look healthier than they really are. Such practices are commonly called:
questions.explanation: Window dressing means presenting financial statements in a way that hides a bank's true weakness, and it is both a cause and a symptom of distress. Options C and A are supervisory approaches used by regulators, and purchase and assumption (B) is a method of resolving a failed bank.

questions.question: Which of the following is an endogenous cause of bank failure arising from a bank's operations?

options.c: A relatively open and undiversified economy
options.d: Type and ease of entry into the market

questions.explanation: Breakdown of a bank's IT systems is an internal operational failure that can disrupt records, payments and controls. Options D, C and A are exogenous causes: they come from market structure, the wider economy and the regulator, not from the bank's own operations.

questions.question: Lambda Bank's bad loans keep piling up because it rarely follows up defaulters, enforces collateral or takes legal action to recover debts. Which internal cause of failure is this?
questions.explanation: Failing to pursue defaulting borrowers means losses that could have been reduced are left to grow, which is ineffective and inadequate recovery. Credit concentration (C) concerns how loans are spread across borrowers. Options D and B are exogenous causes rather than weaknesses in the bank's own recovery effort.

questions.question: Mu Bank's credit department rarely reviews existing loans after disbursement, so loans that start to go bad are noticed only when they are long overdue. Which internal cause of failure does this describe?
questions.explanation: A laissez-faire (hands-off) credit review process fails to monitor loans after they are granted, so problems are caught too late. Insider lending (D) concerns who receives the loans. A weak supervisory framework (A) is a weakness of the regulator, not the bank, and dipping into reserves (B) is an accounting abuse.

questions.question: Weak credit policies, connected lending and insider loans, and credit concentration are grouped together as failures arising from banks':
questions.explanation: These causes all come from how a bank decides to lend, which is its credit and risk policy. Operational failures (D) include fraud, IT failure and ineffective audit, while mismanagement failures (A) are accounting abuses such as under-provisioning. The regulatory environment (C) relates to exogenous causes.

questions.question: Bank failure causes that originate outside the bank, such as an unstable macroeconomy or an asset price bubble, are called:
questions.explanation: Exogenous causes come from the environment in which banks operate, such as the economy, markets, regulation and supervision. Endogenous causes (B) come from inside the bank, and operational (C) and policy (D) failures are both subgroups of endogenous causes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an exogenous cause of bank failure?

options.b: Type and ease of entry into the market

questions.explanation: How easily new banks can enter the industry is set by licensing policy and market structure, so it is outside any individual bank. Options C, A and D are internal weaknesses in staffing, controls and lending judgement, which makes them endogenous causes.

questions.question: After the 1986 Structural Adjustment Programme liberalised bank licensing, the number of banks in Nigeria rose sharply into the early 1990s, stretching supervisory capacity. Which exogenous cause of distress does this illustrate?

options.b: Type and ease of entry into the market
options.d: A relatively open and undiversified economy

questions.explanation: Easy entry let many new banks open quickly, often with weak capital and management, which raised competition and the risk of distress. A rise in asset prices (A) is a market bubble, and credit concentration (C) is an internal lending problem. An open undiversified economy (D) refers to vulnerability to external shocks, not the number of banks.

questions.question: In July 2004 the CBN raised banks' minimum capital to N25 billion, to be met by 31 December 2005, and banks that could not comply lost their licences. For those banks, the new rule is an example of which exogenous cause of failure?

options.b: A relatively open and undiversified economy
options.c: Type and ease of entry into the market

questions.explanation: A sudden, large change in rules, such as a much higher capital requirement, can push weaker banks into failure if they cannot adjust. A rise in asset prices (D) and an open undiversified economy (B) are market and economic causes. Ease of entry (C) refers to lax licensing that lets too many banks in, which is the opposite of this tightening.

questions.question: Suppose property prices in a city rise rapidly for several years and banks lend heavily against land and houses. Prices then collapse, the collateral loses value and many loans go bad. Which exogenous cause of bank failure is this?

options.b: Type and ease of entry into the market
options.c: Rapid rise in asset prices (boom and burst)

questions.explanation: A boom and burst occurs when asset prices climb far above sustainable levels and then crash, destroying the value of collateral and borrowers' wealth. Ease of entry (B) concerns licensing of new banks. Options D and A are internal weaknesses of a bank, not market-wide price movements.

questions.question: A country earns most of its export income from one commodity and imports much of what it consumes. When the world price of that commodity crashes, borrowers default and banks come under pressure. Which exogenous cause is shown?

options.a: A relatively open and undiversified economy susceptible to external shocks
options.b: Type and ease of entry into the market

questions.explanation: An economy that depends on one export and on imports is exposed to shocks from abroad, which then hit borrowers and banks. A weak supervisory framework (C) is about the quality of oversight. Insider lending (D) is an internal cause, and ease of entry (B) concerns licensing.

questions.question: Regulators know that several banks routinely break single-borrower lending limits, but no sanctions are imposed for years. Which exogenous cause of bank failure does this reflect?

options.c: Non-compliance and weak enforcement of regulation

questions.explanation: Rules only protect banks and depositors if they are obeyed and enforced; when breaches go unpunished, risky behaviour spreads. Major regulatory change (B) is about new rules, not failure to enforce existing ones. Options D and A are economic and market causes.

questions.question: High inflation, a sharp fall in the naira and rising interest rates leave many bank borrowers unable to repay their loans. Which broad exogenous cause of bank distress is this?

options.b: Type and ease of entry into the market

questions.explanation: Inflation, exchange rates and interest rates make up the macroeconomic environment, and when it turns hostile, borrowers struggle and banks' assets weaken. Frauds (D) and credit concentration (A) are internal causes. Ease of entry (B) concerns licensing, not economic conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the pre-crisis conditions said to have made banks vulnerable before the global financial crisis?

options.a: A large amount of system-wide liquidity that encouraged excessive risk taking
options.b: Outsourcing of due diligence to rating agencies
options.c: Regulatory gaps that left parts of the financial system under-regulated

questions.explanation: Before the crisis, underwriting standards were poor, not too strict, so loans were granted too easily. Options C, B and A are genuine pre-crisis weaknesses: gaps in regulation, reliance on rating agencies instead of banks' own checks, and abundant liquidity that fuelled risk taking.

questions.question: Before the global financial crisis, weaknesses in banks' risk management were described as only a symptom of a deeper problem. That deeper problem was:

options.a: Fundamental shortcomings in financial institutions' governance
options.d: Deposit insurance coverage that was too low

questions.explanation: Poor risk management reflected poor governance: boards and senior management failed to set and enforce sound risk-taking. Option B is wrong because thin capital and high leverage were the problem, not excess capital. Options C and D were not identified as root causes; regulatory gaps meant too little oversight, not too much.

questions.question: Why can increased competition among banks contribute to bank distress, even though competition is generally good for customers?

options.a: It forces banks to stop accepting deposits
options.b: It can encourage banks to take excessive risks with depositors' funds
options.c: It removes the need for any bank supervision
options.d: It always reduces banks' capital to zero

questions.explanation: Under strong competition banks may chase market share and profits by lending to riskier borrowers or underpricing risk, putting depositors' money in danger. That is why small depositors need protection. Options A, C and D are exaggerations that do not follow from competition.

questions.question: Before the NDIC was established, the government was unwilling to let any bank fail and propped up inefficient banks, especially those owned by state governments. Under the Structural Adjustment Programme, policy shifted towards:

options.a: Banning state governments from owning banks
options.d: Protecting depositors, especially small ones, rather than directly supporting weak banks

questions.explanation: The new approach accepted that weak banks could fail, and focused on protecting depositors, particularly small, less-informed ones, through an explicit deposit insurance scheme. Options B and C would have continued, or widened, unlimited support for banks. Option A was not the policy shift.

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely an early warning sign that a bank is becoming distressed?

options.a: Prompt and accurate submission of regulatory returns
options.b: A steady rise in non-performing loans alongside falling capital
options.d: A steady fall in non-performing loans

questions.explanation: Growing bad loans eat into earnings and capital, and capital erosion is one of the clearest signals that a bank is sliding towards failure. Options C, D and A are signs of a healthier bank: stronger capital, better asset quality and reliable reporting.

questions.question: Nu Bank regularly borrows overnight from other banks at rates well above the market, delays customers' withdrawals and keeps missing its cash reserve requirement. These are symptoms of:
questions.explanation: A bank that must borrow desperately, cannot meet withdrawals on time and falls short of reserve requirements does not have enough liquid funds, which is liquidity distress. Excess liquidity (A) is the opposite situation. Options D and B describe strength or caution, not a cash shortage.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of bank distress?

options.b: Desperate borrowing on the interbank market
options.d: Consistently timely and accurate regulatory returns

questions.explanation: A bank that files timely, accurate returns is showing good governance and controls. Boardroom squabbles (C) point to governance breakdown, window dressing (A) hides losses, and desperate interbank borrowing (B) signals a liquidity shortage, so all three are symptoms of distress.

questions.question: During an on-site examination, NDIC examiners find that Xi Bank's actual loan losses are far larger than those shown in the returns it sent for off-site analysis. Besides the losses themselves, this gap is a warning sign of:

options.a: Effective risk management by the bank

questions.explanation: A wide difference between on-site findings and off-site returns shows the bank's reported data cannot be trusted, which often hides deeper distress. Options B and A are the opposite of what the gap shows. Option C is unrelated to misreporting of loan losses.

questions.question: In the mid-1990s, the CBN and NDIC imposed 'holding actions' on many distressed banks. Holding actions were:

options.a: Payments of insured deposits to depositors
options.b: Sales of failed banks to new investors
options.d: Corrective or self-restructuring measures imposed on distressed banks
