questions.explanation: Holding actions restricted a distressed bank's activities and required it to restructure itself, as an early form of open bank intervention. Option A is deposit payout, which happens after closure. Option B is an acquisition and sale, and option C is the end point of failure rather than a corrective step.

questions.question: When depositors lose confidence in a distressed bank and rush to withdraw their funds at the same time, the event is called:
questions.explanation: A bank run is a sudden wave of withdrawals driven by fear that the bank will fail, and it can bring down even a solvent bank because banks keep only a fraction of deposits in cash. A liquidation dividend (B) is paid after closure. Options A and C are resolution and corrective measures used by the authorities.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a likely consequence of widespread bank distress?

options.a: Increased public confidence in the banking system
options.b: Disruption of credit to businesses and households

questions.explanation: Distress damages confidence rather than increasing it. Uninsured depositors (D) may lose part of their money, fear can spread and trigger runs on other banks (C), and credit to the real economy (B) dries up as banks shrink or close.

questions.question: Mr Okafor had N9 million in a deposit money bank whose licence was revoked in 2025. If the liquidator later pays a liquidation dividend of 40 percent on uninsured deposits, how much does he recover in total under the coverage limits in force since May 2024?
questions.explanation: He first receives the insured N5 million; the uninsured part is N9m - N5m = N4m, and 40 percent of that is N1.6m, giving N6.6m in total. Option B takes 40 percent of the whole N9m and ignores the insured payment. Option D wrongly adds 40 percent of the whole deposit to the N5m, and option A ignores the liquidation dividend.

questions.question: Chioma had N3.2 million in a microfinance bank whose licence was revoked in 2025. Under the coverage limits introduced in May 2024, her insured amount is:
questions.explanation: Since May 2024 microfinance bank depositors are covered up to N2 million, so she receives N2 million as insured deposit and claims the remaining N1.2 million from liquidation dividends. Option A applies the N5 million limit meant for deposit money banks, and option D is the older N200,000 limit. Option C ignores the limit.

questions.question: In December 2025 the CBN revoked the licences of Aso Savings and Loans Plc and Union Homes Savings and Loans Plc, two primary mortgage banks. A depositor with N1.5 million in one of them should receive:

options.a: Only N500,000, the old mortgage bank limit
options.b: The full N1,500,000, because it is within the N2 million limit
options.c: Nothing, because mortgage bank deposits are not insured

questions.explanation: Primary mortgage banks are insured institutions, and since May 2024 their depositors are covered up to N2 million, so a N1.5 million balance is fully protected. Option A uses the pre-2024 limit, and option D is an even older figure. Option C is wrong because PMBs must insure their deposits with the NDIC.

questions.question: Under the resolution cost (AMCON sinking fund) arrangement, the CBN contributes N50 billion a year for 10 years and each bank pays an annual levy on its total assets. When the levy was 0.5 percent, what were the CBN's total 10-year contribution and the annual levy of a bank with total assets of N3 trillion?
questions.explanation: The CBN pays N50bn x 10 = N500bn, and the bank pays 0.5 percent x N3 trillion = N15bn a year. Option B counts only one year of the CBN's contribution. Option D misplaces the decimal (0.05 percent), and option C inflates both figures tenfold.

questions.question: In 1994 the Federal Government promulgated the Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Decree. Its main purpose was to:

options.b: Merge distressed banks with healthy banks
options.c: Speed up recovery of debts owed to failed banks and punish financial malpractice in banks
options.d: Raise the deposit insurance coverage limit

questions.explanation: The decree targeted two problems behind the distress of the 1990s: unpaid loans, often to insiders, and malpractice by bank officials, through special recovery and prosecution powers. Option D concerns coverage, which this decree did not set. Option A is wrong because the NDIC was created in 1988, and option B describes a resolution method, not this law.

questions.question: On 16 January 1998 the CBN revoked the licences of 26 banks at once. What role did the NDIC play for these banks?
questions.explanation: Once the licences were revoked, the NDIC was appointed liquidator to pay insured depositors, realise the banks' assets and pay liquidation dividends. Purchase and assumption (D) was first used only in 2006, and bridge banks (B) came in 2011. The lender of last resort (A) is the CBN, not the NDIC.

questions.question: In July 2004 the CBN required every bank in Nigeria to have a minimum capital base of ____ by 31 December 2005.
questions.explanation: The 2004-2005 consolidation set a minimum capital of N25 billion, which forced mergers and acquisitions and cut the number of banks sharply. Options D, B and A are not the figure set for that exercise.

questions.question: In 2009 a CBN/NDIC special examination of 24 banks found 10 in grave condition. Which of the following was NOT among the problems it identified?

options.c: Excess capital and too little lending

questions.explanation: The examination found the troubled banks weighed down by bad loans, with eroded capital, weak risk management and poor governance; excess capital was the opposite of their condition. Options B, D and A were all genuine findings.

questions.question: Following the 2009 special examination of Nigerian banks, roughly how much was injected into the banks found to be in grave condition?
questions.explanation: About N620 billion was injected in 2009, starting with N400 billion into five banks on 14 August 2009 when their chief executives were removed. Option A is the 1989 accommodation to 10 banks, option C is the CBN's annual contribution to the resolution cost fund, and option D is the 2005 minimum capital figure.

questions.question: On 14 August 2009 the CBN removed the chief executives of five banks and injected N400 billion into them, keeping the banks open. This intervention is best described as:
questions.explanation: The banks kept their licences while the authority replaced management and supplied funds, which is open bank assistance, often called a bailout. Purchase and assumption (B) requires a failed bank's business to pass to another institution. Deposit payoff (D) and liquidation (C) happen only after a bank is closed.

questions.question: In 2010 the CBN revoked the licences of 224 microfinance banks, but 121 of them had their licences restored after capital verification. How many microfinance banks were finally closed?
questions.explanation: The banks finally closed equal those revoked minus those restored: 224 - 121 = 103. Option B is the number restored, option C the number first revoked, and option D wrongly adds the two figures.

questions.question: During the global financial crisis some countries gave blanket guarantees on deposits. Their main aim was to:

options.a: Encourage depositors to move funds abroad
options.b: Maintain depositor confidence and prevent systemic runs

questions.explanation: A blanket guarantee protects deposits beyond the normal limit so that frightened depositors do not rush to withdraw from all banks at once. Option C is the opposite of a blanket guarantee. Options A and D would weaken rather than restore confidence.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT among the deposit insurance policy measures taken in the fall of 2008?

options.a: Introducing or increasing co-insurance for depositors
options.b: Taking steps to ensure timely access to insured deposits
options.d: Extending coverage to a wider range of deposits

questions.explanation: In late 2008 authorities reduced the role of co-insurance, because making depositors bear part of the loss encouraged runs. Options C, B and D were genuine measures taken to strengthen confidence.

questions.question: After the crisis, countries with implicit protection reconsidered explicit schemes. Which country launched explicit deposit insurance on 1 May 2015 with cover of 500,000 yuan?
questions.explanation: China moved from implicit to explicit deposit insurance on 1 May 2015, with cover of 500,000 yuan that protects over 99 percent of depositors. India (A) has had deposit insurance since 1962, Kenya (D) since the 1980s, and Japan (B) does not use the yuan.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the key new measures in deposit insurance introduced after the global financial crisis?

options.a: Higher and more harmonised coverage levels
options.b: Reducing coordination between deposit insurers and other safety-net participants
options.c: Greater convergence of deposit insurance practices across jurisdictions
options.d: Identification and resolution of systemically important financial institutions

questions.explanation: The crisis led to more, not less, information sharing and coordination among deposit insurers, central banks, supervisors and finance ministries. Options D, A and C were all genuine post-crisis reforms.

questions.question: Which of the following was a lesson of the global financial crisis concerning deposit insurance premiums and supervision?

options.a: Premiums should be abolished and replaced by government grants
options.b: Supervision should be reduced to cut costs for banks
options.c: Premium assessment was adjusted towards risk-based pricing, backed by enhanced risk-based supervision
options.d: All banks should pay the same flat premium regardless of risk

questions.explanation: Risk-based premiums, such as Nigeria's Differential Premium Assessment System, make riskier banks pay more, and enhanced risk-based supervision discourages unnecessary risk taking. Option D is the flat-rate approach that risk-based pricing replaces. Options A and B would weaken the system and are not lessons of the crisis.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A series of systematic actions designed to end a bank's distressed condition with minimal disruption and without exposing taxpayers to losses is known as ____
questions.explanation: Bank resolution covers all the actions used to deal with a failing bank in an orderly way, such as purchase and assumption, bridge banks or mergers, with liquidation as the last resort. Option B is narrower: liquidation means closing the bank and selling off its assets, which is only one possible outcome of resolution. Option A describes the troubled condition itself, not the remedy, and consolidation in option D is about mergers to meet capital rules.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: After the CBN revokes the licence of an insured bank in Nigeria, which body is by law appointed as its liquidator?
questions.explanation: Once a bank's licence is revoked, the NDIC becomes its statutory liquidator: it pays insured depositors, sells off the bank's assets and pays liquidation dividends to uninsured depositors and creditors. Option D is tempting because the CBN revokes the licence, but it hands the winding-up to the NDIC. AMCON buys bad loans and has funded bridge banks, and the Ministry of Finance is a part-owner of the NDIC, not a liquidator.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a bank failure resolution option used by the NDIC?
questions.explanation: Realignment is not a recognised failure resolution tool, so it is the odd one out. The NDIC's resolution options include purchase and assumption (option C), where a healthy bank takes over the failed bank's deposits and good assets, paying off insured depositors (option A), and setting up a bridge bank (option D) to keep a failed bank's business running until a buyer is found, as was done with Mainstreet, Keystone and Enterprise banks in 2011.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: The resolution method in which a healthy bank takes over the deposits and some or all of the assets of a failed bank is known as ____
questions.explanation: In a purchase and assumption, a healthy bank buys some or all of the failed bank's assets and assumes its deposit liabilities, so depositors simply become customers of the acquiring bank. Option A, a bail out, means injecting public money to keep the troubled bank itself alive, not handing it to another bank. Options C and D close the bank down: liquidation sells off its assets, and a payout reimburses insured depositors directly without any bank taking over the business.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Effective failure resolution, as practised by the NDIC, is best described as:

options.a: A series of systematic actions designed to end a bank's distressed condition with minimal disruption
options.b: A single action by shareholders to raise new capital
options.c: The immediate liquidation of every distressed bank
options.d: A government guarantee of all bank liabilities

questions.explanation: Resolution is a planned set of steps aimed at ending a bank's distress while limiting disruption to the financial system and avoiding losses to taxpayers. Option C is wrong because liquidation is only one tool and usually the last resort. Option B describes just one possible step, and option D is a blanket guarantee, which shifts losses to taxpayers rather than resolving the bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of an effective failure-resolution process?

options.b: Ensure depositors are reimbursed promptly and accurately
options.c: Maximize recoveries on the failed bank's assets
options.d: Protect shareholders of the failed bank from any loss

questions.explanation: In a bank failure, shareholders are the owners who took the risk, so they are expected to bear losses first; shielding them would reward bad management and create moral hazard. Options A, B and C are all genuine aims of good resolution: the insurer honours its guarantee, depositors get paid quickly and correctly, and asset recoveries are maximized to cut the cost of the failure.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Broadly, bank failure resolution methods are grouped into which two categories?

options.d: Ex ante and ex post resolution

questions.explanation: Resolution methods are grouped by whether the bank keeps operating: open-bank methods (such as financial assistance or takeover of management) keep it running, while closed-bank methods (such as purchase and assumption, bridge banks or deposit payout and liquidation) follow licence revocation. Option A describes types of deposit insurance, not resolution. Option C names deposit insurer mandates, and option D refers to ways of funding a deposit insurance scheme.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a failure resolution option available to the NDIC?
questions.explanation: Lending to banks as a lender of last resort is a CBN power, used to ease temporary liquidity shortages, so it is not one of the NDIC's own resolution tools. Options A, C and D are all NDIC resolution options: it can assist a bank while it stays open, pay insured depositors when a bank is closed, or arrange for a healthy bank to buy assets and assume deposits of a failed one.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of an effective bank failure resolution regime in Nigeria?

options.a: Maximising the returns of the failed bank's shareholders
options.b: Minimising reliance on public sector support
options.c: Ensuring continuity of basic banking functions

questions.explanation: Resolution aims to protect depositors and the financial system, not to secure profits for the owners whose bank has failed; shareholders are expected to bear losses first. Options B, C and D are all genuine resolution objectives, together with protecting depositors and limiting harm to financial stability.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the stated objectives of bank failure resolution in Nigeria?

options.a: Minimising adverse effects on banking and financial system stability
options.b: Keeping the failed bank's management in office
options.c: Ensuring that no bank is ever closed
options.d: Guaranteeing every creditor of the failed bank in full

questions.explanation: Resolution seeks to limit the damage a failure does to the wider banking and financial system. Option D goes beyond deposit insurance, which protects insured depositors only up to a limit, while option B is wrong because those who mismanaged the bank are usually removed. Option C is wrong since closure and liquidation remain valid resolution options.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A well-designed resolution regime tries to deal with a failing bank without exposing which group to losses?

options.a: Uninsured creditors of the failed bank

questions.explanation: Good resolution keeps public money out of the picture, so taxpayers should not end up paying for a bank's failure. Options A and D are exactly the parties expected to absorb losses in order of seniority, and option C describes people who may even be held responsible for the failure.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Bank failures have a greater impact than failures of ordinary businesses. Which of the following is NOT a reason for this?

options.a: Banks hold a low cash-to-assets ratio under fractional reserve banking
options.b: Banks are closely linked through interbank lending and payments
options.c: Banks generally have a high capital-to-assets ratio
options.d: Banks have a high share of demand deposits and short-term debt

questions.explanation: Banks actually have a LOW capital-to-assets ratio (high leverage), which leaves little room to absorb losses, so a high ratio would make them safer, not riskier. Option A explains why banks may have to sell earning assets to pay depositors, option D explains their exposure to runs, and option B explains how one failure spreads to others.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the FSB Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes, resolution authorities should be able to allocate the losses of a non-viable institution to:

options.a: The deposit insurer and central bank in equal shares
options.b: Insured depositors before any other party
options.c: Shareholders and unsecured or uninsured creditors in order of seniority

questions.explanation: The FSB framework wants losses borne first by the owners and then by unsecured or uninsured creditors, following their legal ranking. Option D is exactly what the framework tries to avoid, option B reverses the protection given to insured depositors, and option A would shift private losses onto public safety-net bodies.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the FSB Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions?
questions.explanation: Risk-based premiums are a funding design feature of deposit insurance systems, not one of the twelve FSB Key Attributes. Options B, C and D all appear on the FSB list, alongside items such as scope, resolution authority, resolution powers and safeguards.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: How many key attributes are listed in the FSB Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions?
questions.explanation: The FSB framework lists twelve key attributes, from scope and resolution authority through to access to information and information sharing. Options A and B are the numbers of IADI Core Principles for deposit insurance in the 2014 and 2025 versions, which is a common mix-up, and option C is simply too few.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: The FSB Key Attributes are mainly designed to let authorities manage the failure of which type of institution without severe disruption or use of public funds?

options.a: Large, complex and internationally active financial institutions

questions.explanation: The FSB framework targets big, complicated, cross-border financial firms whose failure could cause severe disruption, aiming to resolve them without taxpayer support. Options B, C and D wrongly restrict the framework to small or narrow groups that are not its main focus.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which FSB Key Attribute requires authorities to regularly check whether the resolution strategy for a firm is feasible and credible?
questions.explanation: Resolvability assessments test whether a firm could actually be resolved under the chosen strategy, and the framework expects these feasibility checks to be reviewed regularly. Option C protects creditors' rights during resolution, option D concerns how financial contracts are treated, and option B deals with financing a firm while it is being resolved.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which FSB Key Attribute deals with agreements between home and host authorities on how a particular cross-border financial firm will be resolved?
questions.explanation: Institution-specific cross-border cooperation agreements set out how authorities in different countries will work together on one named firm. Option C defines which institutions the regime covers, option D is about having a designated body with resolution powers, and option B concerns protections for creditors and counterparties.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In Nigeria, which body shares bank failure resolution responsibility with the NDIC?
questions.explanation: The NDIC resolves failing banks together with the CBN, which licenses banks and acts as lender of last resort. The SEC regulates capital markets, NAICOM regulates insurance companies and the CAC registers companies, so options A, B and C do not resolve failing banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following resolution tools belongs to the NDIC rather than to the CBN or AMCON?
questions.explanation: The NDIC has the power to set up and run a bridge bank to take over a failed bank's business. Option A is the CBN's role, option B is AMCON's mandate, and option D is done by the CBN, after which the NDIC steps in as liquidator.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A solvent Nigerian bank faces a sudden, temporary cash shortage and obtains short-term funding from the CBN to tide it over. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Lending to a solvent bank facing temporary liquidity pressure is the CBN's lender of last resort role. Options A and C involve transferring a failed bank's business to another entity, and option D is the reimbursement of insured depositors after closure.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In Nigeria's bank resolution framework, the main resolution role of the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) is to:

options.a: Act as lender of last resort to solvent banks
options.b: Revoke the licences of insolvent banks
options.c: Pay insured depositors of closed banks
options.d: Purchase non-performing loans and recapitalise distressed banks

questions.explanation: AMCON was set up to buy bad loans from banks and inject capital into technically insolvent banks. Option C is the NDIC's deposit guarantee role, while options A and B are functions of the CBN.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: AMCON, which bought non-performing loans and recapitalised distressed Nigerian banks, was established by an Act in:
questions.explanation: AMCON was created by the AMCON Act of 2010 in response to the 2009 banking crisis. Option D is the year banks that failed consolidation were resolved, option C is when the three bridge banks were set up, and option A is when Skye Bank was resolved through Polaris Bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, an insured institution whose licence has been withdrawn is described as a:
questions.explanation: Under the 2006 Act a 'failed' insured institution is one whose licence has been withdrawn. Option B is the term for a bank whose capital ratio has fallen below the CBN minimum but which still holds its licence, while options A and D were not the statutory terms for a bank that has lost its licence.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, Bank Q still holds its licence but its capital adequacy ratio has fallen below the minimum prescribed by the CBN. Bank Q is a:
questions.explanation: A 'failing' insured institution under the 2006 Act is one whose capital adequacy ratio is below the CBN minimum while it is still licensed. Option C applies only once the licence has been withdrawn, option B follows licence revocation, and option A is a temporary bank set up by the deposit insurer.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which resolution option helps a distressed bank while it remains open and licensed, for example through financial assistance, holding actions or a takeover of its management?
questions.explanation: Open bank assistance supports a troubled bank without closing it, so it keeps its licence and continues serving customers. Option A transfers a failed bank's business to another institution, while options B and C follow the closure of the bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In 1989 the NDIC granted accommodation facilities of N2.3 billion to 10 banks that had serious liquidity problems. This was an example of:

options.b: Open bank assistance through financial assistance

questions.explanation: The 1989 facilities were money given to banks that stayed open, which is financial assistance under open bank assistance. Options A and D involve moving a failed bank's assets and liabilities to another entity, and option C involves closing the banks, which did not happen here.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Corrective or self-restructuring measures imposed on a distressed bank, such as restrictions on its activities until it improves, are called:
questions.explanation: Holding actions are restrictive, corrective measures placed on a distressed bank so it can restructure while still open. Option D is a payment to uninsured depositors and creditors after closure, option A is a temporary bank run by the deposit insurer, and option C moves insured deposits of a closed bank to another bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Regulators order distressed Bank R to stop opening new branches, stop granting new loans and cut its expenses until it restructures, while it continues to serve customers. Which resolution measure is this?
questions.explanation: Restricting a bank's activities while it stays open so it can put its house in order is a holding action, a form of open bank assistance. Options A and D transfer the bank's business to another institution, and option B applies only after a bank is closed.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a form of open bank assistance?

options.c: Takeover of management and control by CBN/NDIC
options.d: Financial assistance to an illiquid bank

questions.explanation: A deposit payoff happens after a bank has been closed, so it is not open bank assistance. Options B, C and D are all ways of helping or controlling a distressed bank while it stays open.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: When the NDIC or CBN removes the board and management of a distressed bank and runs the bank itself to safeguard its assets, the measure is known as:
questions.explanation: Taking over management and control means the regulators run the distressed bank directly while it remains open, which protects its assets from further abuse. Option B involves another bank buying assets and assuming liabilities, and options C and D follow closure of the bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In 2009, after a special examination of 24 banks, the authorities injected about N620 billion into troubled banks as loan capital and liquidity support and guaranteed their interbank takings. Which resolution approach was this?

options.c: A government bailout through the CBN

questions.explanation: Injecting public money and giving guarantees to keep troubled banks open is a bailout, carried out through the CBN. Option D would have closed the banks, option A came later in 2011 for three banks that could not recapitalise, and option B imposes losses on creditors rather than injecting public funds.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: What is the key difference between a bailout and a bail-in?

options.a: A bailout protects only shareholders while a bail-in protects only insured depositors
options.b: A bailout closes the bank while a bail-in always sells it to a foreign bank
options.c: A bailout uses outside, often public, funds while a bail-in imposes losses on the bank's shareholders and creditors
options.d: A bailout is done only by the deposit insurer while a bail-in is done only by courts

questions.explanation: In a bailout, money from outside the bank, usually the government, is injected to rescue it, whereas a bail-in writes down or converts claims of shareholders and unsecured creditors to absorb losses. Options A, B and D misdescribe both tools, and none of them captures the question of who bears the loss.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A resolution measure in which a failing bank's losses are absorbed by writing down or converting the claims of its shareholders and unsecured creditors, instead of using public funds, is called:
questions.explanation: A bail-in recapitalises a failing bank from within by making its owners and unsecured creditors absorb losses. Option A is the opposite approach, rescuing the bank with outside money, option B restricts a distressed bank's activities, and option D reimburses insured depositors after closure.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: The 2009 public assurance that 'no bank would be allowed to fail', together with large public rescues, raises which concern for future bank behaviour?
questions.explanation: When bankers expect to be rescued, they have an incentive to take more risk because others will bear the cost, which is moral hazard. Option C is the healthy pressure from depositors and creditors that such assurances actually weaken, while options B and D are unrelated to rescue expectations.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A resolution method in which a healthy financial institution or a group of investors buys some or all of the assets and assumes some or all of the obligations of a failed institution is called:
questions.explanation: Purchase and assumption (P&A) transfers a failed bank's assets and liabilities, especially deposits, to a healthy acquirer. Option B helps a bank while it remains open, option A restricts a distressed bank's activities, and option D simply pays insured depositors without any acquirer taking over the business.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In a purchase and assumption transaction, the acquiring institution:

options.a: Pays insured depositors in cash and takes no assets
options.b: Buys some or all of the failed bank's assets and assumes some or all of its liabilities
options.c: Lends money to the failed bank so that it can stay open
options.d: Runs the failed bank temporarily on behalf of the deposit insurer

questions.explanation: In P&A a healthy bank or investor group purchases assets and assumes obligations, usually including deposits, of the failed bank. Option C describes open bank assistance or lender of last resort lending, option A describes a deposit payoff, and option D describes a bridge bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Purchase and assumption was first used in Nigeria in 2006 to resolve banks that:

options.a: Were found in grave condition in the 2009 special examination
options.b: Were later taken over by AMCON as bridge banks
options.c: Received accommodation facilities from the NDIC in 1989
options.d: Failed to meet the N25 billion minimum capital requirement of the banking consolidation

questions.explanation: The 2004-2005 consolidation required banks to have N25 billion capital, and in 2006 P&A was used to resolve those that failed to meet it. Option C refers to open bank assistance in 1989, while options A and B relate to the 2009 crisis and the 2011 bridge banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason the NDIC adopted purchase and assumption for banks that failed the 2005 consolidation?

options.a: To encourage depositors to build relationships with the acquiring banks
options.b: To allow the failed banks' shareholders to keep control of their banks
options.c: To keep banking services running in the failed banks' premises
options.d: To give depositors easy access to their funds without disruption

questions.explanation: P&A moves the failed bank's business to an acquirer, so the old shareholders lose control rather than keep it. Options A, C and D are the stated benefits: easy access to funds, continuity of service in the same premises, and promoting banking relationships with the acquiring bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: How does purchase and assumption differ from open bank assistance?

options.a: In P&A the failed bank's business passes to an acquirer, while in open bank assistance the troubled bank itself stays open
options.b: In P&A the deposit insurer lends to the bank, while open bank assistance closes it
options.c: In P&A depositors lose all funds, while open bank assistance pays them in full
options.d: In P&A the bank keeps its management, while open bank assistance replaces its owners with AMCON

questions.explanation: Open bank assistance supports a distressed bank while it continues to operate, whereas P&A follows failure and transfers assets and liabilities to a healthy institution. Option B reverses the two methods, option C is wrong because P&A is designed to protect depositors, and option D is not how either method works.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: From a depositor's point of view, why is purchase and assumption usually less disruptive than a deposit payoff?

options.a: Depositors receive payments above the coverage limit from the deposit insurer
options.b: The failed bank's shareholders guarantee all deposits personally
options.c: Depositors receive liquidation dividends before insured payments
options.d: Deposits move to the acquiring bank, so customers keep banking without waiting for payment from the insurer

questions.explanation: In P&A the acquirer assumes the deposits, so customers continue banking, often in the same premises, with no break in service. Option A is wrong because coverage limits still apply to insurer payments, option B has no basis, and option C reverses the normal order in which insured sums are paid first.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A temporary bank set up and operated by the deposit insurer to acquire the assets and assume the liabilities of a failed bank until a final resolution can be achieved is called a:
questions.explanation: A bridge bank is a temporary institution run by the deposit insurer that keeps a failed bank's business going until a buyer or permanent solution is found. Option B only helps pay depositors on the insurer's behalf, option D is a healthy permanent buyer in a P&A, and option A provides services to other banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which word best captures the intended life of a bridge bank?
questions.explanation: A bridge bank is meant to be temporary, bridging the gap until the failed bank's business can be sold or otherwise finally resolved. Option C is the opposite of its purpose, and options A and D describe types of arrangements or ownership unrelated to how a bridge bank works.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, a bridge bank was to last for how long from the date of its licensing, before any extension?
questions.explanation: Under the 2006 Act a bridge bank had an initial life of two years, which could be extended by up to three one-year periods. Option A is far too long for a temporary bank, option D is too short, and option B is the maximum reached only if all three extensions were granted.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, a bridge bank lasted two years from licensing and could be extended by up to three one-year periods. What was the maximum total life of a bridge bank?
questions.explanation: The initial two years plus three possible one-year extensions gives 2 + 3 = 5 years. Option B ignores the extensions, option D counts only the extensions, and option C wrongly adds an extra year.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, which section gave the NDIC power to establish a bridge bank?
questions.explanation: Section 39 of the 2006 Act provided for bridge banks and was the basis for the 2011 bridge banks. Options B, C and D are other sections of the Act that deal with different matters.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In August 2011, which bridge bank was set up by the NDIC to take over the business of the failed Bank PHB?
questions.explanation: Keystone Bank was the bridge bank for Bank PHB. Option A took over Afribank, option C took over Spring Bank, and option B was the 2018 bridge bank for Skye Bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Why did the NDIC set up bridge banks for Afribank, Bank PHB and Spring Bank in 2011?

options.a: They had voluntarily asked to be wound up by their shareholders
options.b: They had been sold to foreign investors who later withdrew
options.c: They could not recapitalise, merge or find an acquirer by the September 30, 2011 deadline
options.d: They had refused to pay their deposit insurance premiums

questions.explanation: The three banks were among those found in grave condition in 2009 and failed to recapitalise, merge or find a buyer by the 30 September 2011 deadline, so a bridge bank was used. Options A, B and D are not the reasons given for these resolutions.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason for adopting the bridge bank option for the three troubled banks in 2011?

options.a: The banks' shareholders had injected enough fresh capital
options.b: The banks had attractive franchises that deterioration would make harder to sell
options.c: Outright liquidation would have had dire consequences for stakeholders
options.d: Continuity of banking services would protect depositors and confidence

questions.explanation: If the shareholders had recapitalised the banks, there would have been no need for a bridge bank at all; the banks failed precisely because they could not recapitalise. Options B, C and D are the reasons given: preserving franchise value, protecting depositors through continuity, and avoiding the harm of outright liquidation.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In 2018 the CBN revoked the licence of Skye Bank Plc, and a new bank took over all its assets and liabilities so customers kept operating their accounts and over 6,000 jobs were saved. Which resolution option was used?
questions.explanation: Polaris Bank was set up as a bridge bank to take over Skye Bank's entire assets and liabilities, keeping services running. Option C would have closed the bank and paid insured depositors only, option B applies while the original bank is still licensed, and option A would have transferred only insured deposits.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Since a bridge bank is temporary, how does its life normally end?

options.a: Its business is sold to, or merged with, a private acquirer as the final resolution
options.b: It is converted into the deposit insurance fund
options.c: It automatically becomes a permanent government-owned bank
options.d: Its depositors are paid off and it is renamed an agent bank

questions.explanation: A bridge bank holds the failed bank's business only until a final resolution, usually a sale to investors; Polaris Bank, for example, was eventually sold to private investors (completed in 2022). Option C contradicts its temporary nature, and options B and D do not describe how bridge banks are wound up.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: How does a bridge bank differ from a purchase and assumption transaction?

options.a: A bridge bank is a temporary bank run by the deposit insurer, while P&A transfers the business to an existing healthy acquirer
options.b: A bridge bank is used only for microfinance banks, while P&A is used only for large banks
options.c: A bridge bank pays only insured deposits, while P&A pays only uninsured deposits
options.d: A bridge bank is created by shareholders, while P&A is ordered by the courts

questions.explanation: A bridge bank is set up and operated by the deposit insurer as a stopgap when no buyer is ready, whereas in P&A a healthy institution or investor group takes over immediately. Options B, C and D invent restrictions that do not exist for either method.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: When regulators arrange for a healthy bank to acquire a distressed bank and support the deal with capital injections, the resolution method is called:
questions.explanation: An assisted merger is an acquisition of a weak bank by a stronger one, facilitated and financially supported by the authorities. Option D pays insured depositors after closure, option A restricts a bank's activities while it stays open, and option C winds the bank up.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In the 2011 assisted mergers in Nigeria, Intercontinental Bank was acquired by:
questions.explanation: Access Bank acquired Intercontinental Bank in the 2011 assisted mergers, with AMCON providing capital injection. Option D acquired Oceanic Bank, option A acquired Finbank, and option C acquired Equitorial Trust Bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In 2011, AMCON injected capital into the troubled Oceanic Bank so that Ecobank could acquire it. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Regulators facilitated Ecobank's acquisition of Oceanic Bank with AMCON capital support, which is an assisted merger. Option B would involve a temporary NDIC-run bank, option A would close the bank and pay insured depositors, and option D only restricts a bank's activities.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: When a failed bank is closed and the deposit insurer directly pays each insured depositor up to the coverage limit, the method is called:
questions.explanation: In a deposit payoff the insurer works out each depositor's insured amount and pays it directly, while the failed bank's assets stay with the liquidator. Options A and B transfer the bank's business to another institution, and option C keeps the troubled bank open.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A resolution method in which the insured deposits of a closed bank are moved to a healthy agent bank, which then pays the depositors or opens new accounts for them, is called:
questions.explanation: In an insured deposit transfer only the insured deposits are moved to an agent bank that makes them available to depositors. Option A usually involves the acquirer buying assets and assuming a wider set of liabilities, option C applies to a bank that is still open, and option D combines a weak bank with a healthy one.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: What is the main difference between a straight deposit payoff and an insured deposit transfer?

options.a: A payoff is done by the CBN, while a transfer is done by AMCON
options.b: A payoff covers uninsured deposits, while a transfer covers only insured deposits
options.c: A payoff keeps the failed bank open, while a transfer closes it
options.d: In a payoff the insurer pays depositors directly, while in a transfer the insured deposits are moved to another bank for depositors

questions.explanation: Both methods follow closure and protect only insured deposits; the difference is that in a payoff the insurer pays each depositor itself, while in a transfer the insured balances are placed in a healthy bank. Option B is wrong because neither pays uninsured sums from the insurance fund, option C is wrong because both apply to closed banks, and option A names the wrong bodies.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: How does an insured deposit transfer differ from a purchase and assumption?

options.a: An insured deposit transfer is a form of lender of last resort, while P&A is a form of bail-in
options.b: An insured deposit transfer moves only insured deposits, while in P&A the acquirer buys assets and assumes a wider set of liabilities
options.c: An insured deposit transfer keeps the failed bank open, while P&A closes it
options.d: An insured deposit transfer pays shareholders first, while P&A pays depositors first

questions.explanation: In an insured deposit transfer the healthy bank only takes the insured deposits to pay out or hold for customers, whereas in P&A it purchases assets and assumes liabilities of the failed bank. Option C is wrong since both follow closure, option A confuses the methods with unrelated tools, and option D reverses the priority of depositors over shareholders.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In Nigeria's resolution framework, liquidation of a failed bank is regarded as:

options.a: The last option, used when all other resolution options have failed
options.b: The first option, applied as soon as a bank shows any weakness
options.c: A form of open bank assistance granted by the CBN
options.d: An option reserved for profitable banks wishing to exit

questions.explanation: The NDIC and CBN treat liquidation as a last resort after other options such as open bank assistance, P&A or bridge banks have been tried in vain. Option B reverses this, option D describes a voluntary exit rather than resolution of a failed bank, and option C is wrong because liquidation closes the bank.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: The liquidation of a failed bank in Nigeria aims at an orderly and efficient closure that ensures:

options.a: Continued operation of the failed bank under its old management
options.b: Transfer of the failed bank's losses to taxpayers
options.c: Full repayment of shareholders before any depositor
options.d: Little or no disruption to the banking system and cost-effective realisation of assets

questions.explanation: Liquidation seeks an orderly closure with minimal disruption, cost-effective sale of assets and settlement of claims of uninsured depositors, creditors and, where possible, shareholders. Option C reverses the order of payment, option A contradicts closure, and option B goes against a key aim of resolution.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the bank failure resolution options that have been used in Nigeria?

options.d: Nationalisation of all banks by the Ministry of Finance

questions.explanation: Nigeria has not resolved failing banks by nationalising the whole banking system. Options A, B and C have all been used, alongside open bank assistance and deposit payoff with liquidation.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: On 16 January 1998 the CBN revoked the licences of 26 banks at once and the NDIC was appointed to wind them up and pay their depositors. Which resolution option was applied to these banks?
questions.explanation: The 1998 banks lost their licences and were wound up by the NDIC as liquidator, with insured depositors paid off. Option D would have kept their business running through a temporary bank, option B would have combined them with healthy banks, and option A applies only to banks that remain open.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Skye Bank (2018) and Heritage Bank (2024) both had their licences revoked by the CBN. How were they resolved?

options.a: Both through liquidation by the NDIC
options.b: Both through bridge banks set up by AMCON
options.c: Skye Bank through liquidation; Heritage Bank through an assisted merger
options.d: Skye Bank through a bridge bank (Polaris Bank); Heritage Bank through liquidation by the NDIC

questions.explanation: Skye Bank's business was moved to Polaris Bank, a bridge bank, while Heritage Bank was placed in liquidation with the NDIC as liquidator and insured depositors paid off. Options A and B wrongly treat the two cases as the same, and option C reverses and misnames the methods.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: As at September 2024, the NDIC had liquidated 651 failed institutions. Which category made up the largest number?
questions.explanation: Of the 651 institutions liquidated by September 2024, 546 were microfinance banks, compared with 55 primary mortgage banks and 50 deposit money banks. Options B and D are much smaller groups, and option A did not feature in that total.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: The rule that a deposit insurer should choose the resolution option that costs its fund the least, compared with all alternatives including liquidation, is known as the:
questions.explanation: The least-cost principle compares the expected cost of each resolution option and selects the cheapest for the insurance fund. Option D relates to insuring each beneficiary of a pooled account, option B is about sharing proceeds in proportion to claims, and option A is the insurer stepping into depositors' shoes after paying them.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 2014 IADI Core Principles, a resolution regime should include at least one resolution option whose cost to the deposit insurer is lower than that of:

options.a: Merging the bank with a healthy acquirer
options.b: Granting the bank a lender of last resort loan
options.c: Paying out insured depositors and liquidating the bank
options.d: Keeping the bank open with holding actions

questions.explanation: IADI uses the cost of liquidation, meaning paying out insured depositors and winding up the bank, as the benchmark that at least one other resolution method should beat. Options A, B and D are themselves alternative tools, not the benchmark used for the least-cost comparison.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A failed bank has insured deposits of N40 billion. The NDIC estimates: deposit payoff would cost N40 billion with expected recoveries of N25 billion from the estate; a P&A would require the NDIC to pay the acquirer N12 billion; a bridge bank would cost N18 billion; and open bank assistance would cost N20 billion. Under the least-cost principle, which option should be chosen?
questions.explanation: The net cost of the payoff is N40bn - N25bn = N15bn, so the options cost N15bn, N12bn, N18bn and N20bn, and P&A at N12bn is cheapest. Option C looks cheapest only if you forget it costs N15bn after recoveries, and options A and D are more expensive.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: When a bank fails, the NDIC pays insured deposits of N8 billion and expects to recover 65% of that amount from the liquidation estate through its subrogated claim. What is the NDIC's expected net cost of the payoff?
questions.explanation: Net cost equals the amount paid minus expected recoveries: N8bn - (65% x N8bn) = N8bn - N5.2bn = N2.8bn. Option C is the amount recovered, not the cost, option B ignores recoveries entirely, and option A wrongly adds the recovery to the payout.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which event formally starts the liquidation of a failed deposit money bank in Nigeria?

options.a: Revocation of the bank's licence by the CBN
options.b: A court order obtained by the bank's shareholders
options.c: Expiry of the bank's deposit insurance premium
options.d: A vote by the bank's depositors

questions.explanation: Liquidation follows once the CBN revokes the bank's licence, after which the NDIC acts as liquidator. Option B is wrong because the bank's owners do not trigger it, and they often challenge revocations in court instead, while options C and D are not the legal trigger.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, who acts as liquidator of an insured bank whose licence has been revoked by the CBN?

options.a: A liquidator elected by the shareholders

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act names the NDIC as liquidator of failed insured institutions, as it did for Heritage Bank in 2024. Option B revokes the licence but does not wind up the bank, option C buys bad loans and recapitalises banks, and option A reflects ordinary company winding-up, which does not apply to failed banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the winding up of a failed insured bank follows the NDIC Act rather than the general winding-up rules of which law?
questions.explanation: Section 56 of the NDIC Act 2023 disapplies the winding-up provisions of CAMA 2020 for banks, so liquidation is run under the NDIC Act. Option C governs the central bank, option B created AMCON, and option D dealt with recovering debts owed to failed banks rather than the winding-up rules.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct order of the main steps in the liquidation of a failed bank in Nigeria?

options.a: Sale of assets; liquidation dividends; licence revocation; NDIC appointed liquidator; payment of insured deposits
options.b: Licence revocation; NDIC appointed liquidator; verification and payment of insured deposits; sale of assets and liquidation dividends; closure
options.c: Verification of claims; licence revocation; closure; liquidation dividends; payment of insured deposits
options.d: NDIC appointed liquidator; sale of assets; licence revocation; payment of insured deposits; closure

questions.explanation: The CBN first revokes the licence, the NDIC takes over as liquidator, verifies claims and pays insured sums, then realises the assets to pay liquidation dividends before the estate is finally closed. Options A, C and D each put a step out of place, for example selling assets or appointing the liquidator before the licence has been revoked.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: During liquidation, the stage at which the NDIC checks each depositor's identity and balance against the failed bank's records before paying is called:
questions.explanation: Verification confirms who the depositors are and how much each is owed, so that only valid claims are paid; insured sums are paid to verified depositors. Option D is the sale of the failed bank's assets, option B comes later once assets have been sold, and option C relates to charging premiums to insured banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason the NDIC has struggled to settle insured deposit claims promptly in some failed banks?

options.a: Poor state of the records of many closed banks
options.b: Banks that stopped operating long before their licences were revoked
options.c: Too much accurate and up-to-date information in the failed banks' records
options.d: Banks that were not fully computerised and had wide branch networks

questions.explanation: Delays came from poor or missing records, not from having too much accurate information. Options A, B and D are genuine causes: bad records, long gaps before revocation, and manual systems spread over many branches, such as the 26 banks closed in 1998 with about 342 branches.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: When the NDIC pays the insured deposits of a failed deposit money bank under the NDIC Act 2023, the money comes from:

options.a: The failed bank's shareholders' fresh capital
options.b: CBN lender of last resort facilities
options.c: The Deposit Insurance Fund built from premiums

questions.explanation: Insured deposits of DMBs are paid from the Deposit Insurance Fund, which is held in trust for depositors and built from premiums paid by insured banks. Option D meets the NDIC's running costs and is kept separate, option A is not available once a bank has failed, and option B is a liquidity loan to solvent banks.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: After paying insured depositors of a failed bank, the NDIC takes over their rights to claim that amount from the liquidation estate. This is called:
questions.explanation: Subrogation means the insurer steps into the shoes of the insured depositors it has paid and recovers from the failed bank's estate. Option A is offsetting a depositor's balance against a debt, option C insures each beneficiary of a pooled account, and option B imposes losses on shareholders and creditors.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Pro rata payments made to uninsured depositors and other creditors as the assets of a failed bank are sold are called:
questions.explanation: Liquidation dividends are shares of the proceeds from selling a failed bank's assets, paid to uninsured depositors and creditors in proportion to their claims. Option C comes from the insurance fund up to the coverage limit, option D is a refund of premiums to insured banks, and option B is assistance to banks still operating.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Liquidation dividends are paid to uninsured depositors 'on a pro rata basis'. This means each depositor receives:

options.a: The same naira amount regardless of the size of the claim
options.b: The same percentage of his or her outstanding claim as every other depositor in the class
options.c: Payment in order of who filed a claim first
options.d: Payment only if the claim is below the coverage limit

questions.explanation: Pro rata means in proportion, so if a 40% dividend is declared every uninsured depositor receives 40% of what is owed to him or her. Option A ignores claim size, option C describes first-come payment, and option D confuses dividends with insured payments.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, how do deposit liabilities rank when a failed bank is liquidated?

options.a: They are paid only after liquidation expenses and taxes
options.b: They rank equally with shareholders' capital
options.c: They rank after all unsecured creditors
options.d: They have priority over all other liabilities

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act gives deposit liabilities priority over all other liabilities of the failed bank, so depositors are paid ahead of other creditors. Options A, B and C all place depositors lower than the law does, and shareholders in particular rank last.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In the liquidation of a failed bank, which group is paid only if something remains after depositors and creditors have been settled?
questions.explanation: Shareholders are the owners and residual claimants, so they receive something only where possible, after depositors and creditors. Options A and C rank ahead because deposit liabilities have priority, and option D is also settled before shareholders.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A liquidator announces a 'final liquidation dividend of 100%' for a closed bank. What does this mean for its uninsured depositors?

options.a: They have received only the insured portion of their deposits
options.b: They have recovered the full amount of their deposits
options.c: They must pay back 100% of any loans before receiving anything
options.d: They will receive nothing because assets were exhausted

questions.explanation: A 100% final dividend means the sale of the bank's assets was enough to repay depositors' claims in full. Option A describes the insured payment only, option D is the opposite outcome, and option C confuses dividends with loan repayment.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Mrs Bello has N7.5 million in a single savings account with a deposit money bank whose licence is revoked in 2025. With the NDIC coverage limit for DMBs of N5 million (set in May 2024), how much will the NDIC pay her as insured deposit?
questions.explanation: Insured payment is the smaller of the balance and the coverage limit, so Mrs Bello receives N5m from the NDIC. Option B ignores the limit, option A is her uninsured balance, which she can recover only through liquidation dividends, and option C is the limit for MFBs, PMBs and PSBs, not DMBs.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Mrs Bello had N7.5 million in a deposit money bank that failed in 2025 and received the N5 million insured amount (May 2024 DMB limit). The liquidator later declares a total liquidation dividend of 40% on uninsured deposits. How much does she recover in total?
questions.explanation: Her uninsured balance is N7.5m - N5m = N2.5m, and 40% of that is N1.0m, so her total recovery is N5m + N1m = N6m. Option C ignores the dividend, option B wrongly applies 40% to the whole N7.5m and adds it to N5m, and option D is just 40% of N7.5m.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Mr Okafor has N3.2 million in a microfinance bank whose licence is revoked in 2025. Under the coverage limits set in May 2024, how much of his deposit is uninsured and must be recovered through liquidation dividends?
questions.explanation: The MFB limit since May 2024 is N2m, so N3.2m - N2m = N1.2m is uninsured. Option C is the insured amount, option D wrongly applies the N5m DMB limit, and option B assumes no cover at all.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Assume a coverage limit of N5 million per depositor and that all accounts held by one depositor in the same right and capacity in a failed bank are added together. Mr Musa has N3 million in savings and N4 million in a current account, both in his own name, at a deposit money bank that fails in 2025. How much is insured?
questions.explanation: Because the two accounts are in the same right and capacity, they are added to N7m and the limit of N5m applies to the total, so N5m is insured. Option B ignores the limit, option A wrongly applies the limit to each account separately, and option D insures only the larger account.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A failed bank's uninsured depositors have total verified claims of N60 billion, and N24 billion is available from the sale of its assets for distribution to them. If Chinedu has an uninsured claim of N3 million, what liquidation dividend should he receive?
questions.explanation: The dividend rate is N24bn / N60bn = 40%, and 40% of N3m is N1.2m. Option B assumes full repayment, option A is the 60% he does not recover, and option C wrongly divides 24 by 60 to get 0.4 and then treats it as N0.4m.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: A liquidator pays an interim liquidation dividend of 25% and later a final dividend of 15% on uninsured claims. Funmi's uninsured claim is N4 million. How much does she receive in liquidation dividends altogether?
questions.explanation: Total dividends equal (25% + 15%) x N4m = 40% x N4m = N1.6m. Option A counts only the interim dividend, option D counts only the final dividend, and option B is the 60% of her claim that remains unpaid.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, assistance funding from an insurance fund is capped at 10% of the fund's balance unless the Board prescribes otherwise. If the fund balance is N1.2 trillion, what is the maximum assistance under this default cap?
questions.explanation: Ten per cent of N1.2 trillion is N120 billion. Option B uses 1% instead of 10%, option C uses 0.1%, and option A is the 90% that remains in the fund after the cap.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, the NDIC was required to pay insured depositors within how many days of the revocation of a bank's licence?
questions.explanation: Section 21(1) of the 2006 Act required payment within 90 days of licence revocation. Option B is the IADI best-practice standard, option A is the NDIC's 2023 Service Charter target, and option C was the period after which unclaimed insured deposits were forfeited under the 2006 Act.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 1988 NDIC Decree, insured depositors of a failed bank were to be paid as soon as possible but not later than:
questions.explanation: The 1988 Decree required payment as soon as possible and within three months of the bank's failure. Option D is the later IADI standard, option A is the NDIC's 2023 Service Charter target, and option C relates to forfeiture of unclaimed deposits under the 2006 Act.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Service Charter of 2023, the NDIC aims to pay insured depositors within how long?

options.b: 30 days of its appointment as liquidator

questions.explanation: The 2023 Service Charter sets a target of paying insured depositors within 30 days of the NDIC's appointment as liquidator. Option C was the NDIC Act 2006 rule, option D was the 1988 Decree rule, and option A was the old period for filing claims.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following ranks Nigeria's reimbursement deadlines from the LONGEST to the SHORTEST?

options.a: NDIC Act 2006 (90 days); NDIC Service Charter 2023 (30 days); IADI 2014 standard (7 working days)
options.b: IADI 2014 standard (7 working days); NDIC Act 2006 (90 days); NDIC Service Charter 2023 (30 days)
options.c: NDIC Service Charter 2023 (30 days); NDIC Act 2006 (90 days); IADI 2014 standard (7 working days)
options.d: NDIC Act 2006 (90 days); IADI 2014 standard (7 working days); NDIC Service Charter 2023 (30 days)

questions.explanation: 90 days is longer than 30 days, which is longer than 7 working days, showing how payout targets have tightened over time. Options B, C and D each place at least one deadline in the wrong position.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: After Heritage Bank's licence was revoked on 3 June 2024, the NDIC began paying insured depositors within days. What mainly made this speed possible?

options.a: Requiring every depositor to file a paper claim within 18 months
options.b: Transferring Heritage Bank to AMCON as a bridge bank
options.c: Waiting for the sale of Heritage Bank's assets before paying anyone
options.d: Paying insured sums into depositors' other bank accounts linked by their BVN

questions.explanation: The NDIC used Bank Verification Numbers to identify depositors' alternative accounts and credit their insured sums quickly. Option C describes how liquidation dividends, not insured payments, are funded, option A reflects the old slow claim-filing approach, and option B is wrong because Heritage Bank was liquidated.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Why is prompt reimbursement of insured depositors important when a bank fails?

options.a: It allows the failed bank's shareholders to recover their capital first
options.b: It cushions the effects of failure and reduces the chance of runs on other banks
options.c: It removes the need to sell the failed bank's assets
options.d: It makes the coverage limit unnecessary for small depositors

questions.explanation: Quick payment softens the shock to depositors and keeps confidence high, so customers of other banks are less likely to panic and withdraw. Option A ignores that shareholders rank last, option C is wrong because assets must still be realised to pay uninsured depositors and creditors, and option D confuses speed with the amount covered.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, insured deposits that were not claimed within what period after a bank's closure were forfeited?
questions.explanation: Section 22(4) of the 2006 Act provided for forfeiture of insured deposits not claimed within six years. Option A was the rule under the earlier 1988 Decree, option D was the 2006 Act's deadline for the NDIC to pay, and option C is the IADI payout standard.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In the past, insured depositors had to file claims with the NDIC, and many never did even where 100% liquidation dividends were declared. Which factor best explains this low response?

options.a: Absence of any coverage limit for small depositors
options.b: Prohibition on depositors filing claims through agent banks
options.c: Depositor ignorance and apathy, especially among those with small balances
options.d: A rule that only shareholders could file claims

questions.explanation: Many depositors did not claim because they were unaware, unconcerned, or had small balances, despite public enlightenment efforts. Option B is wrong because agent banks were appointed to help pay claims, option A is false since limits have always existed, and option D has no basis.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Apart from paying insured depositors directly, the NDIC has also reimbursed depositors of closed banks through:

options.a: Agent banks appointed to pay claims on its behalf
options.d: The CBN's lender of last resort window

questions.explanation: The NDIC has paid insured deposits both directly and through agent banks that pay depositors on its behalf. Option B is wrong because directors of failed banks play no role in paying depositors, and options C and D are different safety-net functions, not payout channels.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a challenge faced in bank failure resolution and liquidation in Nigeria?

options.b: A deep secondary market for the risk assets of failed banks
options.c: Poor record keeping in failed banks
options.d: Cumbersome judicial process and long litigation

questions.explanation: A deep secondary market would make asset sales easier; in fact the lack of a secondary market for risk assets is one of the problems. Options A, C and D are genuine challenges that slow down liquidation and recoveries.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the NDIC finds it hard to realise the loans and other assets of failed banks?

options.a: Strict IFRS rules that forbid asset sales
options.b: The coverage limit on insured deposits
options.c: Large insider loans, poor loan documentation and lack of a secondary market
options.d: Excess demand from investors for failed banks' loans

questions.explanation: Asset realisation is difficult because many loans went to insiders, were poorly documented, are of low quality and have no ready market. Option D is the opposite of the real situation, option A has no basis, and option B concerns depositor protection, not asset sales.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which law was introduced in 1994 to help recover debts owed to failed banks and deal with financial malpractices in banks?

options.b: Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria Act 2010
options.c: Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020
options.d: Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Decree/Act 1994

questions.explanation: The 1994 Failed Banks law created a faster route to recover debts owed to failed banks, which helps liquidators realise assets. Option A is general company law, option B created AMCON to buy bad loans, and option C is the later banking law under which banks are licensed.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: Which resolution-related challenge in Nigeria is linked to the establishment of AMCON?

options.a: The lack of a deposit insurance coverage limit
options.b: The absence of any body to buy non-performing loans
options.c: The moral hazard it may create by encouraging banks to expect bad loans to be bought
options.d: The prohibition of bridge banks by AMCON law

questions.explanation: Because AMCON buys non-performing loans and recapitalises distressed banks, bankers may take more risk expecting a rescue, which is moral hazard. Option B is wrong because AMCON is exactly such a body, and options A and D are false statements.

questions.topic: Bank Liquidation and Failure Resolution by the NDIC
questions.question: In every case, Nigeria's choice of a particular resolution measure has been largely guided by the need to:

options.a: Avoid ever paying out insured depositors
options.b: Preserve the jobs of the failed bank's directors
options.c: Ensure cost-effectiveness, protect depositors and limit the use of taxpayers' funds
options.d: Maximise the fees earned by the deposit insurer

questions.explanation: The guiding considerations are cost-effectiveness, confidence, depositor protection, minimal disruption and limited recourse to taxpayers' money. Option D is not an aim of a public deposit insurer, option B conflicts with holding parties at fault responsible, and option A is wrong because deposit payout is itself one of the options used.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 1988 decree that established the NDIC, insured banks paid an annual premium equal to ____ of their total deposit liabilities.
questions.explanation: The original decree set a flat annual premium of 15/16 of 1 percent (about 0.9375 percent) of total deposit liabilities. Option D, 8/16 of 1 percent, was the ceiling the 2006 Act set for other deposit-taking institutions such as microfinance and mortgage banks, not the 1988 rate for banks. The other figures were never the statutory premium rate.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: A deposit insurance scheme that collects premiums from member banks regularly, so that a fund is built up before any bank fails, is said to be funded:
questions.explanation: Ex ante funding means the money is collected in advance and accumulated in a fund that is ready before any failure happens. Option C, ex post funding, is the opposite: money is raised from surviving banks only after a failure. Options A and D describe forms of protection, not a way of building up a fund.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under which funding method does a deposit insurer raise the money needed to pay depositors from the surviving member institutions only after a bank has failed?
questions.explanation: Ex post funding means nothing is set aside in advance; the cost of a failure is recovered afterwards by levying the banks that are still standing. Option A is the reverse, with money collected before failures. Options B and C both belong to an ex ante system that charges premiums and builds a fund over time.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In the country of Zamora there is no standing deposit insurance fund. When Prime Bank failed, the government paid insured depositors and then imposed a special levy on the remaining banks to recover the money. Zamora's scheme is best described as:
questions.explanation: Paying first and collecting from the surviving banks afterwards is the mark of ex post funding. Option C would require a fund built up in advance, which Zamora does not have.
