Options A and B are ways of pricing regular premiums in an ex ante fund, and no regular premium is charged here.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Australia's Financial Claims Scheme, set up in 2008, pays depositors with government money when an authorised deposit-taking institution fails and then recovers the cost from the liquidation and, if needed, a levy on the industry. This is an example of:

options.c: A pay box funded by premiums
options.d: An implicit guarantee with no legal basis

questions.explanation: Because no fund is accumulated beforehand and costs are recovered after the event, the Australian scheme is funded ex post. Option A is wrong because there is no pre-built fund from premiums, which also rules out option C. Option D is wrong because the scheme is set out in law, so it is explicit, not implicit.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is a weakness of ex post funding of deposit insurance?

options.a: Banks pay premiums even in years when no bank fails
options.b: The failed bank itself never contributes to the cost of its own failure
options.c: Money collected in advance lies in a fund and has to be invested
options.d: The insurer holds a ready pool of cash when a bank fails

questions.explanation: Under ex post funding the levy is collected only after a failure, so the bank that failed escapes paying and the surviving, often healthier, banks carry the cost. Options A and C are features of ex ante funding, not ex post. Option D is actually a strength of ex ante funding.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is the main advantage of ex ante funding of a deposit insurance scheme?

options.a: Banks pay nothing at all until a failure actually occurs
options.b: Money is already available to reimburse depositors promptly when a bank fails
options.c: Surviving banks bear the whole cost after each failure
options.d: The insurer never has to manage or invest any funds

questions.explanation: With ex ante funding the fund exists before the failure, so the insurer can pay insured depositors quickly and boost public confidence. Options A and D describe ex post funding, where nothing is collected or invested in advance. Option C is a drawback of ex post funding, not an advantage of ex ante.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: A levy charged on surviving banks during a banking crisis, exactly when they are under the greatest strain, can deepen the crisis. Because of this, ex post funding is described as:
questions.explanation: Pro-cyclical means a measure moves with the cycle and makes a downturn worse, which is what happens when weak banks must pay large levies in a crisis. Option A, counter-cyclical, describes ex ante funding, where money is gathered in good times and used in bad times. Options B and C are unrelated ideas about premium pricing and international cooperation.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 2014 IADI Core Principles, which funding arrangement is recommended for a deposit insurer?

options.a: Ex post funding only, levied after each failure
options.b: Voluntary donations from the largest banks
options.c: Annual appropriations from the national budget
options.d: Ex ante funding built up towards a target fund size

questions.explanation: IADI's 2014 funding principle (Core Principle 9) calls for ex ante funding with a target fund size, so money is ready before failures occur. Option A is wrong because relying only on levies after each failure leaves no money ready when a bank fails. Options B and C are not the regular, member-funded arrangement IADI recommends.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 2014 IADI Core Principles, the principle titled 'Sources and uses of funds' is Core Principle:
questions.explanation: Core Principle 9 of the 2014 set deals with how a deposit insurer is funded and how it may use its funds. Option A, Core Principle 8, is about coverage, option D, Core Principle 10, is about public awareness, and option C, Core Principle 14, covers failure resolution.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 2014 IADI Core Principles, which statement about a deposit insurer's emergency or back-up funding is correct?

options.a: Borrowing in the market should be the insurer's only back-up
options.b: Emergency funding should be arranged only after a failure occurs
options.c: Emergency funding should be pre-arranged, for example with the government or the central bank
options.d: A deposit insurer should never be allowed to borrow

questions.explanation: IADI wants emergency liquidity lined up in advance from the government, the central bank or market borrowing, so the insurer is not caught short in a crisis. Option A is wrong because market borrowing should not be the sole back-up. Option B defeats the purpose of pre-arranged funding, and option D contradicts the principle.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The NDIC builds up its deposit insurance funds from premiums collected every year from insured institutions, whether or not any bank fails in that year. This means the NDIC's deposit insurance is funded:
questions.explanation: Collecting premiums every year to build a standing fund before failures happen is ex ante funding. Option B would mean raising money only after a failure. Option D is wrong because the NDIC does not depend on government subvention, and option C describes an informal scheme with no fund at all.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a source of funds for the NDIC?

options.a: Recoveries from the assets of failed banks
options.b: Income from investing its funds in government securities
options.d: Annual government subvention for its operations

questions.explanation: The NDIC is self-financing and does not receive government subvention for its operations. Options A, B and C are genuine inflows: premiums build the deposit insurance funds, investment income pays for operations, and recoveries come back to the NDIC after it pays depositors of failed banks.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is a genuine source of income for the NDIC?

options.a: Income earned from investing its funds in Federal Government securities
options.b: An annual allocation from the federal budget
options.c: Premiums paid directly by individual depositors
options.d: A charge on every customer's ATM withdrawal

questions.explanation: The NDIC invests its funds in government securities and uses the income to run the Corporation. Option B is wrong because the NDIC gets no budget subvention, and option C is wrong because premiums are paid by the insured banks, not by depositors. Option D is invented and has no basis in NDIC law.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The initial take-off capital of the NDIC was contributed by:

options.a: The Central Bank of Nigeria (60%) and the Federal Ministry of Finance (40%)
options.b: The Central Bank of Nigeria (50%) and the insured banks (50%)
options.c: The Central Bank of Nigeria alone (100%)
options.d: The Central Bank of Nigeria (40%) and the Federal Ministry of Finance (60%)

questions.explanation: The NDIC is publicly owned, with its capital provided 60 percent by the CBN and 40 percent by the Federal Ministry of Finance. Option D reverses the shares, and option C leaves out the Ministry of Finance. Option B is wrong because the insured banks pay premiums but do not own the NDIC.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the authorised capital of the NDIC is:
questions.explanation: Section 16 of the NDIC Act 2023 fixes the NDIC's authorised capital at N50 billion, paid up by the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance in a 60:40 ratio. Option B, N500 billion, is ten times that figure, the level that matters for the General Reserve Fund. Option D is close to the combined balance of the deposit insurance funds in 2024, not the capital.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Suppose the NDIC's paid-up capital is N20 billion, shared between its two owners in the proportion fixed by the NDIC Act 2023. How much of this would the Central Bank of Nigeria have paid?
questions.explanation: The CBN holds 60 percent of the NDIC's paid-up capital, so 60% x N20 billion = N12 billion. Option A, N8 billion, is the 40 percent share of the Federal Ministry of Finance. Option D assumes an equal split, and option C wrongly gives the whole capital to the CBN.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The NDIC is described as 'self-financing' because:

options.a: Its staff salaries are paid from the Deposit Insurance Fund
options.b: Depositors pay a fee each time they open an account
options.c: It does not receive government subvention to run its operations
options.d: It finances its operations by borrowing from the CBN every year

questions.explanation: Self-financing means the NDIC meets its running costs from its own income, mainly from investing its funds, rather than from government grants. Option D is wrong because borrowing is not its regular way of paying for operations. Option A is wrong because the deposit insurance funds cannot be used for running costs, and option B has no basis.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the salaries and allowances of NDIC staff are charged to the:
questions.explanation: Section 18 of the 2023 Act sets up an Operating Fund, and staff pay, Board allowances and administrative costs are charged to it. Options A and D are deposit insurance funds held for depositors and cannot be used for running costs. Option C holds year-end surpluses to support depositor payments.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, which of the following is NOT credited to the NDIC's Operating Fund?

options.a: Money borrowed with the approval of the Board
options.b: Investment income other than income of the deposit insurance funds
options.d: Premiums assessed on deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Premiums from deposit money banks go into the Deposit Insurance Fund, which is held for depositors, not into the Operating Fund. Options A, B and C are all listed in section 18 as amounts credited to the Operating Fund.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The NDIC has long been barred by law from paying its operating expenses out of the Deposit Insurance Fund. From what is it expected to meet these expenses?

options.b: Fines imposed on failed banks' customers
options.c: Income generated by investing its funds
options.d: Grants from the Federal Ministry of Finance

questions.explanation: Operating costs are paid from the income earned by investing the NDIC's funds, while the premium pool itself is kept for depositors. Option A is wrong because depositors do not pay premiums. Option D is wrong because the NDIC receives no government subvention, and option B is invented.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The NDIC Act 2023 specifically names which class of securities for investing NDIC funds not immediately required?

options.a: Shares of listed deposit money banks
options.c: Foreign currency deposits in insured banks
options.d: Commercial papers issued by microfinance banks

questions.explanation: Section 20 allows the NDIC to invest idle funds in Federal Government securities, or other securities the Board approves. Government securities are chosen because they are safe and easy to sell. Options A, C and D would expose the fund to the very banks it insures, which would defeat its purpose.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Why has the NDIC's revenue base been described as vulnerable?

options.a: Insured banks often refuse to pay their premiums
options.b: Its funds are restricted to treasury instruments whose yields swing with economic conditions
options.c: Depositors' premium contributions are too small
options.d: Its government subvention is irregular and often delayed

questions.explanation: Because operating costs are paid from investment income, and the fund may only be invested in treasury instruments, falling or volatile yields directly shrink the NDIC's income. Option D is wrong because the NDIC receives no subvention at all. Option C is wrong because depositors do not pay premiums, and option A is not the reason given.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The main reason a deposit insurer invests its fund in government securities rather than in high-yield assets is to ensure:

options.a: Control over the insured banks' boards
options.b: Support for share prices on the stock exchange
options.c: Safety and liquidity, so the money is available when banks fail
options.d: The highest possible return in every year

questions.explanation: A deposit insurance fund must be there, in cash, when a bank fails, so safety and liquidity come before yield. Option D is wrong because chasing high returns adds risk to money held for depositors. Options A and B are not the purpose of investing the fund.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: How many separate deposit insurance funds does section 17 of the NDIC Act 2023 establish?
questions.explanation: The 2023 Act sets up five funds: the DIF, NIDIF, SIIF, NISIIF and PSBIF, each for a different category of insured institution. The Board may create more, but the Act itself establishes five. Options B, C and D miscount them.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) is the fund for:

options.a: Deposit money banks and mobile money operators
options.c: Microfinance banks and primary mortgage banks

questions.explanation: Section 17 says the DIF covers deposit money banks and mobile money operators. Option C describes the SIIF, option D the PSBIF, and option B the NIDIF.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Swiftpay Payment Service Bank pays its annual deposit insurance premium to the NDIC in 2025. Under the NDIC Act 2023, the premium is credited to the:
questions.explanation: Each fund receives the premiums of its own category, and payment service banks have a separate fund, the PSBIF. Option C is for deposit money banks and mobile money operators, option A is for microfinance and primary mortgage banks, and option B is for non-interest deposit money banks.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the premiums paid by a conventional microfinance bank in Ibadan are credited to the:
questions.explanation: Microfinance banks and primary mortgage banks are 'special insured institutions', and their conventional members pay into the SIIF. Option C is for deposit money banks and mobile money operators, option A is for non-interest deposit money banks, and option B is for payment service banks.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the premiums of a non-interest (Islamic) deposit money bank are credited to the:
questions.explanation: The 2023 Act keeps non-interest deposit money banks in their own fund, the NIDIF, separate from conventional banks. Option A is for conventional deposit money banks and mobile money operators. Option B is for non-interest microfinance and mortgage institutions, and option D is for payment service banks.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the deposit insurance funds established under section 17 of the NDIC Act 2023?
questions.explanation: The Operating Fund is created separately under section 18 to pay the NDIC's running costs, so it is not a deposit insurance fund. Options A, B and D are among the five insurance funds in section 17, along with the SIIF and NISIIF.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the NDIC manages each deposit insurance fund:

options.a: On behalf of its shareholders, the CBN and the Ministry of Finance
options.b: As part of the Federation's Consolidated Revenue Fund
options.c: For the benefit of the insured banks' shareholders
options.d: In trust for depositors of the corresponding category of insured institutions

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act says each fund is held in trust for the depositors of its own category, which stresses that the money belongs to the protection of depositors. Option A is wrong because the owners' stake is the capital, not the insurance funds. Options B and C would put the money outside depositor protection.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, each insurance fund is held for depositors of its own category of institution. A key effect of this arrangement is that:

options.a: Mobile money subscribers lose cover under pass-through insurance
options.b: Deposit money bank premiums are used to pay the NDIC's staff
options.c: Premiums paid by microfinance banks are kept to protect microfinance depositors rather than mixed with deposit money bank premiums
options.d: All insured institutions pay the same premium rate

questions.explanation: Separate funds held in trust for each category keep each group's premiums for its own depositors, which limits cross-subsidy between, for example, microfinance banks and deposit money banks. Option D is wrong because rates differ by category and by risk. Option B is wrong because staff costs come from the Operating Fund, and option A is wrong because mobile money operators sit in the DIF.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, which of the following is NOT a permitted use of a deposit insurance fund?

options.a: Refunding excess premiums paid by insured institutions
options.b: Paying insured depositors of a failed insured institution
options.c: Paying salaries and allowances of NDIC staff
options.d: Giving financial assistance to a failing insured institution, within a set cap

questions.explanation: Staff pay is charged to the Operating Fund, not to the insurance funds. Options A, B and D are the uses allowed by section 17: paying deposit insurance obligations, assisting institutions within a cap, and refunding excess premiums or special contributions.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, unless the Board prescribes otherwise, financial assistance to insured institutions from a deposit insurance fund is capped at what percentage of that fund's balance?
questions.explanation: Section 17(7)(b) limits assistance to 10 percent of the fund's balance unless the Board sets a different percentage. The cap protects money that is meant first of all for paying insured depositors. Options B, C and D are not the figure in the Act.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, if the Deposit Insurance Fund stands at N1.8 trillion and the Board has not prescribed a different limit, what is the most the NDIC may give a failing deposit money bank as assistance from the fund?
questions.explanation: The default cap is 10 percent of the fund balance, so 10% x N1.8 trillion = N180 billion. Option C uses 1 percent instead of 10 percent. Option D uses 25 percent, and option B slips by two decimal places.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, which of the following is NOT credited to a deposit insurance fund?

options.a: Money borrowed by the NDIC with the Board's approval
options.b: Special contributions required from insured institutions
options.c: The share of investment income the Board needs to keep the fund at its target
options.d: Premiums assessed on institutions in that category

questions.explanation: Borrowed money goes into the Operating Fund under section 18. Options B, C and D are all credited to the insurance funds by section 17, together with any share of general reserves the Board allocates.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, who sets the minimum target size of each deposit insurance fund and the timeframe for reaching it?

options.a: The International Association of Deposit Insurers

questions.explanation: Section 17 leaves the minimum target fund size, its timeframe and its periodic review to the NDIC Board. Option C passes laws but does not set the target. Option B heads the regulator, and option A issues international guidance but does not set targets for member insurers.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: A deposit insurer's target fund ratio expresses the size of its fund as a percentage of:

options.c: Total (or insured) deposits of the institutions it covers
options.d: The total loans of insured banks

questions.explanation: A target fund ratio measures the fund against the deposits it must protect; under the NDIC Act 2023 the target is tied to total deposits of each category. Option A is the basis for the General Reserve Fund rule, not the fund target. Options B and D are not the measure of what the fund may have to pay.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Suppose the NDIC Board set a minimum target of 5 percent of total deposits for a category whose total deposits are N40 trillion, and that category's fund stood at N1.6 trillion. By how much would the fund fall short of its target?
questions.explanation: The target is 5% x N40 trillion = N2 trillion, and N2 trillion - N1.6 trillion = N400 billion still to be built up. Option A is the target itself, not the shortfall. Option B is the existing balance, and option D uses 10 percent instead of 5 percent.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The European Union's Single Resolution Fund, built up between 2016 and 2023, had a target size of at least what share of covered deposits in the Banking Union?
questions.explanation: The Single Resolution Fund had a target of at least 1 percent of covered deposits, about EUR 80 billion by end-2023. It is a good example of a fund built up ex ante towards a target. Options A, C and D are not the target that was set.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In May 2024, the NDIC announced that the combined balance of its deposit insurance funds had exceeded:
questions.explanation: In May 2024 the NDIC's Managing Director said the deposit insurance funds together exceeded N2 trillion. Option C is ten times too small and option D ten times too large. Option B, N50 billion, is the NDIC's authorised capital under the 2023 Act.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the General Reserve Fund receives the NDIC's year-end surplus mainly so that it can:

options.a: Pay the annual salaries of NDIC staff
options.b: Fund the CBN's lender of last resort loans
options.c: Buy shares in distressed deposit money banks
options.d: Support payments to insured depositors when a deposit insurance fund falls short

questions.explanation: The General Reserve Fund builds a cushion from surpluses that can be drawn on to maintain the insurance funds or cover a shortfall in paying depositors. Option A belongs to the Operating Fund. Options B and C are not functions of the reserve.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the special rule for sharing the NDIC's net operating surplus applies once the General Reserve Fund is more than ten times the authorised capital. With an authorised capital of N50 billion, this threshold is:
questions.explanation: Ten times the N50 billion authorised capital is 10 x N50 billion = N500 billion. Option C is the capital itself, option A divides by ten instead of multiplying, and option B multiplies by one hundred.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, once the General Reserve Fund exceeds ten times the authorised capital, what share of the net operating surplus must go to the General Reserve Fund?
questions.explanation: Section 19(2) sends 75 percent of the net operating surplus to the reserve; the remaining 25 percent is split between premium reduction and the shareholders. Option C is the balance that is shared, not the reserve's portion. Options A and D do not match the Act.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, assume the General Reserve Fund is already above ten times the authorised capital and the NDIC makes a net operating surplus of N60 billion. How much goes to the shareholders?
questions.explanation: 75 percent (N45 billion) goes to the reserve, and the remaining 25 percent (N15 billion) is split in half, so N7.5 billion may go to premium reduction and N7.5 billion to the shareholders. Option D gives the shareholders the whole 25 percent. Option C is the reserve's share, and option B is half of the entire surplus.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, the General Reserve Fund already exceeds ten times the authorised capital and the year's net operating surplus is N24 billion. How much must go to the General Reserve Fund?
questions.explanation: When the reserve is above the threshold, 75 percent of the surplus goes to it: 75% x N24 billion = N18 billion. Option A is the 25 percent balance that is shared out. Option B assumes a 50:50 split, and option D sends the whole surplus to the reserve.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, part of the NDIC's surplus may be used to reduce the annual premiums of insured institutions. This shows that:

options.a: Depositors receive a cash refund from the NDIC each year
options.b: Premiums are fixed by the Act and can never change
options.c: The Federal Government pays part of every bank's premium
options.d: A well-funded insurer can pass some of its surplus back to the banks that pay premiums

questions.explanation: Once the reserve is large enough, half of the 25 percent surplus balance may go to lowering premiums, which eases the burden on the institutions that fund the scheme. Option B is wrong because rates can be changed and differ by risk. Option A is wrong because depositors do not pay premiums, and option C has no basis.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 1988 Decree and the NDIC Act 2006, the NDIC was specifically empowered to borrow from:
questions.explanation: Both the 1988 Decree and the 2006 Act let the NDIC borrow from the CBN, and from other lenders with Board approval, if its funds ran short. Option B is not the named lender. Option A would make no sense because depositors are the people the NDIC protects, and option D is a stock exchange, not a lender.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2023, money the NDIC borrows with the approval of its Board is credited to the:
questions.explanation: Section 18 lists money borrowed from any lender with Board approval among the items credited to the Operating Fund, and repaying it with interest is charged to the same fund. Options C and D receive premiums, special contributions and allocated income. Option B receives year-end surpluses.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the 1988 Decree the premium rate was 15/16 of 1 percent. Expressed in basis points, this is:
questions.explanation: One percent is 100 basis points, so 15/16 x 100 = 93.75 basis points. Option C is ten times too small, option D ten times too large, and option B simply writes the fraction as a number.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In 1990, Unity Commercial Bank had total deposit liabilities of N600 million. Under the flat-rate premium of the 1988 Decree, what annual premium would it pay the NDIC?
questions.explanation: Premium = 0.9375% x N600 million = N5,625,000, or N5.625 million. Option C uses 9.375 percent, option B uses 0.09375 percent, and option D wrongly uses 0.5 percent.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, the annual premium of an insured institution was assessed on its:

options.a: Total assets as at 31 December of the current year
options.b: Total deposit liabilities as at 31 December of the preceding year
options.c: Insured deposits only, on the date its licence is revoked
options.d: Paid-up share capital at the date of assessment

questions.explanation: The 2006 Act based the premium on total deposit liabilities as shown at 31 December of the previous year. Option A confuses the premium base with the total-asset levy used for the bank resolution cost fund. Options C and D are not the assessment base in the Act.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, the maximum premium rate for licensed banks was 15/16 of 1 percent. What was the maximum rate for other deposit-taking institutions such as microfinance banks?
questions.explanation: The 2006 Act set a lower ceiling, 8/16 of 1 percent or 0.5 percent, for other deposit-taking institutions. Option D is the ceiling for licensed banks. Option A is not in the Act, and option B misreads the fraction as 8 percent.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, a microfinance bank with total deposit liabilities of N2.4 billion is charged the maximum premium rate allowed for other deposit-taking institutions. What is its annual premium?
questions.explanation: The maximum for other deposit-taking institutions was 8/16 of 1 percent, or 0.5 percent, so 0.5% x N2.4 billion = N12 million. Option A wrongly applies the bank ceiling of 0.9375 percent. Options B and D are decimal slips of ten times too much and ten times too little.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: What is the main weakness of a flat-rate deposit insurance premium?

options.a: It makes premium income impossible to forecast
options.b: It is too complicated for banks to calculate
options.c: Sound banks end up subsidising risky banks, which encourages moral hazard
options.d: It charges the riskiest banks the highest rates

questions.explanation: A flat rate charges every bank the same percentage whatever its risk, so careful banks pay for the extra risk taken by reckless ones, and risk-taking goes unpenalised. Option B is wrong because a flat rate is the simplest system. Option D describes a risk-based system, and option A is not the main problem.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Bank A is well run and Bank B takes heavy risks, but both have N100 billion of deposits and both pay exactly the same deposit insurance premium. The premium system in use is:
questions.explanation: Charging every bank the same rate on its deposits, regardless of its risk, is a flat-rate system. Options A and C are the same idea, a risk-based approach that would charge Bank B more. Option B is wrong because premiums are being charged in advance, not levied after a failure.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In NDIC premium assessment, DPAS stands for:
questions.explanation: DPAS is the Differential Premium Assessment System, under which each bank's premium depends on its risk. Options A, B and D are look-alike expansions that do not exist.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In which year did the NDIC adopt the Differential Premium Assessment System (DPAS) in place of the flat-rate premium?
questions.explanation: After a framework issued in 2007, the NDIC adopted DPAS in 2008. Option D is when the NDIC started, with a flat rate. Option C is the year of the NDIC Act that allowed risk-reflecting rates, and option B is when the DPAS base rate was cut to 35 basis points.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Under the NDIC's Differential Premium Assessment System, a bank's premium rate is made up of:

options.a: A base rate plus an add-on that depends on the bank's riskiness
options.b: A single flat rate charged to every bank
options.c: A rate set by the bank's own board each year
options.d: The CBN's monetary policy rate plus a margin

questions.explanation: DPAS starts with a base rate that all banks pay and adds an extra charge that rises with the bank's risk rating. Option B is the old flat-rate system. Options C and D have nothing to do with how deposit insurance premiums are set.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: When the NDIC's Differential Premium Assessment System began in 2008, the base rate was:
questions.explanation: DPAS started with a base rate of 0.50 percent, or 50 basis points. Option A came after the first cut, and option D after the cut that took effect in January 2015. Option C is the old flat rate under the 1988 Decree.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Effective January 2015, the NDIC reduced the DPAS base rate for deposit money banks to:
questions.explanation: The NDIC Board cut the base rate from 40 to 35 basis points with effect from January 2015. Option C was the rate before that cut, and option D was the starting rate in 2008. Option A is the top of the range charged to riskier banks in 2024.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: As at May 2024, the DPAS premium rates paid by deposit money banks ranged from:

options.a: A flat 93.75 basis points for every bank
options.b: 35 basis points for the soundest banks up to 65 basis points for riskier banks
options.c: 10 basis points up to 35 basis points
options.d: 50 basis points up to 100 basis points

questions.explanation: In 2024 the NDIC said deposit money banks paid a base rate of 35 basis points, rising to as much as 65 basis points for riskier banks. Option A is the 1988 flat rate. Options C and D do not match the published range.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In 2024 a deposit money bank under DPAS pays the 35 basis point base rate plus a risk add-on of 20 basis points. If its assessable deposits are N3.2 trillion, what is its annual premium?
questions.explanation: The total rate is 35 + 20 = 55 basis points, or 0.55 percent, and 0.55% x N3.2 trillion = N17.6 billion. Option A charges only the 35 basis point base rate and forgets the add-on. Options B and D are decimal slips.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In 2024, under DPAS rates of 35 to 65 basis points, how much more premium would a deposit money bank at the top of the range pay than one at the bottom, if each had assessable deposits of N1 trillion?
questions.explanation: The gap is 65 - 35 = 30 basis points, or 0.30 percent, and 0.30% x N1 trillion = N3 billion. Option C is the full premium of the riskier bank, not the difference. Options A and B are decimal slips.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: When the DPAS base rate fell from 40 to 35 basis points in January 2015, how much would a group of deposit money banks with N12 trillion of assessable deposits save on base-rate premiums each year?
questions.explanation: The cut is 5 basis points, or 0.05 percent, and 0.05% x N12 trillion = N6 billion. Option A is the full premium still payable at 35 basis points, not the saving. Options B and C are decimal slips.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: A deposit money bank with assessable deposits of N500 billion compares the 1988 flat premium rate (15/16 of 1 percent) with the 35 basis point DPAS base rate in force from 2015. How much more would it pay a year at the 1988 flat rate?
questions.explanation: The difference in rates is 0.9375% - 0.35% = 0.5875%, and 0.5875% x N500 billion = N2.9375 billion. Option B is the whole premium at the flat rate, and option C is the whole premium at 35 basis points. Option A is a decimal slip.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: In 2016 a deposit money bank rated in the lowest-risk category paid only the 35 basis point DPAS base rate, and its premium came to N4.2 billion. What were its assessable deposits?
questions.explanation: Deposits = premium / rate = N4.2 billion / 0.0035 = N1.2 trillion. Options B and D are off by a factor of ten. Option C wrongly multiplies the premium by the rate in basis points instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Why does IADI encourage differential (risk-based) premiums such as the NDIC's DPAS?

options.a: They guarantee that every bank pays exactly the same premium
options.b: They make riskier banks pay more and so help reduce moral hazard
options.c: They remove the need for any bank supervision
options.d: They allow depositors to choose how much premium to pay

questions.explanation: Risk-based premiums put a price on risk-taking, so banks have a reason to behave prudently, and IADI lists them among tools that reduce moral hazard. Option A describes a flat rate. Option C is wrong because premiums work alongside supervision, and option D is wrong because banks, not depositors, pay premiums.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Around 2020, which category of insured institutions still paid a flat-rate premium rather than risk-based DPAS premiums?
questions.explanation: NDIC reported that microfinance banks paid a flat-rate premium while deposit money banks and primary mortgage banks were on risk-based premiums. Options A and C were on risk-based premiums, and option B, commercial banks with national licences, are themselves deposit money banks.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The NDIC cut the DPAS base rate from 50 to 40 basis points after the 2009 banking crisis mainly to:

options.a: Punish banks that had taken excessive risks
options.b: Ease the burden on banks that were also contributing to a new fund for bank resolution costs
options.c: Raise more money for the Deposit Insurance Fund
options.d: Bring the rate back to the 1988 flat level

questions.explanation: After the 2009 crisis, banks began paying an annual levy into a fund set up with the CBN to meet resolution costs, so the NDIC lowered the base rate to reduce their combined burden. Option C is the opposite effect of a cut. Option A would call for higher, not lower, rates, and option D is wrong because the 1988 rate was much higher.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: To meet the cost of resolving banks after the 2009 crisis, the CBN agreed with the banks to set up a fund (variously called the Financial Stability Fund or the AMCON Resolution Cost Fund). How much was the CBN to contribute each year for ten years?
questions.explanation: The CBN committed N50 billion a year for ten years, while each bank paid an annual levy based on its total assets. Option C, N500 billion, is roughly the CBN's total over the whole ten years, not its yearly share. Options B and D are not the agreed figure.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: The banks' annual contribution to the post-2009 bank resolution cost fund was calculated on their total assets. NDIC deposit insurance premiums, by contrast, are calculated on:
questions.explanation: Deposit insurance premiums are a rate applied to a bank's deposit liabilities, because deposits are what the NDIC insures. Option B is the base of the resolution cost fund levy, which is exactly the contrast in the question. Options A and D are not used as the premium base.

questions.topic: Funding and Funding Management of the NDIC
questions.question: Mr Okafor keeps N3 million in a deposit money bank in Enugu and asks who pays the premium for the NDIC cover on his account. The correct answer is that:

options.a: The bank pays the premium; Mr Okafor pays nothing for the cover
options.b: The Federal Government pays the premium on behalf of depositors
options.c: Mr Okafor pays the premium through a monthly charge
options.d: The CBN pays the premium out of its own profits

questions.explanation: In deposit insurance the insured institution pays the premium, while the depositor is protected without paying, which is why there are three parties rather than two. Option C confuses deposit insurance with ordinary insurance, where the insured person pays. Options B and D are wrong because neither the government nor the CBN pays bank premiums.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a challenge of public awareness of deposit insurance?

options.d: Scarcity of data to measure awareness progress

questions.explanation: Radio is simply one channel deposit insurers use to reach people, so 'radio waves' is not a challenge to public awareness. Real challenges include limited budgets for campaigns (option C), low literacy levels that make messages hard to understand (option A), and the lack of good data for measuring whether awareness is actually improving (option D).

questions.question: The NDIC has identified public awareness of deposit insurance in Nigeria as generally ____
questions.explanation: Low public awareness is one of the challenges the NDIC itself lists: many depositors do not know their deposits are insured or how to claim, which is one reason many small insured balances go unclaimed after a bank closes. Options B, A and C all suggest awareness is already good, which is why the NDIC keeps running awareness campaigns.

questions.question: Some of the key challenges of public awareness programmes for deposit insurance include:

options.c: Scarcity of relevant information to measure public awareness progress

questions.explanation: Running a public awareness campaign is not easy: money is limited, so budgets restrict how widely a deposit insurer can advertise, and low literacy levels mean messages must be simplified or delivered through radio, local languages and other channels. Measuring progress is also hard, because there is often little reliable information to show whether awareness has actually improved. Since options A, B and C are all genuine challenges, D is the best answer.

questions.question: After a government agency was set up to buy bad loans from distressed banks, the managers of Kogi Trust Bank began granting large risky insider loans, expecting that any losses would be absorbed by the agency. This behaviour is an example of:
questions.explanation: The managers take extra risk because they expect someone else to carry the losses, which is exactly moral hazard; this is why the creation of AMCON is listed as a challenge in Nigerian bank resolution. Option C is about who chooses to join a scheme, D means lenders limiting loans, and B refers to depositors failing to claim their money.

questions.question: Which institution's establishment is listed among the challenges of bank failure resolution in Nigeria because of the moral hazard it created?
questions.explanation: AMCON was created by the AMCON Act 2010 to buy non-performing loans and recapitalise distressed banks, and bank managers expecting such rescues may take excessive risks. Option C is a coordinating forum for regulators, B issues national identity numbers, and D regulates insurance companies; none of them buys bad bank loans.

questions.question: Allowing a deposit insurer to take legal action against directors and other parties at fault in a bank's failure mainly helps to:

options.a: Shift supervision of banks from the CBN to the courts
options.b: Hold culpable insiders responsible and discourage reckless banking
options.c: Increase the coverage limit for insured depositors
options.d: Reduce the premium rates paid by healthy banks

questions.explanation: When those who caused a failure can be pursued for losses, insiders have less incentive to abuse the bank, which reduces moral hazard; this was one of the gaps NDIC wanted closed in its law ('dealing with parties at fault'). Option C concerns coverage, not accountability. Options A and D are not effects of suing parties at fault.

questions.question: The 'cumbersome judicial process' challenge faced by the NDIC mainly results in:

options.a: Long-drawn-out litigation on winding-up actions and debt recovery
options.b: Automatic revocation of bank licences by the courts
options.c: Higher premium rates for all insured banks
options.d: Payment of depositors above the coverage limit

questions.explanation: Slow and cumbersome court procedures mean that winding-up cases and suits to recover debts owed to failed banks drag on for years, delaying liquidation and dividends. Option B is wrong because licences are revoked by the CBN, not the courts. Options C and D have nothing to do with court delays.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the challenges Nigeria has faced in resolving failed banks?

options.a: Poor record keeping in the failed banks
options.b: Problems of realising the failed banks' assets
options.d: Too many investors competing to buy failed banks' loans

questions.explanation: The real difficulty was the opposite: there was no secondary market for risk assets, so failed banks' loans were hard to sell. Options A, B and C are all genuine challenges: broken IT systems and missing records, lawsuits by former owners, and difficulty turning loans and physical assets into cash.

questions.question: As liquidator of a failed bank, the NDIC tries to sell the bank's portfolio of loans but finds there is no secondary market for such risk assets in Nigeria. This is an example of which challenge?
questions.explanation: Asset realisation means turning a failed bank's loans and property into cash to pay depositors and creditors; without buyers for risk assets, this becomes slow and recoveries fall. Option C is about depositors not filing claims, B is about unreliable data from banks, and A is about NDIC's own income.

questions.question: After the CBN revoked the licence of a bank, its former shareholders went to court to challenge the revocation, stalling the liquidation for years. This illustrates which challenge facing the NDIC?

options.a: Legal actions by owners of closed banks
options.c: Moral hazard created by deposit insurance

questions.explanation: Suits by erstwhile shareholders and owners of closed banks are listed as a legal constraint because they delay the winding-up and recovery process. Option C is about excessive risk-taking, B is about poor quality data from banks, and D is about depositors failing to claim; none involves a court challenge by owners.

questions.question: The 'inadequate legal provisions' challenge refers to the view that a deposit insurer acting as liquidator of a closed bank should be vested with:

options.a: Power to set the monetary policy rate
options.b: Power to guarantee all deposits without limit
options.c: Special powers suited to winding up banks
options.d: Power to issue and revoke banking licences

questions.explanation: A liquidator that works only through ordinary company law and courts is slow, so deposit insurers argue they need special powers when winding up banks. Option A belongs to the CBN, and D is also a CBN power in Nigeria. Option B would be blanket cover, which creates moral hazard and is not what the challenge is about.

questions.question: The Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Decree of 1994 was mainly a response to which problem?

options.a: Lack of a regional deposit insurance body in Africa
options.b: Delays by insured banks in paying annual premiums
options.c: Low coverage limits for small savers in insured banks
options.d: Slow recovery of failed banks' debts in the regular courts

questions.explanation: Debtors of failed banks were exploiting slow regular courts, so the 1994 Decree set up special arrangements for recovering such debts and punishing malpractice. Options A, B and C are not problems that a debt-recovery law addresses.

questions.question: Before the NDIC Act 2023, NDIC proposed a provision allowing it to pay insured deposits 'pending action in court'. The aim was to:

options.a: Reimburse depositors without waiting for court cases to end
options.b: Stop former shareholders from going to court at all
options.c: Allow courts to fix the coverage limit in each case
options.d: Pay uninsured creditors ahead of insured depositors

questions.explanation: Court cases by owners of closed banks could hold up payments for years, so the proposal let NDIC pay insured depositors while the litigation continued. Option B is wrong because the provision does not take away anyone's right to sue. Options D and C would reverse depositor priority and remove the fixed statutory limit.

questions.question: One reason the public misunderstands deposit insurance is that it differs from conventional insurance. How many parties are involved in a deposit insurance arrangement, and who are they?

options.a: Two: the insurer and the insured depositor
options.b: Two: the insured bank and the CBN
options.c: Three: the deposit insurer, the depositor and the insured bank
options.d: Three: the depositor, the bank and the CBN

questions.explanation: Conventional insurance is a contract between two parties, but deposit insurance has three: the insurer (NDIC), the depositor who is protected, and the bank that pays the premium. Option A describes ordinary insurance, while D and B wrongly put the CBN in the insurer's place.

questions.question: Unlike in motor or life insurance, in a deposit insurance scheme the premium is paid by the:
questions.explanation: In deposit insurance the bank pays the premium while the depositor enjoys the protection without paying anything directly. Option A is the common misunderstanding that comes from comparing it with conventional insurance. Options C and B are NDIC's owners, not premium payers.

questions.question: Unreliable returns submitted by insured banks most directly weaken which NDIC supervisory tool?
questions.explanation: Off-site surveillance analyses the periodic returns banks submit, so poor data hides problems and delays early warning. Options A and D are CBN functions, not NDIC supervisory tools. Option B is about refunds of premiums, not monitoring bank health.

questions.question: Many insured depositors of closed banks never file claims for their money, even where a 100 percent liquidation dividend has been declared. This challenge is known as:
questions.explanation: Despite public enlightenment efforts, many depositors, often with small balances, simply do not come forward, which NDIC attributes largely to ignorance and apathy. Option D is about excessive risk-taking, C about who joins a scheme, and B about depositors rushing to withdraw, the opposite of not claiming.

questions.question: Which group was noted to default in filing their own claims against closed banks, even though they had been appointed to pay depositors' claims on behalf of the NDIC?
questions.explanation: NDIC appoints healthy banks as agent banks to pay depositors of closed banks, yet some of these same agent banks failed to file their own claims. Options A, B and C are not the institutions that act as NDIC's paying agents.

questions.question: Mr Okafor had N3.2 million in a microfinance bank whose licence was revoked in 2025. He is paid his insured deposit under the May 2024 limits, and the liquidator later declares a 25 percent liquidation dividend on uninsured claims. What is the total he receives?
questions.explanation: The MFB cover since May 2024 is N2m, leaving an uninsured claim of N1.2m; a 25% dividend on that is N300,000, so he gets N2.3m in total. Option A wrongly applies 25% to the whole N3.2m, B ignores the dividend, and D wrongly applies 25% to the insured N2m.

questions.question: In 2025, Aisha holds N6 million in her wallet with a mobile money operator, whose pooled trust account is kept at a deposit money bank. If that bank fails, how much of Aisha's money is protected under the pass-through cover set in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Pass-through cover treats each subscriber as if they held the deposit directly, and since May 2024 the limit is N5m per subscriber per mobile money operator, so N5m of her N6m is protected. Option D is the pre-2024 limit, B is the limit for MFBs, PMBs and payment service banks, and A assumes unlimited cover.

questions.question: Which was a major reason the NDIC could not meet target periods for paying insured depositors of many closed banks?

options.a: Poor records in banks closed long before licence revocation
options.b: Coverage limits that were too complex to compute
options.c: Excess capital still held by the failed banks
options.d: Too many healthy banks bidding for the failed banks

questions.explanation: Many closed banks had incomplete records, were not fully computerised and had wide branch networks, so compiling depositor information was slow. Option B is wrong because a fixed limit is easy to apply, D would speed up resolution rather than delay payout, and C is the opposite of a failed bank's condition.

questions.question: NDIC liquidators taking over a closed bank find broken-down IT systems and missing mandate records, making it hard to confirm who owns which account. This is the challenge of:
questions.explanation: Poor record keeping covers missing financial records, mandate records and broken IT systems in failed banks, and it slows verification of claims and payout. Option C is about excess risk-taking, D about NDIC's income, and B about banks operating in several countries.

questions.question: Prompt reimbursement of insured depositors contributes to financial stability mainly by:

options.a: Allowing the failed bank's shareholders to recover their capital
options.b: Reducing the likelihood of runs on other banks
options.c: Removing the need for bank supervision
options.d: Increasing the profits of the failed bank

questions.explanation: When depositors of a failed bank are paid quickly, the public sees the guarantee working, which cushions the effects of the failure and discourages panic withdrawals from other banks. Options D and A are not effects of payout, and C is wrong because supervision remains essential.

questions.question: Under the NDIC Act 2006, the Corporation's operating expenses were to be met from:

options.a: Annual grants from the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: Income earned from investing the Deposit Insurance Fund
options.d: The premium balances in the Deposit Insurance Fund itself

questions.explanation: NDIC was prohibited from spending the Deposit Insurance Fund on running costs; those had to come from the income generated by investing the fund. Option D is the very thing the law forbade, A is not how running costs were funded, and C is wrong because depositors pay nothing for the cover.

questions.question: The proposal for a General Reserve Fund, now provided for in section 19 of the NDIC Act 2023, was meant to:

options.a: Replace premiums as NDIC's main inflow of funds
options.b: Finance the CBN's lender of last resort operations
options.c: Build a reserve that backs up payments to insured depositors
options.d: Pay dividends to shareholders of failed banks first

questions.explanation: Year-end surpluses go to the General Reserve Fund so that NDIC can meet depositor payments if an insurance fund is short, addressing the risk of an inadequate fund. Option B is a CBN function, D is wrong because failed banks' shareholders rank last, and A is wrong because premiums remain a key inflow.

questions.question: To guard against a deposit insurance fund that is too small relative to insured deposits, the 2014 IADI Core Principles expect a deposit insurer to have:

options.a: An ex ante fund with a target size, plus pre-arranged emergency funding
options.b: A fund raised only after a bank has failed (ex post)
options.c: Unlimited access to taxpayers' money for every failure
options.d: Borrowing from the market as its only backup funding

questions.explanation: IADI's funding principle favours collecting premiums in advance towards a target fund size and having emergency liquidity lined up, for example from the central bank or government. Option B is the ex post approach, C would create moral hazard, and D is wrong because market borrowing should not be the only backup.

questions.question: IADI requires the public to be informed of both the benefits and the LIMITATIONS of deposit insurance. Which of these is a limitation?

options.a: Small savers are protected against loss
options.b: Deposits above the coverage limit are not fully protected
options.c: Insured depositors are paid promptly when a bank fails
options.d: Membership is compulsory for all licensed banks

questions.explanation: A limitation is something deposit insurance does not do; balances above the cover limit may be lost in part, so depositors should know this. Options C and A are benefits of the scheme, and D is a feature that strengthens the scheme rather than a limitation on depositors.

questions.question: A public awareness programme of a deposit insurer conveys all the following EXCEPT:

options.a: Which types of deposits and depositors are covered
options.b: The monthly profit figures of each member bank
options.c: Which banks are members and how they can be identified

questions.explanation: IADI says awareness programmes cover the scope of cover, the list of member banks and how to identify them, the coverage limits and other information such as the insurer's mandate. Bank profit figures are a matter of financial disclosure, not deposit insurance awareness, while A, C and D are all required content.

questions.question: A bank has just failed and the NDIC is issuing press releases and newspaper adverts to its depositors. Which of the following MUST the notice tell insured depositors?

options.a: How to apply to the CBN for a new banking licence
options.b: The new lending rates the bridge bank will charge
options.c: How they can buy shares in the failed bank's successor
options.d: Where, how and when they will get access to their funds

questions.explanation: When a bank fails, IADI requires the deposit insurer to tell depositors where, how and when they can access their funds, what information they must provide, whether interim payments are made, and whether anyone will lose money. Options A, B and C are not part of a payout notice.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a clearly defined public awareness objective for the NDIC?

options.a: Advertise in as many newspapers and radio stations as possible
options.b: Raise awareness that deposits are insured to a set target level
options.c: Tell people more about banking and finance in general
options.d: Make the NDIC more popular than all other regulators

questions.explanation: IADI expects awareness objectives to be clearly defined, for example as target awareness levels, and consistent with the scheme's public policy objectives. Option A is an activity rather than an objective, while D and C are vague and cannot be measured.

questions.question: Requiring insured banks to display the NDIC 'insured' sign or logo in their banking halls and on their websites mainly helps the public to:

options.a: Know the CAMEL rating of each bank
options.b: Identify which institutions are insured members
options.c: Find out the bank's lending limits
options.d: Compare the interest rates of different banks

questions.explanation: Signs and logos are a simple awareness tool that tells depositors their bank is a member and their deposits are insured. Banks are also expected to present deposit insurance information in the format the insurer prescribes. Options A, C and D are not what the insured sign communicates; supervisory ratings in particular are confidential.

questions.question: According to IADI guidance, the most practical way for a deposit insurer to measure whether a public awareness campaign has worked is to:

options.a: Ask member banks to rate how good the campaign was
options.b: Compare the campaign budget with last year's budget
options.c: Count the number of brochures and adverts produced
options.d: Survey awareness independently before and after the campaign

questions.explanation: A before-and-after survey shows whether people's knowledge actually changed, and IADI also calls for periodic independent evaluations. Option C is only an output measure of activity, and A and B do not tell you whether depositors' awareness improved.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a challenge for deposit insurance public awareness programmes?

options.a: Compulsory membership of all licensed deposit takers
options.b: Awareness levels that fall quickly after a campaign
options.d: Budgetary constraints and the high cost of mass media

questions.explanation: Compulsory membership is a design feature that makes the scheme simpler to explain, not an obstacle to awareness. Options B, C and D are recognised challenges: limited budgets, literacy barriers and the fact that awareness fades unless it is maintained.

questions.question: After a slow and confusing payout to depositors of a failed bank, a survey shows public confidence in deposit insurance has fallen, despite a costly advertising campaign. This shows that:

options.b: Depositors never pay attention to bank failures
options.c: Public confidence depends heavily on the actual payout experience
options.d: Payout speed has no link to public awareness

questions.explanation: IADI observes that one poor payout can undo the gains of an awareness campaign, because people judge the scheme by how it performs when a bank fails. Options A, B and D all contradict what the survey revealed.

questions.question: Low public awareness of deposit insurance can make bank runs MORE likely because:

options.a: Unaware depositors panic and withdraw at the first rumour
options.b: Insured banks stop paying their deposit premiums
options.c: The CBN can no longer act as lender of last resort
options.d: Coverage limits automatically fall to lower levels

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance prevents runs only if depositors know their money is protected; without that knowledge, small depositors may rush to withdraw at the first rumour. Options B, C and D are not consequences of low public awareness.

questions.question: Many Nigerian banks now operate subsidiaries in other African countries. What challenge does this create for the NDIC?

options.a: Insuring the deposits of all foreign banks worldwide
options.b: Having to adopt the currency of every host country
options.c: Coordination and information-sharing with foreign authorities
options.d: Losing its power to liquidate banks in Nigeria

questions.explanation: Cross-border groups expose Nigerian banks to risks abroad, so supervisors need consolidated and cross-border supervision and formal arrangements with foreign authorities; IADI's 2014 Core Principle 5 deals with these cross-border issues. Options A, B and D are not consequences of cross-border banking.

questions.question: Where banks operate across borders through foreign branches or subsidiaries, IADI's 2014 public awareness principle requires that depositors be clearly told:

options.a: Which deposit insurer covers them, and the cover's limits and scope
options.b: How to open an account in the parent bank's home country
options.c: The exchange rate policy of the parent bank's home country
options.d: The names and nationalities of the bank's foreign shareholders

questions.explanation: Depositors of cross-border banks can be confused about who protects them, so they must be told which deposit insurer is responsible and what the cover is. Options B, C and D do not help a depositor know whether and how much of their money is protected.

questions.question: The NDIC responded to the growth of mobile money by extending protection to subscribers through:

options.a: Co-insurance in which subscribers bear the first loss
options.b: Pass-through cover on operators' pooled trust accounts
options.c: A blanket government guarantee of all e-wallets
options.d: An implicit promise with no written rules

questions.explanation: Under pass-through cover, introduced by NDIC guidelines in 2016, a mobile money operator's pooled trust account at a bank is insured as if each subscriber held the deposit directly, up to the limit per subscriber. Option C would be unlimited cover, A is a different design not used here, and D describes implicit protection, whereas Nigeria's scheme is explicit.

questions.question: Rapid growth of fintech apps and digital wallets creates a public awareness challenge for the NDIC mainly because:

options.a: Fintech apps make bank supervision unnecessary
options.b: Digital wallets are unable to hold naira balances
options.c: Fintech firms do not pay company income tax
options.d: Users may wrongly assume every digital wallet is insured

questions.explanation: Deposit insurers must tell the public which products and institutions are covered and which are not; new products blur this line, so people may believe funds are protected when they are not. Options C and B are untrue or irrelevant, and A is wrong because innovation increases rather than removes the need for supervision.

questions.question: A cyber attack that corrupts a bank's customer account database would most directly threaten the NDIC's ability to:

options.a: Set the coverage limit for deposit money banks
options.b: Choose which agencies sit on the FSRCC
options.c: Determine and pay insured amounts promptly on failure
options.d: Fix the CBN's monetary policy rate

questions.explanation: Fast payout depends on accurate, complete depositor records; if those records are lost or corrupted, NDIC cannot quickly confirm balances, just as poor record keeping delayed payouts in the past. Options A and B are policy matters unaffected by one bank's data, and D is a CBN function.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways the NDIC supports financial inclusion in Nigeria?

options.c: Guaranteeing deposits, especially of small and poor savers

questions.explanation: NDIC supports financial inclusion by guaranteeing deposits of small savers, protecting consumers, resolving distress and educating the public. Issuing national identity numbers is the job of the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), while C, A and D are genuine NDIC roles.

questions.question: Why do financial literacy and consumer protection matter for financial inclusion and depositor protection in Nigeria?

options.a: Nigeria has one central consumer council for finance
options.b: Financial literacy removes the need for deposit insurance
options.c: Information imbalance puts consumers at a disadvantage
options.d: Consumers usually know more about products than banks

questions.explanation: Providers know far more about their products than ordinary customers, so literacy and consumer protection are needed to correct the imbalance; this is why they complement financial inclusion. Option D reverses the imbalance, A is wrong because no such central council exists and each regulator covers its own sector, and B is wrong because the two work together.

questions.question: ____ is an international body that monitors and makes recommendations about the global financial system.
questions.explanation: The Financial Stability Board (FSB) brings together national authorities and standard-setters to monitor the global financial system and make recommendations to keep it stable, and it lists the IADI Core Principles among the standards it promotes for sound financial systems. Option C, IADI, sets standards only for deposit insurance, not the whole financial system. Options A and B are lending and economic institutions; the IMF does monitor economies, but the body described in these exact terms is the FSB.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the financial safety net?
questions.explanation: The financial safety net is made up of functions such as prudential regulation and supervision, the lender of last resort, failure resolution and deposit insurance, and in many countries the Ministry of Finance also plays a part. Disclosure is a useful tool for transparency and market discipline, but it is not one of the safety-net functions. Options D, C and A are all core parts of the net; in Nigeria, for example, the NDIC provides deposit insurance and the CBN acts as lender of last resort.

questions.question: Membership of the FSRCC includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee (FSRCC) brings together Nigeria's financial regulators, including the CBN (whose Governor chairs it), the NDIC, the SEC, NAICOM and PenCom. The NDDC (Niger Delta Development Commission) is a regional development agency, not a financial regulator, so it is not a member. Options B, C and D are all members.

questions.question: The financial safety-net participants in Nigeria collectively interact through a common organ called the:
questions.explanation: The FSRCC is the forum where Nigeria's financial regulators, including the CBN, NDIC, SEC, NAICOM and PenCom, coordinate and share information; it was renamed FSRCC in 1994 and given legal backing in 1998. Option C is the CBN committee that sets interest rates, option D is an international body rather than a Nigerian one, and option B is a forum of the CBN and bank chief executives, not of the regulators.

questions.question: In deposit insurance and financial stability work, FSAP refers to:
questions.explanation: FSAP stands for Financial Sector Assessment Program, an in-depth review of a country's financial sector, including how well its deposit insurance and supervision meet international standards. The important word is 'assessment', because the program assesses the stability and soundness of the sector. Options D, B and C sound similar but do not describe what the program actually does.

questions.question: The Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP), launched in 1999, is a joint programme of:

options.d: the IMF and the World Bank

questions.explanation: The FSAP was set up in 1999 as a joint effort of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to assess countries' financial sectors. In developing and emerging economies such as Nigeria, both institutions take part in the review. Options A and B each name only one of the two partners, and option C names the body that hosts IADI and the Basel Committee, not the FSAP.

questions.question: CBRG is an acronym for:

options.d: Crisis Backed by Bank Resolution Group

questions.explanation: CBRG is the Cross-border Bank Resolution Group of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which studied how to resolve banks operating in more than one country. Its name reflects the problem it tackled: cross-border banks need coordinated resolution. Options C, D and B mix up the words and do not describe a real body.

questions.question: Financial system stability requires ________ among the various safety-net participants.

options.b: Strict separation with no information sharing

questions.explanation: The safety net only works when the deposit insurer, the central bank and the supervisors coordinate closely and share information, because a bank problem spotted by one agency often needs action by another. Option B is wrong because withholding information is exactly what weakens crisis response. Options A and C describe rivalry and wasted effort, which create gaps and confusion rather than stability.

questions.question: The main purpose of financial safety-net arrangements is to:

options.a: Guarantee that every bank makes a profit
options.b: Ensure the stability and integrity of the financial system and protect depositors
options.c: Prevent any bank from ever failing
options.d: Replace the need for bank supervision

questions.explanation: A financial safety net (deposit insurance, supervision and the lender of last resort) exists to keep the financial system stable and to protect depositors and other consumers of financial services. Option C is wrong because the safety net cannot stop all failures; it limits the damage when they happen. Option A is not a policy goal, and option D is wrong because supervision is itself part of the safety net.

questions.question: The component(s) of the financial safety net in Nigeria is/are:

options.a: Lender of last resort facility of the CBN to address financial institutions' liquidity problems
options.b: Deposit insurance provided by the NDIC

questions.explanation: A financial safety net usually has three parts: a lender of last resort to handle liquidity problems (the CBN), deposit insurance to protect depositors (the NDIC), and bank supervision to spot problems early (done jointly by the CBN and NDIC). Because A, B and C are each one of these parts, D is correct; picking only one of them leaves out the other two pillars.

questions.question: In Nigeria's financial safety net, which institution acts as the lender of last resort?
questions.explanation: The lender of last resort lends to solvent banks facing a temporary shortage of cash, and in Nigeria that role belongs to the CBN as the bank of banks. Option A is wrong because the NDIC provides deposit insurance and handles failure resolution, not emergency central bank liquidity. Options B and C buy bad loans and regulate the capital market respectively.

questions.question: The interrelationship between financial safety-net players is:

options.a: Unique, and therefore managed by a single agency or the central bank
options.b: Irrelevant, because each agency works in isolation
options.c: Multi-dimensional, and therefore managed by more than one agency
options.d: Limited to the NDIC and commercial banks only

questions.explanation: The safety net involves several players with different roles, such as the CBN (lender of last resort and regulator), the NDIC (deposit insurer and resolver) and the Ministry of Finance, so the relationships run in many directions and require coordination among several agencies. Option A is wrong because no single agency handles all these roles. Options B and D ignore the need for coordination and leave out major players like the CBN.

questions.question: The set of public functions made up of prudential regulation, supervision, bank resolution, lender of last resort and deposit insurance, which together protect depositors and the financial system, is called the
questions.explanation: The financial safety net is the collection of functions - regulation, supervision, resolution, lender of last resort and deposit insurance - that stand behind banks and their depositors. Option C is about controlling money supply and interest rates, option A is only the pool of money a deposit insurer holds, and option D is about bringing the unbanked into formal finance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the financial safety net?

options.a: The reserves that each commercial bank keeps with the central bank to meet withdrawals
options.b: A private fund contributed by shareholders to bail out banks that make losses
options.c: The set of rules that decides which depositors are excluded from deposit insurance cover
options.d: The functions of prudential regulation, supervision, resolution, lender of last resort and deposit insurance, sometimes with the Ministry of Finance

questions.explanation: A financial safety net is the whole package of functions that protect depositors and keep the system stable: regulation, supervision, resolution, lender of last resort and deposit insurance, with the finance ministry included in many countries. Option A describes cash reserve requirements, option C describes coverage exclusions, and option B is not a public safety net at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions that make up the financial safety net?
questions.explanation: The safety net covers prudential regulation, supervision, resolution, lender of last resort and deposit insurance. Planning government capital spending is part of fiscal policy, not a safety-net function. Options B, C and D are all genuine safety-net functions.

questions.question: In the simplest description of the financial safety net, the three core components are

options.a: deposit insurance, taxation and exchange control
options.b: deposit insurance, supervision and lender of last resort
options.c: supervision, credit rating and stock exchange listing
options.d: lender of last resort, insurance regulation and pension regulation

questions.explanation: The basic safety net has three legs: deposit insurance to protect depositors, supervision to keep banks sound, and a lender of last resort to supply emergency liquidity. Option A mixes in tax and foreign exchange policy, while options C and D list activities or regulators outside the core three.

questions.question: In Nigeria's bank failure resolution arrangements, the Federal Ministry of Finance is described as the

options.b: guarantor of the lender of last resort

questions.explanation: The finance ministry stands behind the central bank as guarantor of the lender of last resort, since the government ultimately carries large fiscal costs in a crisis. Option A is the NDIC's role, option D is AMCON's role, and option C is wrong because the CBN Governor chairs the FSRCC.

questions.question: Which safety-net participant in Nigeria was set up to purchase non-performing loans and recapitalise distressed banks?
questions.explanation: AMCON was created under the AMCON Act 2010 to buy bad loans from banks and inject capital into distressed ones, which made it part of the resolution side of the safety net. NAICOM, option A, regulates insurance; PenCom, option B, regulates pensions; and the FRC, option C, sets financial reporting standards.

questions.question: Which pairing of a Nigerian safety-net participant with its role is CORRECT?

options.a: NDIC - deposit insurance, failure resolution and liquidation
options.c: Federal Ministry of Finance - on-site examination of banks

questions.explanation: The NDIC guarantees deposits, resolves failing banks and liquidates failed ones.
